faq.q: Can hamsters eat apple seeds?
faq.a: No. Apple seeds contain compounds that can release cyanide, so remove every seed and the core before feeding. If your hamster has eaten seeds, call your vet for advice.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat apple skin?
faq.a: Yes. Washed skin is fine on a small piece of apple.

faq.q: Can hamsters have dried apple or apple sauce?
faq.a: It is best not to. Drying concentrates the sugar, and vets advise avoiding dried fruit and sugary foods for hamsters. Apple sauce often has added sugar too.

hamster.notes: Every hamster source consulted lists seedless apple as safe. ASPCA's cyanogenic glycoside entry is for dogs, cats and horses; applied to hamsters by inference, consistent with PetMD's and Woodgreen's advice to remove apple seeds. Portion and frequency are deliberately stricter than PetMD's dwarf care sheet (about a teaspoon of fruit 1-3 times a week), because Blue Cross limits fruit to Syrian hamsters, UC Davis's exotic service says hamsters cannot tolerate high-sugar items such as fruit, and dwarf species are diabetes-prone.

budgie.short: Yes, in small amounts. Apple flesh is safe for budgies, but it is sugary and the seeds contain cyanide-releasing compounds, so core it and keep it an occasional treat.
budgie.portion: One or two pieces about 1 cm (⅜ in) across, roughly a thumbnail-sized amount
prep: Wash the apple well under running water
Cut out the core and every seed
Chop the flesh, skin on, into pieces about 1 cm (⅜ in) across
Remove any uneaten apple within a couple of hours
budgie.benefits: Apple adds fiber, moisture and variety, and many budgies enjoy picking at it.
budgie.risks: Apple seeds contain amygdalin, which can release cyanide, so avian vets advise removing them every time. The flesh is mostly sugar and water, and budgies are prone to obesity, so fruit should stay a small part of the diet.

faq.q: Can budgies eat apple seeds?
faq.a: No. Apple seeds contain cyanide-releasing compounds and should always be removed. If your budgie swallowed one, watch it closely and call your avian vet for advice, especially if it seems weak, fluffed up or has trouble breathing.

faq.q: Do I need to peel apple for my budgie?
faq.a: No, but wash the skin thoroughly, because birds are very sensitive to pesticide residues. Organic apples are a sensible choice when available.

cockatiel.short: Yes, in small amounts. Cockatiels can eat apple flesh, but always remove the core and seeds, which contain cyanide-releasing compounds, and keep fruit to a small share of the diet.

prep: Rinse the apple thoroughly
Remove the core and all seeds
Cut the flesh into pieces about 1.5 cm (⅝ in) across; the skin can stay on
Take away leftovers after a couple of hours
cockatiel.benefits: Apple is a crunchy, widely accepted fruit that gives cockatiels fiber and something to manipulate with the beak.
cockatiel.risks: VCA notes apple seeds may be toxic to birds; they contain amygdalin, which releases cyanide. Fruit is high in water and natural sugar, so VCA advises feeding it in limited quantities.

faq.q: What if my cockatiel ate an apple seed?
faq.a: Remove any other seeds and call your avian vet for advice, particularly if the seed was chewed open. Watch for weakness, breathing difficulty or unusual sleepiness.

faq.q: Can cockatiels eat dried apple?
faq.a: Only rarely and in tiny amounts. Drying concentrates the sugar, and many dried apple products are sweetened or preserved, so fresh apple is the better choice.

hamster.short: Yes, in small amounts. Banana is safe for hamsters, but it is one of the sweeter, starchier fruits, so offer only a small piece of peeled banana now and then.

Cut a small piece of ripe banana
Offer it by hand or in a dish
Remove any uneaten piece, including from the hoard, within a few hours

faq.q: Can hamsters eat banana peel?
faq.a: No. The peel is tough, hard to chew and may carry residues. Offer only a small piece of the peeled flesh.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat banana chips?
faq.a: No. Banana chips are dried, often fried and sometimes sweetened. Vets advise avoiding dried fruit because it is very high in sugar.

hamster.notes: Portion and frequency are deliberately stricter than PetMD's dwarf care sheet (about a teaspoon of fruit 1-3 times a week), because Blue Cross limits fruit to Syrian hamsters, UC Davis's exotic service says hamsters cannot tolerate high-sugar items such as fruit, and dwarf species are diabetes-prone.

budgie.short: Yes, in small amounts. Banana is safe for budgies but is one of the sweeter, starchier fruits, so offer only a thin slice now and then.
budgie.portion: A thin slice about 5 mm (¼ in) thick, cut into quarters
prep: Peel the banana and discard the skin
Cut a thin slice and quarter it
Serve fresh banana, not dried banana chips
Remove leftovers within a couple of hours, as banana spoils quickly
budgie.benefits: Banana is soft and easy to eat, supplies potassium, and can help coax a budgie into trying fresh food.

faq.q: Can budgies eat banana peel?
faq.a: It is better not to. The peel is not known to be toxic, but it is tough and may carry pesticide residues, so offer only the flesh.

faq.q: Are banana chips okay for budgies?
faq.a: No. Banana chips are usually fried and often sweetened, adding fat and sugar a budgie does not need.

cockatiel.short: Yes, in small amounts. Banana is safe for cockatiels, but it is sweet and starchy, so treat it as an occasional extra rather than an everyday food.

Slice and cut into small pieces
Offer plain fresh banana only
Clear away any leftovers after a couple of hours
cockatiel.benefits: Its soft texture makes banana a useful first fruit for cockatiels that are reluctant to try fresh foods.
cockatiel.risks: Cockatiels are among the species most prone to obesity and fatty liver disease, and banana is energy-dense compared with vegetables.

faq.q: Can cockatiels eat banana every day?
faq.a: It is better not to. Fruit should be a small part of the fresh-food portion, with vegetables making up most of it.

faq.q: Can I mash banana into my cockatiel's food?
faq.a: A little mashed banana can help a cockatiel accept a new food, but keep the amount small and remove the dish within a couple of hours.

hamster.short: Yes, in small amounts. Blueberries are safe and most hamsters love them, but they are still sugary fruit, so keep them to an occasional small treat.

hamster.dwarf: Campbell's, Winter White, their hybrids and Chinese hamsters are prone to diabetes. faq.q: Can hamsters eat dried blueberries?

faq.q: Are frozen blueberries OK?

budgie.risks: Merck also points out that blueberries contain a substantial amount of sugar, so they belong in the treat share of the diet rather than as a staple.

faq.q: Can budgies eat frozen blueberries?
faq.a: Yes, once fully thawed to room temperature. Fresh berries are preferred because their flavonoid content declines when they are frozen.

cockatiel.short: Yes, in small amounts. Blueberries are a good fruit for cockatiels, with fiber and flavonoids, but their sugar content means a few berries at a time is enough.
cockatiel.portion: Two or three blueberries, halved
prep: Wash the blueberries
Halve them so they are easy to hold
Choose fresh berries, or thaw frozen ones completely

cockatiel.benefits: According to Merck, blueberries provide fiber, vitamin C, vitamin K and flavonoids and are accepted by most birds.
cockatiel.risks: They are still sugary. Fruit is high in natural sugar and should be fed in limited quantities.

faq.q: Do blueberries stain cockatiel droppings?
faq.a: They can tint droppings blue or purple for a short time. That is harmless, but contact your vet if droppings stay discolored after you stop feeding them or your bird seems unwell.

cockatiel.notes: Dropping-color FAQ is general knowledge rather than from a cited source.

faq.q: Why is my hamster's fur pink after eating strawberry?

faq.q: Can hamsters eat the tiny seeds on strawberries?

budgie.short: Yes, in small amounts. Strawberries are safe for budgies, but they are sugary and soft berries hold pesticide residues, so wash them well and offer only a small piece.

faq.q: Can budgies eat strawberry seeds?
faq.a: Yes. The tiny seeds on the surface are eaten with the fruit and are not known to be harmful, unlike apple seeds or stone-fruit pits.

faq.q: Can budgies eat strawberry jam?
faq.a: No. Jam is mostly added sugar. Offer a small piece of fresh strawberry instead.

cockatiel.short: Yes, in small amounts. Cockatiels can enjoy fresh strawberry, but it is sugary and needs careful washing, since birds are sensitive to pesticide residues.
cockatiel.portion: Half a small strawberry, cut into pieces about 1.5 cm (⅝ in) across

Clear away leftovers after a couple of hours
cockatiel.benefits: Strawberries are colorful and well liked, which makes them useful as an occasional reward.

faq.q: Are frozen strawberries okay for cockatiels?

hamster.benefits: Provide fibre and are relatively low in sugar compared with most fruit.

hamster.dwarf: Campbell's, Winter White, their hybrids and Chinese hamsters are prone to diabetes. faq.q: Can hamsters eat raspberry seeds?
faq.a: The tiny seeds inside raspberries cannot practically be removed and are eaten with the fruit, as with strawberries. The advice to remove seeds applies to larger pips and stones.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat raspberry leaves?

budgie.short: Yes, in small amounts. Raspberries are safe for budgies and a little lower in sugar than many fruits, but they are still fruit, so keep portions small.
budgie.portion: Half of one raspberry

Pull the berry apart into small pieces
Serve fresh, or fully thawed if frozen

budgie.benefits: Berries are rich in fiber, vitamins and antioxidants, as the AAV points out.
budgie.risks: Raspberries are soft and hard to wash, and birds are very sensitive to pesticides. Their sugar content means they should not replace vegetables.

faq.q: Can budgies eat the small seeds in raspberries?
faq.a: Yes. The tiny seeds are eaten with the fruit and are not known to be harmful.

cockatiel.short: Yes, in small amounts. Raspberries are safe for cockatiels and supply fiber and antioxidants, but like all fruit they should be a small, occasional part of the diet.
cockatiel.portion: One raspberry, torn into pieces
prep: Wash the raspberries carefully

Use plain fresh or fully thawed berries
Take away leftovers after a couple of hours
cockatiel.benefits: The AAV notes that fruits, especially berries, are rich in fiber, vitamins and antioxidants.
cockatiel.risks: Sugar content and potential pesticide residues are the main concerns; neither is a problem in small, well-washed portions.

faq.q: Can cockatiels eat raspberry leaves?
faq.a: Plain fresh fruit is the safe choice. Garden foliage is best avoided unless your avian vet has confirmed it is safe and it has not been sprayed.

hamster.short: No. The RSPCA advises never giving grapes to hamsters because they can be poisonous to rodents. Some vets allow a tiny amount, but with no proven safe dose, it is better to skip them.
hamster.risks: The RSPCA warns that grapes can be poisonous to rodents. Grapes and raisins can cause kidney failure in dogs; how this applies to hamsters is not known, and no safe amount has been established. Grapes are also very sugary.
hamster.ifEaten: Call your vet for advice and say how much was eaten. Watch for diarrhoea, reduced appetite, lethargy or changes in drinking and urination, and see a vet promptly if any appear.

faq.q: Are seedless grapes safe for hamsters?
faq.a: We treat seedless and seeded grapes the same. The concern is about the fruit itself, not only the seeds.

faq.q: Why do some guides say grapes are fine?
faq.a: Some reputable sources, including a UK animal charity and some vet clinics, allow an occasional grape. Because the RSPCA warns grapes can be poisonous to rodents and there is no proven safe amount, we take the cautious view.

hamster.notes: Credible sources disagree. RSPCA: 'Don't give them grapes or rhubarb, as these can be poisonous to rodents.' Woodgreen: grapes are fine as an occasional treat in small amounts. Dogwood Animal Hospital lists seedless grapes as OK. Northgate Veterinary Clinic lists grapes among foods to give 'very rarely or not at all' because of sugar. Merck says confirmed cases are in dogs (anecdotal in cats and ferrets) and the proposed toxin, tartaric acid, harms dogs because they lack organic acid transporters other species have, so the dog mechanism may not apply to hamsters. No hamster toxicity data found. Chose 'no' as the most cautious status per the RSPCA; this is stricter than much popular advice.

budgie.short: Yes, in small amounts. Avian vet guides list grapes as suitable for budgies, but they are very sugary, so offer a small piece only occasionally.
budgie.portion: A quarter of a seedless grape
prep: Wash the grape well under running water
Use seedless grapes or remove the seeds
Cut into quarters
Remove leftovers within a couple of hours
budgie.benefits: Grapes are juicy and appealing, which can help encourage a budgie to try fresh food.
budgie.risks: Grapes are high in sugar for their size. Grapes and raisins can cause kidney damage in dogs, with tartaric acid the suspected cause; this has not been documented in birds, but it is another reason to keep portions small.

faq.q: Aren't grapes poisonous to pets?
faq.a: They are dangerous for dogs. Veterinary bird-care guides from VCA, the University of Florida and the RSPCA list grapes as suitable for pet birds, and no similar poisoning has been documented in birds, but small portions are still sensible.

faq.q: Should I peel grapes for my budgie?
faq.a: No, but wash them well, because the skin can hold pesticide residues.

budgie.notes: Grape/raisin toxicity is documented in dogs (ASPCA: tartaric acid speculated); no avian cases found. VCA, UF and RSPCA list grapes as suitable for birds. Kept at 'limit' because of sugar and residual uncertainty.

cockatiel.short: Yes, in small amounts. Grapes are listed as suitable for pet birds by veterinary sources, but they are high in sugar, so cockatiels should only have a small piece now and then.
cockatiel.portion: Half a seedless grape, cut into pieces
prep: Wash thoroughly
Remove any seeds
Halve or quarter the grape
Take away leftovers after a couple of hours
cockatiel.benefits: A piece of grape can be a handy training reward because most cockatiels like the taste.
cockatiel.risks: The main issue is sugar. Grape toxicity is well known in dogs; it has not been reported in birds, but that uncertainty supports keeping amounts small.

faq.q: My cockatiel ate a whole grape. Is that an emergency?
faq.a: No poisoning from grapes has been documented in birds, so a single grape is not usually an emergency. Watch droppings and appetite, and call your vet if anything seems off.

cockatiel.notes: Same reasoning as budgie: dog toxicity not documented in birds; sugar is the practical limit.

hamster.short: No. Raisins are dried grapes, which the RSPCA warns can be poisonous to rodents, and drying concentrates the sugar. Vets advise avoiding dried fruit for hamsters.
hamster.risks: Raisins carry the same unexplained toxicity concern as grapes, in concentrated form, and are very high in sugar, which is a particular problem for diabetes-prone dwarf hamsters.
hamster.ifEaten: Call your vet for advice and say how many were eaten. Watch for diarrhoea, reduced appetite, lethargy or changes in drinking and urination, and see a vet promptly if any appear.

faq.q: What about sultanas and currants?
faq.a: Treat sultanas and currants (dried grapes) the same as raisins and do not feed them.

faq.q: My hamster's food mix contains raisins. Is that a problem?
faq.a: Pick them out, or choose a complete pellet or mix without dried grapes or added sugar.

hamster.notes: Northgate Veterinary Clinic advises avoiding dried fruit because it is very high in sugar; PetMD lists high-sugar treats among foods never to offer dwarf hamsters. Grape disagreement and dog-specific mechanism as described under grape.

budgie.short: Better not. Raisins are concentrated sugar with little benefit for a budgie, and because grapes and raisins are toxic to dogs for reasons not fully understood, it is safest to skip them.
budgie.portion: Not recommended; offer a small piece of fresh fruit instead
prep: Offer a small piece of fresh fruit instead
Keep raisins, trail mix and fruit cake away from the cage
Check treat mixes for added raisins or sugared dried fruit
budgie.risks: Drying concentrates the sugar in grapes, which works against a budgie's tendency to put on weight. Grape and raisin toxicity is documented in dogs; it has not been documented in birds, but with no real benefit there is no reason to take the chance. Some dried fruit is also treated with preservatives.
budgie.ifEaten: A raisin or two is not an emergency. Offer normal food and water and watch your budgie over the next day or two. Contact your avian vet if it becomes lethargic, fluffs up, drinks or passes noticeably more urine, or has diarrhea.

faq.q: Are raisins poisonous to budgies?
faq.a: No poisoning has been documented in birds. However, grapes and raisins damage the kidneys of dogs, and the cause is still not certain. Given that uncertainty and the high sugar content, it is safest to leave raisins out.

faq.q: What about other dried fruit?
faq.a: Fresh fruit is better. Dried fruit is far more concentrated in sugar and is sometimes sweetened or preserved.

budgie.notes: No avian-vet source found that addresses raisins specifically. Some popular budgie guides list raisins or dried fruit as an occasional treat. Chose the cautious 'avoid' based on sugar density (AAV and LafeberVet list sugary foods as problems) plus the unexplained grape/raisin toxicity in dogs (ASPCA).

cockatiel.short: Better not. Raisins pack a lot of sugar into a small bite and offer cockatiels little, and grape and raisin toxicity in dogs is still not fully explained, so fresh fruit is the safer choice.
cockatiel.portion: Not recommended; use a small piece of fresh fruit instead
prep: Choose fresh fruit as a treat instead
Store raisins and baked goods containing them out of reach
Read treat-mix labels for raisins and sugared fruit
cockatiel.risks: Raisins are dried grapes with the sugar concentrated, which is unhelpful for a species prone to obesity and fatty liver. Kidney damage from grapes and raisins is well recognized in dogs; birds have not been shown to be affected, but the cause is unknown.
cockatiel.ifEaten: One or two raisins do not call for emergency care. Keep an eye on your cockatiel's appetite, droppings and activity for a day or two, and call your avian vet if it becomes quiet, fluffed up, drinks much more than usual or has loose droppings.

faq.q: Can soaked raisins be given to cockatiels?
faq.a: Soaking adds water but does not remove the sugar or resolve the uncertainty about grape toxicity. Fresh fruit remains the better option.

cockatiel.notes: Same reasoning as budgie. Differs from some popular advice that lists raisins as a bird treat.

faq.q: Can budgies eat watermelon seeds?

faq.q: Can budgies eat watermelon rind?

hamster.short: Better not. Vets and UK animal charities advise against citrus fruit such as oranges, lemons and grapefruit for hamsters because it can upset their digestion.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat lemon, lime, grapefruit or clementine?

faq.q: Does my hamster need vitamin C from fruit?

hamster.notes: All sources advise avoiding citrus. PDSA: 'new research suggests that citrus fruits may not only be harmless to hamsters but could potentially offer some health benefits. Cut a small piece from one segment
Serve plain fruit, never juice or canned orange in syrup
Remove leftovers within a couple of hours
budgie.benefits: Veterinary bird-care guides list oranges and other citrus as suitable fruits, and a juicy piece adds variety.

faq.q: Can budgies eat mandarins, clementines or grapefruit?
faq.a: Yes, with the same rules: peeled, pips removed, in small pieces and only occasionally.

faq.q: Can I add orange juice to my budgie's water?
faq.a: No. The AAV advises against putting juice in a bird's water because it encourages bacterial growth.

budgie.notes: Some popular guides say to avoid citrus entirely because of acidity; VCA and UF list orange and other citrus as suitable. cockatiel.short: Yes, in small amounts. Cockatiels can eat peeled orange segments, but citrus is acidic and sweet, so keep it to an occasional small piece without peel or pips.

cockatiel.risks: The peel and pips carry irritating oils and citric acid. The acidity and sugar of the flesh are reasons to keep portions small.

faq.q: Can cockatiels drink orange juice?

Cut the flesh away from the large stone
Cut a small piece of ripe flesh

faq.q: Can budgies eat dried mango?

cockatiel.short: Yes, in small amounts. Mango is a good source of beta-carotene for cockatiels, but it is very sweet, so offer a small peeled piece now and then.

Cut the flesh into bite-sized pieces

faq.q: Can hamsters eat canned or dried pineapple?

faq.q: Can budgies eat pineapple skin or leaves?

cockatiel.benefits: A small piece of pineapple is a juicy, well-liked change from vegetables.

faq.q: Is canned pineapple in juice okay for cockatiels?
