Merck lists cattle, goats, horses, mice, rabbits, guinea pigs, rats, sheep and several birds as susceptible; dogs are relatively resistant. Verdict inferred from closely related rodents; confidence in 'do not feed' is high.

budgie.short: No. Avocado contains persin, which damages the hearts of pet birds, and budgies are among the most sensitive species. Never feed any part of it.
budgie.risks: All parts of the avocado plant, including the flesh, skin, pit and especially the leaves, contain persin, which can cause heart damage, fluid build-up and breathing difficulty. In published reports, budgies given about 1 g of avocado showed signs of distress, and larger amounts were fatal within 48 hours.
budgie.ifEaten: Treat any amount as an emergency. Call your avian vet or an animal poison line straight away, even if your budgie seems fine. Signs such as fluffed feathers, labored breathing, weakness or being unable to perch can appear around 12 hours after eating, and death can follow within one to two days.

faq.q: Is a tiny lick of avocado or guacamole okay for a budgie?
faq.a: No. There is no known safe amount, and budgies are among the most susceptible birds. Guacamole also usually contains onion and garlic, which are harmful too.

faq.q: Are some avocado varieties safe?
faq.a: No. Guatemalan types have been linked to poisoning most often, but no variety is known to be safe for birds.

budgie.notes: Merck: budgerigars fed 1 g avocado developed agitation and feather pulling; 8.7 g mashed avocado caused death within 48 h. Hargis et al. 1989 (JAVMA) found avocado highly toxic to budgerigars; cited within Merck and LafeberVet.

cockatiel.short: No. Avocado contains persin, a toxin that can damage a cockatiel's heart and cause fatal breathing problems. Never offer the flesh, skin, pit or leaves.
cockatiel.risks: The Merck Veterinary Manual lists cockatiels among the birds affected by avocado. Persin causes heart muscle damage, fluid around the heart and lungs, and swelling under the skin of the neck and chest. The leaves are the most toxic part, but the fruit, pit and skin are also dangerous.
cockatiel.ifEaten: Call your avian vet or an animal poison line immediately, whatever the amount, and do not wait for signs. Watch for fluffed feathers, open-mouth or labored breathing, weakness and inability to perch; signs often start within about 12 hours.

faq.q: Can cockatiels eat food that contains avocado, like smoothies or salads?
faq.a: No. Keep all avocado-containing foods, including guacamole and avocado toast, away from your cockatiel.

faq.q: Can I use avocado wood or leaves as a perch or chew toy?
faq.a: No. The leaves are the most toxic part of the plant, and all parts contain persin.

hamster.short: Yes, but only a tiny amount now and then. Fresh coconut flesh is not toxic, but it is very high in fat, and hamsters easily become overweight.
hamster.portion: A thin shaving about 5 mm (¼ in) across for a Syrian; best skipped for dwarf species (see the dwarf note).
hamster.frequency: Once every one to two weeks at most.
prep: Use fresh or plain unsweetened coconut only
Offer a thin shaving of the white flesh
Do not offer coconut milk, cream, oil or sweetened desiccated coconut
Remove any uneaten piece, including from the hoard, within a few hours
hamster.benefits: Adds novelty. A clean, untreated coconut shell also makes a safe gnawing item or hide.
hamster.risks: Coconut flesh is mostly fat and calorie-dense. Hamsters are prone to obesity, and vets recommend low-fat treats.
hamster.dwarf: Research in diabetes-prone Chinese hamsters found that reducing dietary fat or calories helped prevent diabetes developing, so it is best to skip coconut flesh for Campbell's, Winter White, hybrid and Chinese hamsters.

faq.q: Can hamsters have a coconut shell?
faq.a: Yes. PDSA lists coconut shells among safe things for hamsters to gnaw on. Make sure it is clean and untreated.

faq.q: Is coconut water or coconut milk OK?
faq.a: No. Your hamster only needs fresh water. Coconut milk is very fatty, and coconut water adds sugar.

hamster.notes: No cited source discusses coconut flesh for hamsters; PDSA mentions coconut shells only as chews. Verdict based on high fat content (general nutrition), VCA's statement that hamsters are prone to obesity, and PetMD's advice to prioritise low-fat treats. Gerritsen 1982 (abstract): 'Caloric restriction per se or reduction of dietary fat prevented onset of hyperglycemia and hyperinsulinemia in prediabetics.' PubMed page blocked by CAPTCHA; abstract retrieved via NCBI E-utilities / Europe PMC API.

budgie.short: Yes, but only a tiny piece, rarely. Fresh coconut is not toxic to budgies, but it is very high in fat, and budgies are prone to obesity, fatty tumors (lipomas) and fatty liver.
budgie.portion: A sliver about 5 mm (¼ in) across
prep: Use fresh, plain coconut flesh
Avoid sweetened desiccated coconut, coconut sweets and coconut oil
Shave or grate off a thin sliver
Remove leftovers within a couple of hours
budgie.benefits: Coconut offers a novel texture that some budgies enjoy shredding.
budgie.risks: Coconut flesh is rich in saturated fat. VCA lists budgies among the species most prone to obesity, which raises the risk of lipomas and fatty liver disease.

faq.q: Can budgies drink coconut water?
faq.a: Plain water is the best drink. Unsweetened coconut water is not known to be toxic, but it adds sugar, and avian vets advise keeping the water bowl free of additives.

budgie.notes: VCA lists coconut as suitable for budgies. The strict portion/frequency is inferred from coconut's fat content and the species' documented predisposition to obesity, lipomas and hepatic lipidosis.

cockatiel.short: Yes, but only a small piece, rarely. Coconut is not toxic to cockatiels, but its high fat content is a concern for a species prone to obesity and fatty liver disease.
cockatiel.portion: A sliver about 1 cm (⅜ in) across
prep: Offer fresh, unsweetened coconut only
Skip desiccated, sweetened or oil-based coconut products
Cut a thin sliver
Take away leftovers after a couple of hours
cockatiel.benefits: A little fresh coconut can be used as a foraging reward.
cockatiel.risks: High fat. VCA lists cockatiels among the birds most commonly affected by obesity, and Merck associates obesity with fatty liver disease.

faq.q: Is coconut shell safe as a toy for cockatiels?
faq.a: Clean, dry coconut shell is commonly used for toys. Make sure it contains no moldy flesh, glue or sharp edges.

cockatiel.notes: Coconut shell FAQ is a practical note, not from a cited source.

hamster.short: Yes, in small amounts. Carrot is safe and crunchy, but it has more natural sugar than most vegetables, so vets suggest it as an occasional treat rather than a daily food.
hamster.portion: A thin slice or stick about 1 cm (⅜ in) long for a Syrian; about 5 mm (¼ in) for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: Two or three times a week.
prep: Wash or peel to remove soil
Cut into a thin slice or small stick
Serve raw with nothing added
Remove any uneaten piece, including from the hoard, within a few hours
hamster.benefits: Rich in beta-carotene, and the crunch gives hamsters something to gnaw.
hamster.risks: Carrots contain more natural sugar than leafy and green vegetables, so large or frequent portions add calories. Chop into small pieces to reduce the choking risk.
hamster.dwarf: Campbell's, Winter White, their hybrids and Chinese hamsters are prone to diabetes. Keep carrot to a thin 5 mm (¼ in) sliver once or twice a week, and rely mainly on low-sugar vegetables such as cucumber, broccoli and bell pepper.

faq.q: Are baby carrots OK?
faq.a: Yes, but chop them into small pieces first. PetMD recommends this to prevent choking.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat cooked carrot?
faq.a: Plain cooked carrot is safe, but raw is better: it is crunchier and has nothing added. Never offer carrot cooked with butter, salt or seasoning.

hamster.notes: Most sources list carrot as a regular safe vegetable (RSPCA 'cleaned root vegetables', Woodgreen, UC Davis, PetMD dwarf sheet). PetMD's 'What Can Hamsters Eat?' says 'only as occasional treats, as they have a high sugar content', and PetMD's Syrian sheet says 'small portions of root vegetables'. Took the more cautious 'limit'. Many popular guides treat carrot as an everyday vegetable.

budgie.short: Yes. Carrot is a good regular vegetable for budgies: crunchy, well liked and rich in beta-carotene, which helps prevent the vitamin A deficiency common on seed diets.
budgie.portion: About a teaspoon (5 ml) of grated or finely diced carrot as part of the day's vegetables
budgie.frequency: Daily or most days, rotated with other vegetables
prep: Wash or peel the carrot
Grate it or cut it into small dice or thin matchsticks
Serve raw, or lightly steamed and cooled, with nothing added
Remove leftovers within a couple of hours
budgie.benefits: The AAV and VCA name carrots among orange vegetables high in beta-carotene, a vitamin A precursor that seeds lack, and the Royal Veterinary College recommends carrot for budgies.
budgie.risks: Carrot is sweeter than leafy vegetables, so it works best as one part of a varied mix rather than the only vegetable.

faq.q: Can budgies eat carrot tops?
faq.a: Yes. VCA lists carrot tops among suitable foods; wash them well and chop finely.

faq.q: Is raw or cooked carrot better?
faq.a: Raw is fine and keeps more nutrients, as cooking can deplete some foods of their value. Lightly steamed carrot is also fine.

cockatiel.short: Yes. Carrot is an excellent everyday vegetable for cockatiels, supplying beta-carotene that supports vitamin A levels, which are often low in seed-fed birds.
cockatiel.portion: About a tablespoon (15 ml) of grated or diced carrot as part of the day's vegetables
cockatiel.frequency: Daily or most days, rotated with other vegetables
prep: Wash or peel the carrot
Grate, dice or cut into thin sticks
Offer raw or lightly steamed and cooled, unseasoned
Take away leftovers after a couple of hours
cockatiel.benefits: Red-orange vegetables such as carrots are high in beta-carotene, according to the AAV, and vitamin A deficiency is common in birds on all-seed diets.
cockatiel.risks: Few risks. Carrot is a little sweeter than green vegetables, so pair it with others rather than feeding it alone.

faq.q: Can cockatiels eat carrot greens?
faq.a: Yes. Carrot tops are listed by VCA as suitable; wash and chop them before serving.

hamster.short: Yes. Broccoli is a safe, low-sugar vegetable for hamsters. Offer a small floret a few times a week; large amounts can cause gas.
hamster.portion: A piece about 1–1.5 cm (⅜–⅝ in) across for a Syrian; about half that for a dwarf. Keep all fresh food together to about 1–2 teaspoons a day for a Syrian and about half that for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: A few times a week, rotated with other vegetables.
prep: Wash well
Cut a small floret or thin piece of stalk
Serve raw, or lightly steamed with nothing added and cooled
Remove any uneaten piece, including from the hoard, within a few hours
hamster.benefits: Low in sugar and a source of fibre, vitamins and minerals; the stalk gives something to gnaw.
hamster.risks: Broccoli and other cabbage-family vegetables can cause gas if fed in large amounts. Introduce it slowly and cut back if droppings become soft.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat broccoli stalks and leaves?
faq.a: Yes. Washed stalks and leaves are fine in small pieces.

faq.q: Raw or cooked broccoli?
faq.a: Raw is fine and keeps the crunch. If you cook it, it must be plain, with no butter, oil, salt or seasoning, and cooled before serving.

hamster.notes: Universally listed as safe. Northgate says 'very small amounts and only occasionally' (as for all fresh vegetables); Dogwood warns too much may cause gas.

budgie.short: Yes. Broccoli is a nutritious vegetable for budgies, but rotate it with other vegetables rather than feeding large amounts daily, as heavy intake has been linked to goiter in budgies.
budgie.portion: A few small florets or leaves, about a teaspoon (5 ml) chopped, as part of the day's vegetables
budgie.frequency: 2–4 times a week, rotated with vegetables outside the cabbage family
prep: Wash the broccoli well
Chop the florets, leaves and peeled stalk into small pieces
Serve raw or lightly steamed and cooled, unseasoned
Remove leftovers within a couple of hours
budgie.benefits: Broccoli florets and leaves are rich in beta-carotene; the AAV, VCA and the Royal Veterinary College all recommend broccoli for budgies.
budgie.risks: Broccoli belongs to the cabbage family, which contains goitrogens that interfere with iodine use. Budgies are especially prone to thyroid enlargement (goiter), and a published outbreak in a budgie flock was linked to large amounts of broccoli in a diet with no added minerals.

faq.q: Can broccoli give my budgie goiter?
faq.a: The risk comes from large amounts, especially with a seed-only diet that is low in iodine. In the reported outbreak, sick budgies improved once broccoli was removed and iodine was added. Offer broccoli as one of several vegetables alongside a pellet-based or iodine-supplemented diet.

faq.q: Can budgies eat broccoli stalks and leaves?
faq.a: Yes. The leaves are especially nutritious. Peel the tough outer layer of the stalk and chop it finely.

budgie.notes: Recommended for budgies by AAV, VCA and RVC. Quantity caution from Loukopoulos et al. 2015 (goiter outbreak: 45 of 400 budgies ill, 15 died; diet was a commercial mix plus broccoli, oats and carrots with no minerals; resolved after broccoli removal and iodine supplementation) and UF/IFAS listing broccoli and cabbage as goitrogenic feeds; VCA notes budgies are vulnerable to iodine deficiency. Kept at 'yes' with rotation advice rather than 'limit' because the risk was tied to large amounts plus no mineral supplementation.

cockatiel.short: Yes. Broccoli is one of the best vegetables for cockatiels. The florets and leaves are rich in beta-carotene, which supports the vitamin A that seed-heavy diets lack.
cockatiel.portion: About a tablespoon (15 ml) of chopped florets and leaves as part of the day's vegetables
cockatiel.frequency: Several times a week, rotated with other vegetables
prep: Rinse the broccoli thoroughly
Chop florets and leaves into small pieces; peel and dice the stalk
Serve raw or lightly steamed and cooled, without seasoning
Take away leftovers after a couple of hours
cockatiel.benefits: The AAV lists broccoli among dark green vegetables high in beta-carotene, and Merck names broccoli leaves and florets as good vitamin A sources for birds.
cockatiel.risks: Safe for cockatiels. As with any single vegetable, very large daily amounts are unwise, because cabbage-family plants contain goitrogens that can interfere with iodine use.

faq.q: Does my cockatiel need broccoli cooked?
faq.a: No. Raw broccoli is fine and keeps more nutrients; lightly steamed and cooled is also fine if your bird prefers it.

cockatiel.notes: Goiter reports center on budgerigars; the goitrogen note for cockatiels is a general precaution.

hamster.short: Yes. Cucumber is a safe, low-sugar vegetable and a good treat for dwarf hamsters, but it is mostly water, so keep portions small to avoid loose droppings.
hamster.portion: A piece about 1–1.5 cm (⅜–⅝ in) across for a Syrian; about half that for a dwarf. Keep all fresh food together to about 1–2 teaspoons a day for a Syrian and about half that for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: A few times a week, rotated with other vegetables.
prep: Wash well
Cut a small piece; washed skin can stay on
Serve raw
Remove any uneaten piece, including from the hoard, within a few hours
hamster.benefits: Very low in sugar and calories, which makes it a sensible treat for diabetes-prone dwarf hamsters.
hamster.risks: Cucumber is mostly water with little nutrition, so large amounts can cause diarrhoea. Hoarded pieces go off quickly in the bedding.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat cucumber skin?
faq.a: Yes, if it is washed well. Peel it if you cannot wash off a waxy coating.

faq.q: Can cucumber replace my hamster's water?
faq.a: No. Fresh water should always be available in a clean bottle or bowl, changed daily.

hamster.notes: Universally listed as safe. VCA's warning about watery, low-nutrition vegetables names iceberg lettuce and celery, not cucumber. Hamster Society Singapore's fresh-food page (now offline, not cited) advised moderation for high-water vegetables such as cucumber and cabbage.

budgie.short: Yes. Cucumber is safe for budgies and refreshing, but it is mostly water, so treat it as a light extra alongside more nutritious vegetables.
budgie.portion: A thin slice about 5 mm (¼ in) thick, or a few small cubes
prep: Wash well; peeling is optional
Slice thinly or cut into small cubes
The soft seeds can be left in
Remove leftovers within a couple of hours
budgie.benefits: Cucumber is low in calories and many budgies enjoy nibbling it, especially in warm weather.
budgie.risks: It has little nutritional value because it is mostly water, the same reason VCA gives for limiting iceberg lettuce and celery. Large amounts can make droppings watery.

faq.q: Can budgies eat cucumber seeds and skin?
faq.a: Yes. The soft seeds and well-washed skin are fine.

budgie.notes: VCA lists cucumber as suitable; VCA's own reasoning about high-water produce (iceberg lettuce, celery) suggests keeping it a minor item. 'yes' because it is harmless, not because it is nutritious.

cockatiel.short: Yes. Cucumber is a safe, low-calorie vegetable for cockatiels, though it is mostly water and should sit alongside more nutrient-rich vegetables.
cockatiel.portion: Two or three thin slices, or about a tablespoon (15 ml) of cubes
prep: Wash the cucumber
Slice or cube it; skin and seeds can stay
Serve raw and plain
Take away leftovers after a couple of hours
cockatiel.benefits: It is hydrating and low in calories, which suits a species prone to weight gain.
cockatiel.risks: Little nutritional value; large portions displace better vegetables and loosen droppings.

faq.q: Are pickles okay for cockatiels?
faq.a: No. Pickles are soaked in salt and vinegar and often contain garlic. Offer only fresh cucumber.

cockatiel.notes: Same as budgie. Pickle answer supported by AAV/VCA warnings on highly salted foods.

hamster.short: Better not. Ripe tomato flesh is not toxic, but the leaves, stems and unripe fruit contain solanine-type compounds, and some UK charities advise avoiding tomato altogether.
hamster.risks: The green parts of the tomato plant and unripe fruit contain solanine-type glycoalkaloids, which can cause serious digestive upset and weakness. Ripe fruit is acidic and watery. Reputable sources disagree about ripe tomato, so we take the cautious view.
hamster.ifEaten: A small bite of ripe tomato is not an emergency: remove any leftovers and watch for diarrhoea, a wet or dirty tail area, or reduced appetite over the next day or two, and contact a vet promptly if these appear. If your hamster ate leaves, stems or green tomato, call your vet for advice.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat tomato leaves or stems?
faq.a: No. The green parts of the tomato plant contain solanine and are listed as toxic to pets. Keep hamsters away from tomato plants.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat cherry tomatoes, tomato sauce or ketchup?
faq.a: Cherry tomatoes carry the same caution as other tomatoes. Sauces, ketchup and soups often contain onion, garlic, salt or sugar and should never be given.

hamster.notes: Disagreement: PDSA lists tomato among suitable fruits; PetMD says do not offer unripe tomatoes and lists tomato leaves as toxic (implying ripe fruit is acceptable); ASPCA (dogs, cats, horses) says 'ripe fruit is non-toxic'; Woodgreen lists 'Tomato' under foods to avoid. Chose the more cautious 'avoid'. This is stricter than much popular advice, which allows small pieces of ripe tomato.

budgie.short: Yes, in small amounts, ripe flesh only. Ripe tomato is not toxic to budgies, but the leaves, stems and green fruit contain solanine, and the flesh is acidic.
budgie.portion: A piece of ripe tomato about 1 cm (⅜ in) across
budgie.frequency: Once or twice a week at most
prep: Use only fully ripe, red tomato
Remove every bit of stem, leaf and green calyx
Wash and cut into small pieces
Remove leftovers within a couple of hours
budgie.benefits: Ripe tomato adds moisture and variety; VCA lists it among suitable foods for budgies.
budgie.risks: Tomatoes are nightshades: the leaves, stems and unripe fruit contain the glycoalkaloid solanine, while ripe fruit is considered non-toxic. The acidity of the flesh is another reason to keep portions small.

faq.q: What if my budgie nibbled a tomato leaf or green tomato?
faq.a: Remove the plant, note roughly how much was eaten and call your avian vet for advice. Watch for drooling, regurgitation, diarrhea or weakness.

faq.q: Are tomato sauce or ketchup okay?
faq.a: No. They are concentrated, salted and often sweetened, and may contain onion or garlic.

budgie.notes: LafeberVet (2019) says 'birds can eat green tomatoes' and that the plants are toxic, which conflicts with ASPCA (unripe fruit contains solanine) and LafeberVet's own toxic-plant list (tomato green parts). Took the cautious line: ripe fruit only. Some vet-reviewed retailer content advises against tomatoes altogether because of acidity.

cockatiel.short: Yes, in small amounts, ripe flesh only. Cockatiels can eat ripe tomato, but never the leaves, stems or green fruit, which contain solanine, and keep portions small because it is acidic.
cockatiel.portion: One or two pieces of ripe tomato about 1.5 cm (⅝ in) across
cockatiel.frequency: Once or twice a week at most
prep: Choose fully ripe tomatoes
Cut off all green parts, including the stem and calyx
Wash and dice
Take away leftovers after a couple of hours
cockatiel.benefits: A little ripe tomato adds variety to the vegetable mix.
cockatiel.risks: The green parts of the tomato plant, and unripe fruit, contain solanine. Ripe fruit is non-toxic but acidic.

faq.q: Can I let my cockatiel play on my tomato plants?
faq.a: No. The leaves and stems are toxic to birds. Keep cockatiels away from tomato, potato and other nightshade plants.

cockatiel.notes: Same disagreement as budgie.

hamster.short: Yes. Sweet bell peppers are a safe, low-sugar vegetable for hamsters. Remove the seeds and stalk and offer a small strip.
hamster.portion: A piece about 1–1.5 cm (⅜–⅝ in) across for a Syrian; about half that for a dwarf. Keep all fresh food together to about 1–2 teaspoons a day for a Syrian and about half that for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: A few times a week, rotated with other vegetables.
prep: Wash well
Remove the stalk, seeds and white pith
Cut a small strip
Remove any uneaten piece, including from the hoard, within a few hours
hamster.benefits: Crunchy and low in calories, with vitamins including vitamin C and, in red, yellow and orange peppers, carotenoids.
hamster.risks: Very low risk. Do not confuse sweet peppers with hot chilli peppers, which should be avoided. Too much of any fresh food can loosen droppings.

faq.q: Are all colours of bell pepper safe?
faq.a: Yes. Red, yellow and orange peppers are slightly sweeter than green, but all are fine in small amounts.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat pepper seeds?
faq.a: Remove them. They add nothing, and seeds are generally best taken out before feeding.

hamster.notes: PDSA ('Bell Sweet peppers'), PetMD ('Colored peppers, such as bell peppers') and Northgate ('Sweet peppers') list them as safe.

budgie.short: Yes. Bell peppers, especially red, orange and yellow ones, are an excellent vegetable for budgies: crunchy, low in sugar and rich in beta-carotene.
budgie.portion: A few small strips or cubes, about a teaspoon (5 ml), as part of the day's vegetables
budgie.frequency: Daily or most days, rotated with other vegetables
prep: Wash the pepper well
Cut off the stalk
Slice into thin strips or small pieces; the seeds can be left in
Remove leftovers within a couple of hours
budgie.benefits: VCA names bell peppers among the brightly colored vegetables that supply vitamin A precursors, which seed-based diets lack.
budgie.risks: Few risks beyond washing off residues. The leaves and stems of pepper plants, like other nightshades, should not be offered.

faq.q: Can budgies eat bell pepper seeds?
faq.a: Yes. Bell pepper seeds are not known to be harmful, and many budgies enjoy picking them out.

faq.q: Which color pepper is best?
faq.a: Red, orange and yellow peppers are riper and richer in carotenoids than green ones, but all colors are safe.

cockatiel.short: Yes. Bell peppers are a top vegetable for cockatiels: low in sugar, crunchy to shred, and rich in beta-carotene, especially the red, orange and yellow ones.
cockatiel.portion: About a tablespoon (15 ml) of strips or pieces as part of the day's vegetables
cockatiel.frequency: Daily or most days, rotated with other vegetables
prep: Rinse the pepper
Remove the stalk
Cut into strips or chunks; leave some seeds for foraging if you like
Take away leftovers after a couple of hours
cockatiel.benefits: Brightly colored peppers are listed by VCA as good sources of vitamin A precursors, and the University of Florida veterinary hospital recommends various peppers for pet birds.
cockatiel.risks: Very low risk. Keep cockatiels away from the leaves and stems of the pepper plant, which belongs to the nightshade family.

faq.q: Can cockatiels eat stuffed or roasted peppers?
faq.a: Only plain pepper. Stuffed or roasted dishes usually contain salt, oil, onion or garlic.

hamster.short: Better not. Hot chilli peppers contain capsaicin, which irritates the mouth and gut, and vets and UK charities advise keeping spicy peppers away from hamsters.
hamster.risks: Capsaicin causes a burning sensation and can trigger digestive upset. PetMD notes spicy peppers can cause gastrointestinal problems in hamsters, and there is no benefit.
hamster.ifEaten: Offer fresh water, remove any remaining pieces and watch for pawing at the mouth, drooling, diarrhoea or reduced appetite. Contact a vet if signs are severe or last more than a few hours.

faq.q: Are jalapeños, chilli flakes or spicy crisps any different?
faq.a: No. All hot peppers, chilli flakes and spicy seasonings should be avoided.

faq.q: So can hamsters eat bell peppers?
faq.a: Yes. Sweet bell peppers are not hot and are a good vegetable choice in small pieces.

hamster.notes: Woodgreen lists 'Chillies' under foods to avoid; PetMD: 'Spicy peppers and citrus fruit should be avoided, as they can cause gastrointestinal problems.' No source describes acute toxicity, hence 'avoid' rather than 'no'.

budgie.short: Yes, in small amounts. Birds do not feel the burn of capsaicin, and vet sources list hot peppers as suitable, but keep portions small and wash your hands after cutting them.
budgie.portion: A thin ring or small piece about 5 mm (¼ in) across
prep: Wash the chili well
Remove the stalk and cut into small pieces; seeds can stay
Wash your hands and knife afterwards so you do not get capsaicin in your own eyes
Remove leftovers within a couple of hours
budgie.benefits: Chili peppers are rich in carotenoids; the Merck Veterinary Manual lists them among foods that supply vitamin A.
budgie.risks: Research on the capsaicin receptor shows birds are indifferent to capsaicin's pain-producing effect. There is little published data on large amounts in small parrots, so moderation is a precaution rather than a response to known harm.

faq.q: Don't hot chilies burn a budgie's mouth?
faq.a: No. Birds' capsaicin receptor does not respond to capsaicin, which is why wild birds eat chili fruits and spread the seeds.

faq.q: Can budgies have chili flakes or hot sauce?
faq.a: No. Stick to fresh chili. Sauces and seasonings usually contain salt, garlic, onion or vinegar.

budgie.notes: VCA lists 'peppers (red/green/hot)'; Merck (owner edition) lists chili peppers as a vitamin A source. 'limit' is precautionary given limited data on quantity in small species; arguably could be 'yes'. Some internet sources claim chili is toxic to birds; no evidence found for that.

cockatiel.short: Yes, in small amounts. Cockatiels cannot taste the heat of chili, and vets list hot peppers as suitable, but offer small pieces as part of a varied mix.
cockatiel.portion: One or two small pieces about 1 cm (⅜ in) across
prep: Wash the chili
Cut off the stalk and chop; seeds may be left in
Clean your hands and cutting board afterwards
Take away leftovers after a couple of hours
cockatiel.benefits: Fresh chilies supply carotenoids that support vitamin A intake.
cockatiel.risks: Birds lack the capsaicin sensitivity that mammals have, so the heat is not a problem for them. Because data on large quantities is limited, small portions are a sensible precaution.

faq.q: Will chili upset my cockatiel's stomach?
faq.a: Birds are indifferent to capsaicin, and no harm from normal portions of fresh chili is documented. Stop offering it and call your vet if you notice any digestive change.

cockatiel.notes: Same as budgie.

hamster.short: Better not. Celery is not toxic, but VCA vets advise against it because it is mostly water with little nutrition, and PetMD warns its stringy fibres are a choking hazard.
hamster.risks: Long, tough strings can lodge in the mouth or throat, and celery adds little nutrition. Some vets and charities allow small pieces, so this is a precaution rather than a toxicity concern.
hamster.ifEaten: A nibble is not an emergency. Check that your hamster is breathing and eating normally and has no string caught in its mouth. If it is gagging, pawing at its mouth, or its cheeks stay swollen for more than a few hours, contact a vet.

faq.q: Some guides say celery is fine. Who is right?
faq.a: PDSA and some vet clinics list celery as safe, while VCA advises against it and PetMD warns about the strings. Because better vegetables are available, we suggest skipping it. If you do offer it, remove the strings and cut it very small.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat celery leaves?
faq.a: The leaves are less stringy than the stalk, but they still add little. Leafy greens such as romaine lettuce or dandelion leaves are better choices.

hamster.notes: Disagreement: VCA (rodents generally): 'Do not give your rodent iceberg lettuce or celery, as these vegetables are composed mostly of water and provide little to no nutritional value.' PetMD: celery strings 'pose a choking hazard... not a good choice for a snack.' PDSA, Northgate and Dogwood list celery as safe. Chose the more cautious 'avoid'. Differs from much popular advice. PetMD dwarf sheet cited for swollen cheek pouches that do not empty after a few hours warranting a vet visit; it lists spinach as safe.

budgie.short: Yes, in small amounts. Celery is not toxic, but it is mostly water with few nutrients, and its long strings should be cut short for a bird as small as a budgie.
budgie.portion: A few pieces of stalk about 5 mm (¼ in) long, or a few chopped leaves
prep: Wash the celery well
Peel off or cut out the stringy fibers
Chop the stalk into pieces no longer than 5 mm (¼ in)
Chop the leafy tops finely
Remove leftovers within a couple of hours
budgie.benefits: Celery leaves carry more nutrients than the watery stalk, and the crunch can be enriching.
budgie.risks: VCA advises feeding celery sparingly because its high water content gives birds few nutrients. The long fibers in the stalk are a possible choking or crop-blockage hazard for small birds, so cut them short.

faq.q: Can budgies eat celery leaves?
faq.a: Yes. The leaves are more nutritious than the stalk; wash and chop them finely.

budgie.notes: The string/crop-impaction concern is widely repeated but was not found in the cited vet sources; included as a precaution (inferred).

cockatiel.short: Yes, in small amounts. Celery is safe for cockatiels but mostly water, so vets advise feeding it sparingly, cut into short pieces with the strings removed.
cockatiel.portion: A few pieces about 1 cm (⅜ in) long, or about 2 teaspoons of chopped leaves
prep: Wash the celery
Remove the stringy fibers
Cut the stalk into short pieces
Take away leftovers after a couple of hours
cockatiel.benefits: Many cockatiels enjoy the crunch, and the leaves add some extra nutrients.
cockatiel.risks: Low nutritional value because of the high water content. Long stringy fibers are best removed as a precaution.

faq.q: Is celery good for a cockatiel's diet?
faq.a: It is safe but not especially nutritious. Darker and orange vegetables such as broccoli, bell pepper and carrot offer more.

cockatiel.notes: Same as budgie.

hamster.short: Yes. Cabbage is listed as safe by UK charities and vets. Offer a small piece of leaf a few times a week; too much can cause gas or loose droppings.
hamster.portion: A piece about 1–1.5 cm (⅜–⅝ in) across for a Syrian; about half that for a dwarf. Keep all fresh food together to about 1–2 teaspoons a day for a Syrian and about half that for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: A few times a week, rotated with other vegetables.
prep: Wash well and discard wilted outer leaves
Tear or cut a small piece of leaf
Serve raw
Remove any uneaten piece, including from the hoard, within a few hours
hamster.benefits: Low in sugar and calories, with fibre and vitamins.
hamster.risks: Cabbage-family vegetables can cause gas, and watery leaves in large amounts can loosen droppings. Leafy greens rot quickly if hoarded.

faq.q: Are red cabbage, savoy and Chinese cabbage OK?
faq.a: Yes, the same small-portion rule applies to all common cabbages.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat cooked cabbage or coleslaw?
faq.a: Plain cooked cabbage is fine but raw is better. Coleslaw contains mayonnaise and often onion, so never feed it.

hamster.notes: Woodgreen, PDSA and Dogwood list cabbage as safe. Blue Cross advises not giving too many green vegetables because they rot easily when hoarded. Hamster Society Singapore (offline, not cited) advised moderation because of high water content. Gas risk is general brassica knowledge.

budgie.short: Yes, in small amounts. Cabbage is safe for budgies, but it contains goitrogens and budgies are prone to thyroid problems, so offer it now and then as part of a mix.
budgie.portion: A piece of leaf about 2 cm (¾ in) square, finely shredded
budgie.frequency: Once or twice a week, not on the same days as other cabbage-family vegetables
prep: Wash the leaves well
Choose darker outer leaves over the pale inner heart
Shred finely
Remove leftovers within a couple of hours
budgie.benefits: Cabbage adds crunch and variety; the darker leaves carry more nutrients than the pale heart.
budgie.risks: Cabbage-family vegetables contain goitrogens that interfere with iodine use. Thyroid enlargement (goiter) is the most common thyroid disease in budgies, and large amounts of these vegetables, especially with an iodine-poor seed diet, add to the risk.

faq.q: Which vegetables are in the cabbage family?
faq.a: Broccoli, cauliflower, kale, Brussels sprouts, bok choy and turnip are all brassicas. Rotate them with vegetables such as carrot, bell pepper, zucchini and pumpkin.

faq.q: What are the signs of goiter in a budgie?
faq.a: Wheezing, clicking or squeaky breathing, voice changes, regurgitation or difficulty swallowing, because the enlarged thyroid presses on the airway and gullet. In severe cases a swelling may be visible in the neck. See an avian vet promptly.

budgie.notes: VCA lists cabbage as suitable for budgies. 'limit' is a budgie-specific precaution based on UF/IFAS (cabbage listed as goitrogenic feed; goiter most common thyroid disease in budgerigars), Loukopoulos 2015, and VCA noting budgies' vulnerability to iodine deficiency. Cockatiel verdict is 'yes'.

cockatiel.short: Yes. Cabbage is safe for cockatiels as one of several vegetables. Darker leaves offer more nutrients than the pale heart.
cockatiel.portion: About a tablespoon (15 ml) of finely shredded leaf as part of the day's vegetables
cockatiel.frequency: A few times a week, rotated with other vegetables
prep: Wash the leaves
Pick darker outer leaves where possible
Shred or chop finely
Take away leftovers after a couple of hours
cockatiel.benefits: Cabbage gives crunch, fiber and variety, and VCA lists it among suitable vegetables for pet birds.
cockatiel.risks: Like other cabbage-family plants it contains goitrogens, which can interfere with iodine use if fed in very large amounts, so rotate it rather than feeding it every day.

faq.q: Is red cabbage okay for cockatiels?
faq.a: Yes. Red and green cabbage are both fine in moderate amounts; red cabbage may temporarily tint droppings.

cockatiel.notes: Goiter reports center on budgerigars, so cockatiels get 'yes' with rotation advice.

hamster.short: Yes. Cauliflower florets and stalk are safe for hamsters in small amounts. Like broccoli, too much can cause gas.
hamster.portion: A piece about 1–1.5 cm (⅜–⅝ in) across for a Syrian; about half that for a dwarf. Keep all fresh food together to about 1–2 teaspoons a day for a Syrian and about half that for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: A few times a week, rotated with other vegetables.
prep: Wash well
Remove the leaves and cut a small floret or piece of stalk
Serve raw, or lightly cooked with nothing added and cooled
Remove any uneaten piece, including from the hoard, within a few hours
hamster.benefits: Low in sugar and calories, and a source of fibre and vitamins.
hamster.risks: Can cause gas if fed in large amounts. Woodgreen advises not feeding the leaves.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat cauliflower leaves?
faq.a: Woodgreen Pets Charity advises feeding only the florets and stalk and avoiding the leaves, so we suggest removing them.

faq.q: Raw or cooked?
faq.a: Both are fine in small amounts, as long as it is plain, with no cheese sauce, butter or seasoning.

hamster.notes: Woodgreen: 'The florets and stalk are both safe, cooked or raw, in small amounts. Avoid feeding them the leaves.' No reason given for avoiding leaves.

budgie.short: Yes, in small amounts. Cauliflower is safe for budgies, but it offers fewer nutrients than broccoli and shares the cabbage family's goitrogen concern, so keep it occasional.
budgie.portion: One or two tiny florets, chopped
budgie.frequency: Once or twice a week, not on the same days as other cabbage-family vegetables
prep: Wash the cauliflower
Break off small florets and chop them finely; the leaves can be used too
Serve raw or lightly steamed and cooled, unseasoned
Remove leftovers within a couple of hours
budgie.benefits: Cauliflower adds texture and variety and is listed by a veterinary school hospital among suitable vegetables for pet birds.
budgie.risks: It is pale and lower in carotenoids than darker vegetables. As a brassica it contains goitrogens, and budgies are the species most prone to goiter.

faq.q: Can budgies eat cauliflower leaves?
faq.a: Yes. The green leaves are safe and more nutritious than the white florets; wash and chop them finely.

budgie.notes: Cauliflower is not named in the goitrogen sources (UF/IFAS names kale, cabbage, broccoli, turnips), but it is the same species as cabbage and broccoli (Brassica oleracea); the budgie caution is extrapolated.

cockatiel.short: Yes. Cauliflower is safe for cockatiels as part of a varied vegetable mix, though it is less nutritious than broccoli and darker vegetables.
cockatiel.portion: A few small florets, about a tablespoon (15 ml) chopped
cockatiel.frequency: A few times a week, rotated with other vegetables
prep: Rinse the cauliflower
Cut into small florets; include some green leaves
Offer raw or lightly steamed and cooled, plain
Take away leftovers after a couple of hours
cockatiel.benefits: It adds crunch and variety, and the University of Florida veterinary hospital lists it among suitable vegetables.
cockatiel.risks: Low in carotenoids compared with orange and dark green vegetables. Like other brassicas it contains goitrogens, so rotate it rather than feeding large amounts daily.

faq.q: Raw or cooked cauliflower for cockatiels?
faq.a: Either is fine. Raw keeps more nutrients; lightly steamed and cooled can be easier for some birds to accept.

hamster.short: Yes. Zucchini (courgette) is a safe, low-sugar vegetable for hamsters. Offer a small piece a few times a week.
hamster.portion: A piece about 1–1.5 cm (⅜–⅝ in) across for a Syrian; about half that for a dwarf. Keep all fresh food together to about 1–2 teaspoons a day for a Syrian and about half that for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: A few times a week, rotated with other vegetables.
prep: Wash well
Cut a small piece; the skin can stay on
Serve raw, or lightly cooked with nothing added and cooled
Remove any uneaten piece, including from the hoard, within a few hours
hamster.benefits: Low in sugar and calories, which suits dwarf hamsters; adds moisture and variety.
hamster.risks: Very low risk in small amounts; like other watery vegetables, a lot can loosen droppings. Do not feed a zucchini that tastes unusually bitter, as bitterness can indicate natural toxins called cucurbitacins.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat other squash?
faq.a: Yes. Summer and winter squash flesh is listed as safe in small pieces; remove seeds and tough rind.

hamster.notes: PDSA (courgette, squash), Dogwood (zucchini), UC Davis and PetMD (squash). The cucurbitacin caution is general food-safety knowledge (bitter squash poisoning in people), not from a hamster source.

budgie.short: Yes. Zucchini (courgette) is a safe, low-sugar vegetable for budgies that can be offered regularly as part of a varied mix.
budgie.portion: About a teaspoon (5 ml) grated or in small cubes, as part of the day's vegetables
budgie.frequency: Daily or most days, rotated with other vegetables
prep: Wash the skin well
Grate or dice finely, skin on
Serve raw or lightly steamed and cooled
Remove leftovers within a couple of hours
budgie.benefits: It is low in sugar and fat, which suits a species prone to obesity, and its mild taste makes it a good starter vegetable.
budgie.risks: Zucchini is quite watery, so it is best paired with more nutrient-dense orange and dark green vegetables.

faq.q: Can budgies eat other squash?
faq.a: Yes. VCA lists squash as suitable, and orange-fleshed types such as butternut are rich in beta-carotene; cook hard winter squash until soft and serve it plain.

cockatiel.short: Yes. Zucchini is a mild, low-sugar vegetable that cockatiels can have regularly as part of their daily vegetable mix.
cockatiel.portion: About a tablespoon (15 ml) grated, sliced or cubed
cockatiel.frequency: Daily or most days, rotated with other vegetables
prep: Wash the zucchini
Slice, cube or grate it with the skin on
Offer raw or lightly steamed and cooled
Take away leftovers after a couple of hours
cockatiel.benefits: Low in calories and easy to accept, it is a useful base vegetable for cockatiels learning to eat fresh food.
cockatiel.risks: Few risks; its high water content means it should not be the only vegetable offered.

faq.q: Can cockatiels eat zucchini seeds?
faq.a: Yes. The soft seeds inside a zucchini are fine.

hamster.short: Yes, in small amounts, cooked and plain. Sweet potato is not toxic, but it is starchy and sweet, so treat it as an occasional extra rather than an everyday vegetable.
hamster.portion: A cube about 1 cm (⅜ in) for a Syrian; about 5 mm (¼ in) for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: Once a week.
prep: Peel and wash
Boil, steam or bake plain, with no butter, salt, sugar or spices
Let it cool completely
Cut a small cube and remove leftovers within a few hours
hamster.benefits: Rich in beta-carotene and fibre.
hamster.risks: High in starch and natural sugar, so frequent portions add calories. Raw sweet potato is harder to digest, so offer it cooked. It is not related to the ordinary potato, which should not be fed.
hamster.dwarf: Campbell's, Winter White, their hybrids and Chinese hamsters are prone to diabetes. Keep sweet potato to a pea-sized crumb no more than every week or two, or skip it, and rely mainly on low-sugar vegetables such as cucumber, broccoli and bell pepper.

faq.q: Is sweet potato the same as potato?
faq.a: No. Sweet potato is a different plant. Ordinary potatoes, especially raw, green or sprouted ones, should not be fed to hamsters.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat sweet potato skin or fries?
faq.a: Peel it to remove soil and residues. Sweet potato fries and crisps are cooked in oil and often salted, so they are not suitable.

hamster.notes: No cited source names sweet potato for hamsters. VCA lists 'yellow and orange vegetables' as acceptable and PetMD allows 'small portions of root vegetables'. Cooking and 'limit' are cautious choices based on starch content (general nutrition).

budgie.short: Yes, cooked and plain. Sweet potato is one of the best orange vegetables for budgies, rich in beta-carotene; serve it steamed or baked with nothing added.
budgie.portion: About a teaspoon (5 ml) of mashed or finely diced cooked sweet potato
budgie.frequency: 2–3 times a week, rotated with other vegetables
prep: Peel and wash the sweet potato
Steam, boil or bake until soft, with no salt, butter or oil
Cool completely, then mash or dice finely
Remove leftovers within an hour, as cooked food spoils faster
budgie.benefits: The AAV, VCA and the Royal Veterinary College all list sweet potato among recommended vegetables because it is rich in beta-carotene, which birds convert to vitamin A.
budgie.risks: It is starchier than most vegetables, so it should be one part of a varied mix. Seasoned, buttered or candied sweet potato and fries are not suitable.

faq.q: Can budgies eat raw sweet potato?
faq.a: Most guidance recommends serving it cooked, plain and cooled. Cooked sweet potato is softer and easier for a small bird to eat.

budgie.notes: Cooking recommendation is conventional avian guidance; raw sweet potato is not documented as toxic.

cockatiel.short: Yes, cooked and plain. Sweet potato is an excellent source of beta-carotene for cockatiels; steam or bake it and serve it without any seasoning.
cockatiel.portion: About a tablespoon (15 ml) of mashed or diced cooked sweet potato
cockatiel.frequency: 2–3 times a week, rotated with other vegetables
prep: Peel the sweet potato
Cook until soft by steaming, boiling or baking, without salt, butter or oil
Let it cool, then dice or mash
Take away leftovers within an hour
cockatiel.benefits: Red-orange vegetables such as sweet potato are high in beta-carotene, a vitamin A precursor, and Merck lists sweet potatoes among foods rich in vitamin A.
cockatiel.risks: Somewhat starchy, so it should not dominate the vegetable mix. Avoid versions prepared for people with sugar, butter or salt.

faq.q: Can I mix sweet potato with my cockatiel's pellets?
faq.a: A little mashed sweet potato can help a cockatiel accept new foods, but moist food spoils quickly, so remove the dish within an hour.

hamster.short: No. Vets and UK charities advise against potatoes for hamsters. Raw, green or sprouted potatoes and the peel contain solanine, and cooked potato is starchy with no benefit.
hamster.risks: Potatoes belong to the nightshade family; green or sprouting potatoes, the peel and the plant contain solanine, a glycoalkaloid that can cause severe digestive upset, weakness and a slow heart rate. Cooked potato is less risky but starchy, calorie-dense and unnecessary.
hamster.ifEaten: If your hamster ate raw, green or sprouted potato, peel or any part of the plant, call your vet for advice. A crumb of plain cooked potato is unlikely to cause problems, but watch for diarrhoea, a wet or dirty tail area, or reduced appetite over the next day or two, and contact a vet promptly if these appear.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat mashed potato, chips or crisps?
faq.a: No. As well as the potato, these contain butter, milk, oil or salt, which are unsuitable for hamsters.

faq.q: What about sweet potato?
faq.a: Sweet potato is a different plant. It can be offered plain and cooked in small amounts.

hamster.notes: PetMD: do not offer potatoes; Woodgreen: avoid 'Potato (including raw/green potato)'; Dogwood: raw potatoes toxic. Solanine signs cited from ASPCA's tomato plant entry (same family and toxin; ASPCA has no potato entry). Plain cooked potato is widely considered low-risk; chose 'no' because sources do not distinguish.

budgie.short: Yes, in small amounts, cooked and plain only. Cooked potato is not toxic to budgies but offers little, and raw, green or sprouting potatoes and the plant contain solanine.
budgie.portion: A piece of plain cooked potato about 1 cm (⅜ in) across
prep: Use potatoes with no green patches or sprouts
Peel, then boil, steam or bake until soft, with no salt, butter or oil
Cool and cut a small piece
Remove leftovers within an hour
budgie.benefits: Plain cooked potato is a bland food that some budgies accept, but sweet potato and other orange vegetables offer much more.
budgie.risks: Potatoes are nightshades: the leaves, stems, sprouts and green skin contain glycoalkaloids such as solanine, while properly stored potato flesh is considered safe for birds. Chips, crisps and fries are too salty and fatty.

faq.q: Can budgies eat raw potato?
faq.a: It is better not to. Raw potato is hard to digest, and any green or sprouting parts contain more solanine. Offer only plain cooked potato, or better still, sweet potato.

faq.q: What about potato peel?
faq.a: Leave it off. Glycoalkaloids concentrate in and just under the skin, especially where it has turned green.

budgie.notes: VCA lists potato as suitable and LafeberVet says birds can eat potatoes while the plants are toxic. 'limit' reflects low nutritional value and solanine risk in raw/green/sprouted potatoes and the plant; the green-potato and peel details come from general toxicology rather than a bird-specific source.

cockatiel.short: Yes, in small amounts, cooked and plain only. Cockatiels can eat plain cooked potato, but never raw, green or sprouted potato or the plant's leaves, which contain solanine.
cockatiel.portion: One or two pieces of plain cooked potato about 1.5 cm (⅝ in) across
prep: Discard any potato with green skin or sprouts
Peel and cook until soft, without salt, butter or oil
Cool before serving
Take away leftovers within an hour
cockatiel.benefits: Little nutritional benefit compared with sweet potato, pumpkin or carrot, but plain cooked potato is harmless in small amounts.
cockatiel.risks: The potato plant and any green or sprouting tubers contain solanine and related glycoalkaloids. Potato dishes made for people are usually salted and buttered, and chips and fries are high in fat and salt.

faq.q: Can cockatiels eat mashed potato from my plate?
faq.a: No. Mashed potato made for people usually contains butter, milk and salt. Set aside a plain cooked piece before seasoning if you want to share.

cockatiel.notes: Same as budgie.

hamster.short: Yes. Plain pumpkin flesh is safe for hamsters in small pieces, raw or cooked. Avoid pumpkin pie filling and anything with added sugar or spice.
hamster.portion: A piece about 1–1.5 cm (⅜–⅝ in) across for a Syrian; about half that for a dwarf. Keep all fresh food together to about 1–2 teaspoons a day for a Syrian and about half that for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: One to three times a week, rotated with other vegetables.
prep: Wash, peel and remove the seeds and stringy pulp
Cut a small cube of flesh; serve raw or cooked plain and cooled
Never use pie filling, spiced or sweetened pumpkin
Remove any uneaten piece, including from the hoard, within a few hours
hamster.benefits: Contains beta-carotene and fibre, and is moderately low in sugar compared with fruit.
hamster.risks: Low risk in small amounts; large portions can loosen droppings. Soft, cooked pumpkin spoils quickly if hoarded.
hamster.dwarf: Pumpkin is less sugary than fruit, but keep portions small (about 5 mm, ¼ in) for diabetes-prone dwarfs.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat pumpkin seeds?
faq.a: Plain, unsalted pumpkin seeds can be an occasional treat, but they are high in fat: one seed for a Syrian, or a small piece of a shelled seed for a dwarf, once or twice a week at most.

faq.q: Is canned pumpkin OK?
faq.a: Plain canned pumpkin with nothing added is fine in a tiny amount. Pumpkin pie filling contains sugar and spices and should not be given.

hamster.notes: PDSA lists pumpkin and squash as suitable; VCA lists yellow and orange vegetables as acceptable; Dogwood lists unsalted pumpkin seeds as suitable; PetMD lists squash. Sugar comparison is general nutrition knowledge.

budgie.short: Yes. Pumpkin flesh is a nutritious, low-fat vegetable for budgies, rich in beta-carotene, and can be served raw or plainly cooked.
budgie.portion: About a teaspoon (5 ml) of grated raw or mashed cooked pumpkin
budgie.frequency: A few times a week, rotated with other vegetables
prep: Wash and peel the pumpkin and scoop out the stringy pulp and seeds
Grate the raw flesh finely, or steam or bake it plain and let it cool
Never use canned pie filling, which is sweetened and spiced
Remove raw leftovers within a couple of hours and cooked ones within an hour
budgie.benefits: VCA lists pumpkin and squash among vegetables rich in vitamin A precursors, a nutrient often lacking in seed-based diets.
budgie.risks: Few risks when plain. Carved or decorative pumpkins that have been sitting out may be moldy and should not be fed.

faq.q: Can budgies eat pumpkin seeds?
faq.a: Plain, unsalted pumpkin seeds are not toxic, but they are high in fat, so treat them as an occasional treat rather than a vegetable.

cockatiel.short: Yes. Plain pumpkin flesh is a good regular vegetable for cockatiels, supplying beta-carotene with little fat, and it can be offered raw or cooked.
cockatiel.portion: About a tablespoon (15 ml) of diced raw or mashed cooked pumpkin
cockatiel.frequency: A few times a week, rotated with other vegetables
prep: Peel the pumpkin and remove pulp and seeds
Dice or grate raw, or cook plain and cool
Do not use canned pie filling or spiced pumpkin products
Take away leftovers promptly
cockatiel.benefits: Orange squash and pumpkin supply carotenoids that cockatiels convert to vitamin A.
cockatiel.risks: Very low risk when fresh and plain. Avoid moldy or decorative pumpkins.

faq.q: Is canned pumpkin okay for cockatiels?
faq.a: Plain canned pumpkin puree with no added sugar, salt or spice is acceptable in small amounts; pie filling is not.

cockatiel.notes: Canned puree answer is inferred (VCA advises against canned produce packed with salt or sugar).

hamster.short: Yes, in small amounts. Garden peas are safe for hamsters, but they are starchier and sweeter than leafy vegetables, so offer just one or two at a time.
hamster.portion: One or two peas for a Syrian; one pea, or half, for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: Once or twice a week.
prep: Use fresh or frozen peas with nothing added
Thaw frozen peas to room temperature
Remove from tough pods
Remove any uneaten piece, including from the hoard, within a few hours
hamster.benefits: Provide plant protein and fibre, and hamsters enjoy handling them.
hamster.risks: Peas are higher in starch and sugar than most vegetables, so large amounts add calories. Canned peas often contain added salt.
hamster.dwarf: Campbell's, Winter White, their hybrids and Chinese hamsters are prone to diabetes. Keep peas to one pea once a week, and rely mainly on low-sugar vegetables such as cucumber, broccoli and bell pepper.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat dried or split peas?
faq.a: Not raw. Vets warn against feeding raw dried beans and pulses, so stick to fresh or frozen garden peas.

faq.q: Are canned or mushy peas OK?
faq.a: No. They usually contain salt, and mushy peas may also have sugar or other additions.

hamster.notes: Woodgreen, PDSA and Northgate list peas as safe without special limits. 'Limit' reflects higher starch/sugar than leafy vegetables (nutritional reasoning, not a documented problem). Dried-pulse FAQ extrapolates PetMD's 'raw beans' warning.

budgie.short: Yes. Fresh or thawed frozen peas are safe for budgies, and most enjoy nibbling or shelling them; offer a few as part of the day's vegetables.
budgie.portion: Three to five peas, or a short piece of pod
prep: Use fresh peas, or frozen peas thawed to room temperature
Offer whole or halved peas, or young pods to explore
Avoid canned peas, which often contain added salt
Remove leftovers within a couple of hours
budgie.benefits: Peas add plant protein and fiber, and pods make good foraging enrichment.
budgie.risks: Peas are starchier and more energy-dense than leafy or watery vegetables, so they should be one part of the mix. Canned peas may contain salt, which VCA advises against.

faq.q: Can budgies eat pea pods?
faq.a: Yes. Fresh pea pods, including snap peas and snow peas, are safe; wash them and cut them into short pieces.

cockatiel.short: Yes. Peas are a safe vegetable for cockatiels, fresh or thawed from frozen, and pods give them something to open and forage.
cockatiel.portion: About a tablespoon (15 ml) of peas, or one or two pods
prep: Use fresh peas or thawed frozen peas
Offer loose peas or whole washed pods
Skip canned or salted peas
Take away leftovers after a couple of hours
cockatiel.benefits: Peas supply plant protein and fiber, and working pods open is good enrichment.
cockatiel.risks: Somewhat starchy, so they should complement rather than replace lower-calorie vegetables.

faq.q: Should peas be cooked for cockatiels?
faq.a: No. Fresh or thawed frozen peas can be served raw; lightly cooked peas are also fine if plain.

hamster.short: Yes, in small amounts. A few kernels of fresh sweetcorn are safe for hamsters, but corn is starchy and sugary, so keep it an occasional treat.
hamster.portion: Two or three kernels for a Syrian; one kernel for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: Once or twice a week.
prep: Use fresh or frozen kernels, thawed, with nothing added
Avoid canned corn with salt or sugar
Do not feed corn that looks or smells mouldy
Remove any uneaten piece, including from the hoard, within a few hours
hamster.benefits: Adds variety; hamsters enjoy handling kernels.
hamster.risks: Corn is higher in starch and sugar than most vegetables. Mouldy corn can contain fungal toxins.
hamster.dwarf: Campbell's, Winter White, their hybrids and Chinese hamsters are prone to diabetes. Keep corn to one kernel once a week, and check whether their dry food already contains corn, and rely mainly on low-sugar vegetables such as cucumber, broccoli and bell pepper.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat popcorn?
faq.a: Plain popcorn with no butter, salt or sugar is listed by VCA as an occasional treat for hamsters. Buttered, salted or sweet popcorn is not suitable.

faq.q: Is the corn in hamster food mixes a problem?
faq.a: No, it is part of a balanced food. The concern is adding a lot of extra corn on top.

hamster.notes: PDSA (sweetcorn) and Dogwood (corn) list it as safe; VCA lists unsalted popcorn as a treat. 'Limit' reflects starch/sugar content (general nutrition). Mould/mycotoxin caution is general feed-safety knowledge.

budgie.short: Yes, in small amounts. Fresh or thawed sweetcorn is safe for budgies, but it is starchy and sweet, so treat it as an occasional extra rather than a staple vegetable.
budgie.portion: Three to five kernels, or a thin round of cob about 1 cm (⅜ in) thick to pick at, taken away after a short while
prep: Use fresh sweetcorn or frozen kernels thawed to room temperature
Serve raw or lightly cooked, with no butter or salt
Throw away any corn that looks or smells moldy
Remove leftovers within a couple of hours
budgie.benefits: The AAV suggests a piece of corn on the cob as something fun to destroy that doubles as a snack.
budgie.risks: Sweetcorn is higher in sugar and starch than most vegetables. Moldy corn and other grains can carry fungal toxins, so offer only fresh, clean corn.

faq.q: Can budgies eat popcorn?
faq.a: Salted, buttered or sweetened popcorn should not be given; VCA lists salty snacks such as popcorn among foods budgies should never have.

faq.q: Can budgies eat canned corn?
faq.a: It is better not to. Canned corn often contains added salt or sugar.

budgie.notes: VCA lists corn as suitable and AAV mentions corn on the cob for enrichment. 'limit' reflects energy density in an obesity-prone species (inferred).

cockatiel.short: Yes, in small amounts. Cockatiels usually love sweetcorn, and a piece of cob makes good enrichment, but it is starchy and sweet, so keep it occasional.
cockatiel.portion: A round of cob about 2 cm (¾ in) thick, or about a tablespoon (15 ml) of kernels
prep: Use fresh or thawed frozen sweetcorn
Serve raw or lightly cooked and cooled, plain
Discard anything moldy
Take away leftovers after a couple of hours
cockatiel.benefits: Picking kernels off a cob keeps a cockatiel busy, and the AAV mentions corn on the cob as a toy that doubles as a snack.
cockatiel.risks: Energy-dense compared with most vegetables; cockatiels gain weight easily. Moldy corn can carry fungal toxins.

faq.q: Can cockatiels eat dried corn or corn in seed mixes?
faq.a: Dried corn is safe only if it is clean and free of mold. Fresh sweetcorn is the better choice for a treat.

cockatiel.notes: Same as budgie.

hamster.short: Yes, in small amounts, ideally cooked. Green beans are listed as safe, but several vets warn against raw beans, so lightly cook them plain and cool them first.
hamster.portion: A piece about 1 cm (⅜ in) long for a Syrian; about 5 mm (¼ in) for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: Once or twice a week.
prep: Wash and trim the ends
Boil or steam plain until tender, with no salt, butter or seasoning
Cool completely and cut small
Remove any uneaten piece, including from the hoard, within a few hours
hamster.benefits: Low in sugar and calories, with fibre and vitamins.
hamster.risks: Raw beans contain lectins that cooking destroys; levels are highest in dried beans such as kidney beans and lower in green beans. PetMD and two vet clinics list raw or uncooked beans as unsafe for hamsters, so cooking is the cautious choice.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat raw green beans?
faq.a: Woodgreen Pets Charity says both raw and lightly cooked green beans are safe, but because vets list raw beans among foods to avoid, we recommend cooking them first.

faq.q: What about kidney beans, baked beans or other beans?
faq.a: Never feed raw dried beans. Baked beans and beans in sauce contain sugar and salt and are also unsuitable.

hamster.notes: Woodgreen: 'Both raw and lightly cooked green beans are safe'; PetMD's Syrian sheet lists green beans as safe but also says do not offer 'raw beans'; Northgate: never feed 'uncooked beans'; Dogwood: 'raw beans' toxic. These warnings probably refer to dried legumes, but they do not specify, so recommended cooking and 'limit'. Lectin statement is general food science.

prep: Wash and trim the ends
Chop into short pieces
Serve raw or lightly steamed and cooled
Avoid canned beans with added salt
Remove leftovers within a couple of hours
budgie.benefits: Green beans are low in sugar and fat and add fiber and crunch; the University of Florida veterinary hospital lists them among recommended vegetables.
budgie.risks: Few risks when fresh and plain. VCA lists beans as suitable only when cooked; raw dried beans such as kidney beans contain lectins and must be soaked and fully cooked.

faq.q: Can budgies eat raw green beans?
faq.a: Fresh green beans are commonly fed raw. Lightly steaming them is a simple extra precaution, because raw beans contain some lectins. Dried beans must always be fully cooked.

budgie.notes: Lectin detail (phytohaemagglutinin, highest in dried kidney beans) is general food-science knowledge, not from a cited bird source.

cockatiel.short: Yes. Green beans are a good low-sugar vegetable for cockatiels, fresh or lightly steamed. Dried beans are different and must be fully cooked first.
cockatiel.portion: About a tablespoon (15 ml) of chopped beans
prep: Rinse and top-and-tail the beans
Cut into short pieces
Offer raw or lightly steamed and cooled
Take away leftovers after a couple of hours
cockatiel.benefits: Low in sugar and fat, with fiber and crunch that many cockatiels enjoy.
cockatiel.risks: Minimal when fresh. Canned beans may be salted, and uncooked dried beans contain lectins.

faq.q: Can cockatiels eat frozen green beans?
faq.a: Yes, once thawed or lightly cooked, as long as they are plain.

hamster.short: No. Onions contain sulfur compounds that damage red blood cells and can cause anaemia. Vets list onion as unsafe for hamsters in any form: raw, cooked, dried or in sauces.
hamster.risks: Onions and other alliums contain sulfur-containing oxidants that damage red blood cells (Heinz body anaemia). Harm can build up for several days after eating, and concentrated forms such as onion powder are more dangerous.
hamster.ifEaten: Call your vet promptly, even if your hamster seems well, and say how much was eaten and in what form. Signs of anaemia, such as weakness, pale ears, feet and nose, fast breathing or reduced appetite, may take several days to appear.

faq.q: What about spring onions, chives, leeks or shallots?
faq.a: These are all alliums with the same risk and should never be fed.

faq.q: Is cooked onion or onion powder safer?
faq.a: No. Cooking does not remove the risk, and dried or powdered onion is more concentrated. Check that any human food shared with your hamster contains no onion.

hamster.notes: PDSA's hamster page lists 'Onion' among suitable vegetables - an outlier contradicted by PetMD (DVM-authored), Northgate ('Never feed your hamster... onions'), Dogwood ('toxic'), Woodgreen and Allium toxicology. Recommend the site owner flag the PDSA listing as a likely error rather than cite it as support. Merck mechanism and timing (Heinz bodies within 24 h, haemolysis 3-5 days) are from cats, dogs and livestock; no hamster dose data found.

budgie.short: No. Onions contain sulfur compounds that damage red blood cells, and avian vets list them among foods budgies must avoid. Raw, cooked and powdered onion are all unsafe.
budgie.risks: Onions and other alliums (garlic, leeks, chives, spring onions) contain compounds that damage red blood cells and can cause anemia. Concentrated forms such as onion powder are more potent, and fatal poisoning has been reported in geese fed large amounts of green onions.
budgie.ifEaten: Remove any remaining onion and call your avian vet, especially if more than a tiny bit or a concentrated form (powder, soup mix, fried onion) was eaten. Signs can be delayed by a day or more and include weakness, lethargy, fluffed feathers, breathing effort and red-brown or unusually dark droppings.

faq.q: Is cooked onion safe for budgies?
faq.a: No. Cooking does not remove the harmful compounds, and dried or powdered onion is even more potent than raw.

faq.q: Can budgies have food seasoned with onion, like crackers or stock?
faq.a: No. Keep seasoned people food away from budgies; much of it contains onion or garlic powder as well as salt.

budgie.notes: Merck's Allium chapter covers mammals; it is cited for the point that raw, cooked and dried forms are all toxic.

cockatiel.short: No. Onion can damage a cockatiel's red blood cells, and VCA says it should never be offered to a bird. This includes cooked onion and onion powder.
cockatiel.risks: Onion belongs to the Allium family, whose sulfur compounds cause oxidative damage to red blood cells, leading to anemia. VCA's cockatiel feeding guide lists onion alongside avocado as potentially toxic.
cockatiel.ifEaten: Call your avian vet for advice, particularly if your cockatiel ate more than a nibble or a concentrated form such as onion powder. Watch over the next few days for weakness, reduced appetite, fluffed feathers, labored breathing or dark or reddish droppings.

faq.q: What about spring onions, leeks or chives?
faq.a: They are all in the onion family and should be kept away from cockatiels too.

hamster.short: No. Garlic contains the same red-blood-cell-damaging compounds as onion, and veterinary toxicology rates it about 3-5 times more potent. Never feed it to hamsters in any form.
hamster.risks: Garlic, like onion, contains sulfur-containing oxidants that damage red blood cells and can cause Heinz body anaemia; signs can take several days to appear. Garlic powder, oil and supplements are concentrated.
hamster.ifEaten: Call your vet promptly, even if your hamster seems well, and say how much was eaten and in what form. Signs of anaemia, such as weakness, pale ears, feet and nose, fast breathing or reduced appetite, may take several days to appear.

faq.q: Is a small amount of garlic good for hamsters' health?
faq.a: No. There is no proven benefit for hamsters, and garlic can damage red blood cells.

faq.q: What about foods cooked with garlic?
faq.a: Do not share them. Sauces, seasoned vegetables, bread and meat dishes often contain garlic or garlic powder.

hamster.notes: All hamster sources that mention garlic say avoid. Merck: 'Garlic is 3-5 times more toxic than onion' (general statement; species data from cats, dogs and livestock).

budgie.short: No. Garlic damages red blood cells and is considered more potent than onion; a pet conure died after being fed garlic. Keep garlic and garlic powder away from budgies.
budgie.risks: Garlic contains sulfur compounds that destroy red blood cells; in mammals it is considered three to five times more toxic than onion. A published case described a conure that died of sudden red-cell destruction after being fed garlic.
budgie.ifEaten: Call your avian vet promptly, especially if a clove, garlic powder or garlicky food was eaten; a budgie's small size means a small amount matters. Watch for weakness, lethargy, fluffed feathers, breathing effort and reddish or dark droppings.

faq.q: Isn't garlic a natural health supplement for birds?
faq.a: No. Despite claims online, avian vet sources list garlic as a food to avoid. Its harmful effect on red blood cells is documented, and it has no proven benefit for pet birds.

faq.q: Is garlic powder in food a problem?
faq.a: Yes. Concentrated forms such as garlic powder are more potent than fresh garlic.

budgie.notes: Some popular internet sources promote garlic as an immune booster or dewormer for birds; vet sources disagree. In Wade & Newman 2004 the conure had been force-fed a large amount (half a clove found in the crop).

cockatiel.short: No. Garlic is harmful to cockatiels: it damages red blood cells, and fatal poisoning has been reported in a small parrot. Avoid fresh garlic, garlic powder and garlicky foods.
cockatiel.risks: Like onion, garlic causes oxidative damage to red blood cells, but it is more potent. A dusky-headed conure, a parrot not much larger than a cockatiel, died of acute hemolysis after being fed garlic.
cockatiel.ifEaten: Phone your avian vet for advice straight away and say how much was eaten and in what form. Signs of anemia can take a day or more to appear: weakness, sleepiness, fluffed feathers, labored breathing and dark or reddish droppings.

faq.q: Can cockatiels have bird treats flavored with garlic?
faq.a: It is best to avoid them. Garlic is on avian vet lists of foods not to feed.

hamster.short: Better not. Mushrooms add little for hamsters, wild ones can be deadly, and raw button mushrooms contain agaritine, considered a potential weak carcinogen in mice.
hamster.risks: Wild mushrooms can be highly toxic and are hard to identify. Raw cultivated button mushrooms contain agaritine, which a 2020 scientific review describes as a potential weak carcinogen in mice. PDSA lists mushroom as suitable, so sources disagree.
hamster.ifEaten: A nibble of a plain shop-bought mushroom is not an emergency: remove the rest and watch for diarrhoea, a wet or dirty tail area, or reduced appetite over the next day or two, and contact a vet promptly if these appear. If your hamster ate a wild mushroom, call your vet immediately and take a photo or sample.

faq.q: Are cooked mushrooms OK?
faq.a: Cooking reduces the concern about raw mushrooms, but they still add little, and cooked dishes often contain garlic, onion, butter or salt. We suggest skipping them.

faq.q: My hamster ate a mushroom from the garden. What should I do?
faq.a: Call your vet straight away. Many wild mushrooms are poisonous and cannot be reliably identified by sight.

hamster.notes: Disagreement: PDSA lists 'Mushroom' among suitable vegetables; no other credible hamster source found either way. Verdict inferred from toxicology: Lagrange & Vernoux 2020 (review): agaritine in A. bisporus 'is a potential weak carcinogen in mice' and advise avoiding raw or poorly cooked button mushrooms (for people). An older study (Toth & Erickson 1986) reported tumours in mice fed uncooked mushrooms for life; the size of this risk is debated. PubMed page blocked by CAPTCHA; abstract retrieved via NCBI E-utilities / Europe PMC API. Evidence set to 'inferred' because the only direct hamster source supports the opposite verdict.

budgie.short: Better not. Shop-bought mushrooms are not known to poison birds, but avian vets disagree on feeding them and wild mushrooms can be deadly. There is no need to offer them to budgies.
prep: Offer other vegetables instead
Never feed wild or foraged mushrooms
Keep mushrooms growing in the garden, aviary or plant pots out of reach
budgie.risks: LafeberVet states that mushrooms safe for people are considered safe for pets, but some avian vets advise avoiding all mushrooms because they have been linked to digestive upset in parrots. Wild species such as Amanita and false morels are dangerously toxic, and cooking does not make false morels safe.
budgie.ifEaten: A nibble of a plain, shop-bought mushroom is not an emergency; watch for regurgitation, diarrhea or lethargy over the next day and call your vet if they appear. If your budgie ate a wild or unidentified mushroom, call your avian vet or an animal poison line immediately and take a sample with you.

faq.q: Are cooked mushrooms safer for budgies?
faq.a: Cooking does not make toxic wild species safe; LafeberVet notes it does not remove the danger of false morels. For shop-bought mushrooms, there is simply no benefit that justifies offering them.

budgie.notes: Disagreement: LafeberVet (Pollock) says human-edible mushrooms are considered safe for pets; a vet-reviewed retailer article (not cited) says experts recommend avoiding mushrooms because of digestive upset. Chose the more cautious 'avoid'. Popular internet advice is split.

cockatiel.short: Better not. Edible mushrooms are not proven toxic to cockatiels, but opinion among avian vets is divided, and wild mushrooms can be fatal, so it is simplest to leave them out.
prep: Choose other vegetables instead
Do not feed wild or foraged mushrooms
Check the aviary, garden and house plants for mushrooms and remove them
cockatiel.risks: Some sources consider shop-bought mushrooms safe while others advise avoiding them because of digestive upset in parrots. Toxic wild mushrooms, including Amanita and false morels, can cause severe or fatal poisoning.

faq.q: My cockatiel ate a mushroom from the lawn. What should I do?
faq.a: Call your avian vet or an animal poison line immediately. Some wild mushrooms are deadly, and identification matters, so bring a sample.

cockatiel.notes: Same disagreement as budgie.

hamster.short: No. The RSPCA warns rhubarb can be poisonous to rodents. It contains soluble oxalates, especially in the leaves, which can damage the kidneys.
hamster.risks: Rhubarb, particularly the leaves, contains soluble oxalates, which bind calcium and can cause kidney failure, tremors and drooling in animals. The stalks are also very sour.
hamster.ifEaten: Call your vet promptly and say whether leaves or stalk were eaten and how much. Watch for drooling, trembling, weakness, reduced appetite, or changes in drinking and urination.

faq.q: Are rhubarb stalks safe if the leaves are removed?
faq.a: No. The leaves are the most dangerous part, but the RSPCA, Woodgreen and PetMD advise against rhubarb in general for hamsters.

faq.q: What about cooked rhubarb, crumble or jam?
faq.a: No. Cooking does not make rhubarb suitable, and desserts add sugar.

hamster.notes: All sources agree. ASPCA (dogs, cats, horses): toxic principle soluble calcium oxalates; signs kidney failure, tremors, salivation. Leaves are the highest-oxalate part (general botany).

budgie.short: No. Rhubarb leaves are rich in soluble oxalates that can damage the kidneys, and avian vet sources list rhubarb as a toxic plant. Keep the whole plant away from budgies.
budgie.risks: Rhubarb leaves contain high levels of soluble oxalates, which bind calcium and can cause kidney damage. The stalks contain far less, but they are very sour, offer no benefit and are usually cooked with a lot of sugar, so no part of rhubarb is recommended for a bird as small as a budgie.
budgie.ifEaten: If your budgie ate any rhubarb leaf, call your avian vet or an animal poison line promptly. For a small nibble of plain stalk, call your vet for advice and watch for regurgitation, weakness, trembling or changes in drinking and droppings.

faq.q: Is cooked rhubarb or rhubarb crumble okay for budgies?
faq.a: No. Rhubarb desserts are loaded with sugar and butter, and the plant offers no benefit to birds.

budgie.notes: Pet Poison Helpline states stalks contain very little soluble oxalate and are non-toxic (for pets generally); LafeberVet lists Rheum spp. as toxic plants and notes leaf oxalates cause kidney problems. Chose 'no' for the food as a whole; an accidental nibble of stalk is unlikely to be serious.

cockatiel.short: No. Rhubarb leaves contain soluble oxalates that can harm the kidneys, and rhubarb appears on avian vet toxic-plant lists. Do not feed any part of it to cockatiels.
cockatiel.risks: Soluble oxalates in rhubarb leaves can lower blood calcium and injure the kidneys. The stalks carry much less oxalate, but they have no nutritional value for cockatiels and are usually served with sugar.
cockatiel.ifEaten: Call your avian vet or a poison line if your cockatiel ate rhubarb leaf. For a small taste of stalk, ring your vet for advice and watch for regurgitation, weakness, trembling, increased drinking or watery droppings.

faq.q: Is it safe to grow rhubarb near an outdoor aviary?
faq.a: It is best not to. Birds may reach or be offered the leaves, which are the most toxic part.

cockatiel.notes: Same as budgie.

hamster.short: Yes, in small pieces. Romaine is a leafy green that vet sources list as suitable for hamsters, unlike iceberg. Too much at once can loosen droppings, so keep portions tiny.

hamster.frequency: 2–4 times a week, rotating with other vegetables
prep: Wash the leaf well and pat it dry
Use the darker outer leaves rather than the pale heart
Tear into small pieces
Remove uneaten or hoarded leaf the next day
hamster.benefits: Adds fibre, water and vitamins A and K, and brings variety to a pellet-based diet.
hamster.risks: Romaine is mostly water, so a large amount can cause soft droppings, and leaves hoarded in the nest rot quickly. It should add variety, not replace the pellet diet.

faq.q: Is romaine better than iceberg lettuce for hamsters?
faq.a: Yes. Veterinary sources advise against iceberg because it is mostly water with little nutritional value, while romaine and other darker leafy greens can be offered in small amounts.

faq.q: Can romaine lettuce give my hamster diarrhoea?
faq.a: A large portion of any watery leaf can soften droppings, and sudden diet changes can upset a hamster's gut. Introduce it gradually in small pieces. If your hamster develops diarrhoea or a wet bottom, contact a vet promptly.

hamster.notes: PetMD (DVM-reviewed) names romaine as suitable; VCA approves leafy greens and specifically excludes iceberg. PDSA's vegetable list does not include lettuce.
