The diarrhoea caution is reasoned from water content and Veterinary Partner's advice to change diets slowly.

budgie.short: Yes. Romaine is a good everyday green for budgies. Its darker leaves carry far more nutrition than pale iceberg lettuce, and most budgies enjoy shredding it.
budgie.portion: A leaf piece about 5 cm (2 in) square, or 1–2 teaspoons finely chopped, as part of the day's fresh food
budgie.frequency: Daily or most days, rotated with other greens and vegetables
prep: Wash the leaf well under running water
Use crisp, fresh leaves and discard wilted or slimy parts
Offer a whole piece to shred, or chop it finely
Remove uneaten leaves after a few hours
budgie.benefits: Romaine is low in calories and provides beta-carotene, which birds turn into vitamin A, plus vitamin K and folate. Vitamin A deficiency is common in seed-fed birds, so dark leafy greens are worth offering.
budgie.risks: Very few. Unwashed produce can carry pesticide residues or bacteria, and a large amount of watery greens can make droppings wetter for a while. Greens add to a pellet-based diet; they do not replace it.

faq.q: Can budgies eat romaine lettuce every day?
faq.a: Yes. Romaine can be offered daily as part of a mix of vegetables and greens. Together, fresh foods should make up roughly a fifth to a quarter of what a budgie eats, with pellets as the base.

faq.q: Is romaine better than iceberg lettuce for budgies?
faq.a: Yes. Iceberg is mostly water and has little nutritional value, while romaine's darker leaves contain much more beta-carotene and other nutrients.

budgie.notes: VCA lists romaine lettuce among suitable foods for budgies and for pet birds generally. The romaine-versus-iceberg nutrient comparison is general food-composition knowledge, not bird-specific research.

cockatiel.short: Yes. Romaine lettuce is a safe, useful daily green for cockatiels and a much better choice than iceberg. Wash it and offer it as part of a varied fresh-food mix.
cockatiel.portion: A leaf piece about 8 cm (3 in) square, or 2–3 teaspoons chopped, as part of the day's fresh food
cockatiel.frequency: Daily or most days, alongside other vegetables
prep: Rinse the leaf thoroughly
Discard any wilted, brown or slimy parts
Clip a whole piece to the cage or chop it into small pieces
Take away leftovers after a few hours
cockatiel.benefits: Romaine supplies beta-carotene (a vitamin A precursor), vitamin K and folate for very few calories. Cockatiels are prone to vitamin A deficiency, so darker greens help round out the diet.
cockatiel.risks: Minimal. Wash off pesticide residues and bacteria, and expect slightly wetter droppings if a cockatiel eats a lot of watery greens. Romaine is a supplement to pellets, not a complete food.

faq.q: Do cockatiels need greens if they eat pellets?
faq.a: Pellets should form most of the diet, but fresh vegetables and greens, up to about a fifth to a quarter of daily food, add variety, enrichment and extra nutrients.

faq.q: Can cockatiels eat the romaine stalk?
faq.a: Yes. The crunchy rib is safe; many cockatiels enjoy chewing it, though the leafy parts hold more nutrients.

cockatiel.notes: VCA's pet-bird fruit and vegetable list names romaine; VCA's cockatiel page warns against pale, watery lettuces and notes cockatiels are vulnerable to vitamin A deficiency.

hamster.short: Better not. Iceberg lettuce is mostly water with very little nutrition, and vets advise leaving it out. Darker greens such as romaine are a better choice.
prep: Offer a small piece of romaine or another darker leafy green instead
Remove any iceberg leftovers from the enclosure
hamster.risks: Iceberg lettuce is mostly water and provides little nutritional value, so it takes up space in a tiny stomach without adding much. Watery leaves eaten in quantity can also soften droppings. It is not toxic.
hamster.ifEaten: A nibble is not an emergency. Remove any leftover pieces, make sure fresh water and pellets are available, and watch the droppings for a day or two. Contact a vet if your hamster develops diarrhoea, a wet or dirty bottom, or stops eating.

faq.q: Is iceberg lettuce poisonous to hamsters?
faq.a: No, it is not toxic. Vets leave it out because it is mostly water and offers very little nutrition; darker leafy greens make better use of your hamster's small daily fresh-food allowance.

hamster.notes: VCA ('do not give your rodent iceberg lettuce') and PetMD both advise against it on nutritional grounds, not toxicity. 'Avoid' reflects low value, and a nibble needs no treatment.

budgie.short: Better not. Iceberg lettuce is mostly water with very little nutrition, so it fills a budgie up without adding much. It is not toxic, and a nibble is harmless.
budgie.portion: Not recommended. If you offer any, keep it to a torn piece about 2 cm (3/4 in) across
prep: Offer romaine, kale or dandelion leaves instead
If you do give iceberg, wash it first
Use only a small torn piece
Remove leftovers within a few hours
budgie.risks: Iceberg is not poisonous. The problem is that it is pale and watery and offers little, so it can crowd out more nutritious foods, and large amounts may briefly make droppings wetter.
budgie.ifEaten: No action is needed. If droppings stay very watery for more than a day, or your budgie seems fluffed up, quiet or off its food, contact an avian vet, as that suggests illness rather than the lettuce.

faq.q: Is iceberg lettuce poisonous to budgies?
faq.a: No. It is not toxic, but avian vets do not recommend it because it is mostly water and has little nutritional value. Darker greens are a better use of a budgie's small appetite.

faq.q: Will iceberg lettuce give my budgie diarrhoea?
faq.a: It can make droppings look wetter for a few hours because of its water content. That is not true diarrhoea; ongoing loose droppings need a vet check.

budgie.notes: VCA: iceberg or head lettuce is not recommended because it is mostly water with little nutritional value. Popular claims that iceberg is toxic are not supported; 'avoid' reflects low value, not danger.

cockatiel.short: Better not. Iceberg lettuce is pale and watery and gives cockatiels almost nothing they need. It is not poisonous, so a stolen bite is nothing to worry about.
cockatiel.portion: Not recommended. If you offer any, keep it to a torn piece about 3 cm (1 in) across
prep: Swap it for romaine, kale, dandelion leaves or other dark greens
If you give iceberg at all, wash it
Keep the piece small
Take away uneaten pieces after a few hours
cockatiel.risks: Iceberg is not toxic, but it has little nutritional value. Filling up on it leaves less room for pellets and nutrient-rich vegetables, and the high water content can make droppings wetter.
cockatiel.ifEaten: Nothing needs to be done. If your cockatiel has watery droppings for more than a day or seems unwell, see an avian vet, since the lettuce is unlikely to be the cause.

faq.q: Why do vets say not to feed iceberg lettuce to cockatiels?
faq.a: Because it is mostly water and has little nutritional value. Cockatiels are prone to vitamin A deficiency, so darker greens are far more useful.

cockatiel.notes: VCA's cockatiel page specifically names iceberg or head lettuce as offering little nutritional value.

hamster.short: Yes, in small amounts. Vet and welfare sources list spinach as suitable, but it is high in oxalate, so offer it now and then as part of a rotation rather than every day.
hamster.portion: One small leaf, about 2–3 cm (1 in) across, for a Syrian; about half that for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: Once or twice a week
prep: Wash thoroughly, including bagged baby spinach
Serve raw and plain, never creamed, buttered or salted
Tear into small pieces
Remove uneaten leaves the next day
hamster.benefits: A source of vitamins A and K, folate and some fibre.
hamster.risks: Spinach is rich in oxalate, which binds calcium. Because bladder stones are not uncommon in hamsters, rotating spinach with other greens is a sensible precaution, though this is based on its nutrient content rather than a documented hamster problem. Like other watery leaves, too much can soften droppings.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat baby spinach?
faq.a: Yes. Baby spinach is the same plant picked young. Wash it and offer a small leaf once or twice a week.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat cooked spinach?
faq.a: Plain raw spinach is better. Spinach cooked for the family often contains butter, salt, cream or garlic, which are not suitable for hamsters.

hamster.notes: PDSA, UC Davis, PetMD and San Diego Humane Society all list spinach as suitable. 'Limit' rather than 'yes' is our precaution based on spinach's high oxalate content; no fetched source specifically restricts spinach for hamsters. Veterinary Partner notes bladder stones are not uncommon in hamsters but says they generally do not respond to dietary change, so the oxalate concern is theoretical.

budgie.short: Yes, in small amounts. Spinach is nutritious and listed by vets as suitable, but it is rich in oxalate, which binds calcium, so offer it now and then rather than as the main green.
budgie.portion: One or two baby spinach leaves, or about 1 teaspoon chopped

Offer a whole baby leaf or chop it finely
Serve raw or plainly steamed, with nothing added
Rotate with lower-oxalate greens such as romaine, kale and dandelion
budgie.benefits: Spinach provides beta-carotene, vitamin K, folate and iron.
budgie.risks: Spinach is high in oxalic acid, which binds calcium and limits how much of the leaf's calcium a bird can absorb. Seed-heavy diets are already low in calcium, so spinach should be one green among many rather than a daily staple.

faq.q: Is spinach bad for budgies?
faq.a: No. It is not toxic, and veterinary feeding guides list spinach among suitable foods for budgies. The caution is its oxalate content, which reduces calcium absorption, so it is best fed in rotation rather than every day.

faq.q: Can budgies eat cooked spinach?
faq.a: Plain steamed spinach is fine. Never offer spinach cooked with butter, salt, garlic or other seasonings.

budgie.notes: Disagreement: VCA lists spinach as suitable for budgies with no caveat; LafeberVet (Pollock) notes that plant calcium digestibility is limited by binding to oxalate or phytate. No bird study shows harm from normal spinach portions; 'limit' is a cautious call based on calcium binding.

cockatiel.short: Yes, in small amounts. Spinach is safe for cockatiels, but its oxalate binds calcium, and cockatiels are prone to calcium deficiency and egg-binding, so keep it an occasional green.

cockatiel.frequency: Once or twice a week, mixed with other greens
prep: Rinse well
Chop into small pieces or offer a whole leaf
Serve raw or plainly steamed
Make lower-oxalate greens such as kale, romaine and dandelion the everyday choice
cockatiel.benefits: Spinach adds beta-carotene, vitamin K, folate and iron to the diet.
cockatiel.risks: Oxalic acid in spinach binds calcium, so little of its calcium is usable. Calcium deficiency is particularly common in cockatiels and can lead to weakness, seizures and egg-binding in laying hens, so spinach should not be relied on as a calcium source or fed every day.

faq.q: Should I avoid spinach if my cockatiel hen is laying eggs?
faq.a: Keep it occasional and focus on a pellet-based diet. Chronic egg laying drains calcium, and cockatiels are prone to egg-binding, so ask your avian vet about her calcium needs.

faq.q: Is spinach a good calcium source for cockatiels?
faq.a: Not really. It contains calcium, but oxalate binds much of it. Pellets and lower-oxalate greens are more dependable.

cockatiel.notes: VCA's pet-bird list includes spinach; VCA's cockatiel page and Illinois (Marrow) highlight calcium deficiency and egg-binding in cockatiels; LafeberVet notes oxalate limits plant calcium digestibility. 'limit' chosen for caution.

hamster.short: Yes, in small pieces. PDSA lists kale as a suitable vegetable for hamsters. Rotate it with other greens rather than feeding it every day.
hamster.portion: A piece of leaf about 2 cm (¾ in) square for a Syrian; about half that for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: 2–3 times a week, as part of a rotation
prep: Wash well
Strip the leaf from the thick central stem
Tear or chop into small pieces
Serve raw and plain
hamster.benefits: Provides fibre, vitamins A, C and K and some calcium.
hamster.risks: Kale belongs to the cabbage family and is fairly rich in calcium; offering it in rotation rather than daily avoids overdoing any one vegetable. At treat-sized portions no specific problem is known. Large amounts of any new green can upset digestion.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat kale stems?
faq.a: The thick central rib is tough and fibrous. It is not toxic, but it is better to strip it off and offer only the leafy part in small pieces.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat kale chips?
faq.a: No. Kale chips are usually coated in oil and salt or other seasonings. Offer plain raw kale instead.

hamster.notes: PDSA lists kale among suitable vegetables; VCA approves leafy greens in general. Rotation advice is a general precaution for brassicas, not from a hamster-specific source.

budgie.short: Yes. Kale is one of the more nutritious greens you can give a budgie, offering beta-carotene and calcium. Wash it, strip the tough stem and chop it small.
budgie.portion: A leaf piece about 5 cm (2 in) square, or 1–2 teaspoons finely chopped
budgie.frequency: 2–4 times a week, rotated with vegetables outside the cabbage family
prep: Wash well
Strip the leaf from the tough central stem
Chop finely or clip a piece to the cage
Serve raw or plainly steamed, with nothing added
budgie.benefits: Kale provides beta-carotene (for vitamin A), vitamin K, vitamin C and calcium.
budgie.risks: Kale is safe in normal portions. Like other cabbage-family plants it contains compounds that can interfere with iodine use in very large amounts; budgies are prone to iodine deficiency on all-seed diets, so rotate kale with other greens. There is no evidence that normal portions cause problems.

faq.q: Can budgies eat kale every day?
faq.a: It is better not to. Kale is in the cabbage family, whose goitrogens can interfere with iodine use, and budgies are the species most prone to goiter. Offer it a few times a week and rotate it with greens outside the cabbage family, such as romaine and dandelion.

faq.q: Raw or cooked kale for budgies?
faq.a: Raw is fine and keeps more vitamin C. Plain steamed kale is also fine; never add butter, salt or garlic.

budgie.notes: VCA lists kale among suitable foods for budgies. The goitrogen comment is an extrapolation from brassica chemistry plus the known budgie iodine-deficiency risk on seed diets (Merck); no study shows harm from kale in budgies.

cockatiel.short: Yes. Kale is a nutritious regular green for cockatiels, supplying beta-carotene and calcium that seed-heavy diets lack. Wash it and offer it chopped or as a whole leaf to shred.
cockatiel.portion: A leaf piece about 8 cm (3 in) square, or about 2 teaspoons chopped
cockatiel.frequency: Several times a week, alongside other vegetables
prep: Rinse the leaves thoroughly
Remove the thick central rib
Chop or tear into cockatiel-sized pieces
Serve raw or lightly steamed with no seasoning
cockatiel.benefits: Kale is rich in beta-carotene, vitamin K and vitamin C and contains calcium, which is useful for cockatiels, a species prone to vitamin A and calcium deficiencies.
cockatiel.risks: Kale is safe in normal amounts. Very large quantities of cabbage-family greens could in theory affect iodine use, so vary the greens rather than feeding kale alone.

faq.q: Is kale good for cockatiels?
faq.a: Yes. It is one of the better greens for them, as long as it is part of a varied mix and the base diet is pellets.

faq.q: Can cockatiels eat kale stems?
faq.a: The thin stems are fine; the thick central rib is tough and less nutritious, so it is easier to strip it off.

cockatiel.notes: VCA's pet-bird list includes kale. Goitrogen caution is theoretical.

hamster.short: Yes, if unsprayed. A vet-reviewed guide lists dandelion greens as suitable for hamsters. Pick them only from places free of chemicals and animal traffic, and wash well.
hamster.portion: One small leaf, about 3 cm (1¼ in) long, for a Syrian; half a small leaf for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: 2–3 times a week, rotating with other greens
prep: Only pick from ground never treated with weedkiller, slug pellets or fertiliser, away from roads and dog-walking areas
Wash thoroughly
Tear into small pieces
Introduce gradually if your hamster has not had it before
hamster.benefits: Rich in vitamins A and K and a source of calcium and fibre; hamsters often enjoy the bitter leaves.
hamster.risks: The main risk is contamination of wild-picked plants with pesticides, herbicides or animal waste. Dandelion leaves are also relatively rich in calcium and, like other greens, can soften droppings if a lot is eaten at once.

faq.q: Can I pick dandelions from my garden for my hamster?
faq.a: Yes, as long as the area has never been treated with weedkiller, slug pellets or fertiliser and is not used by dogs, cats or wildlife. Wash the leaves well before feeding.

faq.q: Are shop-bought dandelion greens OK?
faq.a: Yes. Salad-grade dandelion greens sold for people are a convenient option. Wash them as you would any leafy green.

hamster.notes: Only PetMD (DVM-reviewed) among the fetched sources names dandelion greens for hamsters. Popular claims that dandelion is a strong diuretic for hamsters could not be confirmed in veterinary sources; the rotation advice is a general precaution. Flowers and roots were not assessed.

budgie.short: Yes. Dandelion leaves are a nutritious green for budgies, provided they come from ground that has not been sprayed or fouled. Wash them well before serving.
budgie.portion: One or two small leaves, or about 1–2 teaspoons chopped
prep: Pick only from places free of weedkillers, fertilisers, traffic fumes and animal waste, or buy them
Wash thoroughly and shake dry
Offer a whole leaf or chop it finely
Remove leftovers after a few hours
budgie.benefits: Dandelion greens provide beta-carotene, vitamin K and calcium, and whole leaves make good foraging material.
budgie.risks: The main risk is contamination: lawn or roadside dandelions may carry herbicides, pesticides or droppings from other animals, and birds are very sensitive to pesticides.

faq.q: Can I pick dandelions from my garden for my budgie?
faq.a: Yes, if you know the ground has not been treated with weedkiller or fertiliser and is not used by dogs or cats. Wash them well first.

faq.q: Can budgies eat dandelion leaves every day?
faq.a: They can be part of the daily fresh food, but rotating them with other greens and vegetables gives a better range of nutrients.

budgie.notes: VCA lists dandelion leaves as suitable for budgies and for pet birds generally, and advises washing produce because birds are very sensitive to pesticides.

cockatiel.short: Yes. Dandelion leaves are a safe, nutritious green for cockatiels. Use leaves from unsprayed ground or a shop, and wash them first.
cockatiel.portion: Two or three leaves, or about 2 teaspoons chopped
prep: Collect only from areas you know are free of sprays, fertiliser and animal waste
Rinse well
Offer whole leaves for shredding or chop them
Take away wilted leftovers after a few hours
cockatiel.benefits: Dandelion leaves add beta-carotene, vitamin K and calcium, and whole leaves encourage natural foraging.
cockatiel.risks: Contamination is the concern: garden and roadside plants may carry pesticides, herbicides or droppings, and birds are very sensitive to these chemicals.

faq.q: Are dandelions safe for cockatiels?
faq.a: Yes. Dandelion leaves appear on veterinary lists of suitable foods for pet birds. Just make sure they have not been sprayed.

cockatiel.notes: VCA's pet-bird list includes dandelion leaves.

hamster.short: Yes, in small amounts. PDSA lists parsley among occasional treats for hamsters. A sprig now and then is plenty.
hamster.portion: One small sprig (2–3 leaves) for a Syrian; a single leaf for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: Once or twice a week
prep: Wash well
Use fresh curly or flat-leaf parsley
Remove thick stems
Remove any uneaten parsley the next day
hamster.benefits: An aromatic herb that adds variety and scent for foraging; contains vitamins A, C and K.
hamster.risks: Parsley is not toxic to hamsters. It is more concentrated in calcium and oxalate than lettuce-type greens, which is one reason to keep it an occasional herb rather than a staple. Large amounts of any herb can upset digestion.

faq.q: Is parsley toxic to hamsters?
faq.a: No. PDSA lists it as a safe occasional treat. The reason to limit it is to keep the diet varied and avoid overdoing calcium- and oxalate-rich greens.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat parsley stems?
faq.a: Thin stems are fine in small amounts. Thick, woody stems are best removed.

hamster.notes: PDSA lists parsley under 'other occasional treats'. The calcium/oxalate reasoning is based on nutrient content, not a documented hamster problem.

budgie.short: Yes, in small amounts. A board-certified avian vet lists parsley as safe, but it has caused sun sensitivity in ducks and ostriches that ate a lot, so keep it to a sprig mixed with other greens.
budgie.portion: One small sprig (a few leaves)
budgie.frequency: Two or three times a week, mixed with other greens
prep: Wash well
Offer a plain sprig of flat-leaf or curly parsley, or chop it
Mix it with other greens rather than serving a pile of parsley
Remove leftovers after a few hours
budgie.benefits: Parsley supplies beta-carotene, vitamin C and vitamin K and adds variety and scent to fresh food.
budgie.risks: Parsley contains natural compounds that can make skin more sensitive to sunlight. A 1988 report described parsley-induced photosensitivity in ostriches and, experimentally, in ducks. No cases in budgies have been reported, so the concern is large amounts, not a sprig.

faq.q: Is parsley toxic to budgies?
faq.a: Not in normal amounts. It appears on some 'toxic' lists because of reports in ducks and ostriches that ate a lot of it, while a board-certified avian vet lists parsley as safe for pet birds. A sprig a few times a week is a sensible middle ground.

faq.q: Can budgies eat parsley stems?
faq.a: Yes, the soft stems are fine. Wash them and offer them with the leaves.

budgie.notes: Disagreement: parsley appears on some owner-facing 'toxic' lists. Perelman & Kuttin (1988) documented photosensitisation in ostriches (natural outbreak) and ducks (experimental). Stephanie Lamb, DVM, DABVP (Avian) states the entire parsley plant is safe for pet birds. No psittacine cases found. The PubMed abstract does not name the compounds; attributing the effect to furanocoumarins is general plant chemistry. 'limit' chosen as the cautious middle.

cockatiel.short: Yes, in small amounts. Parsley is considered safe for cockatiels by an avian vet, but large amounts caused sunlight sensitivity in other birds, so offer a sprig or two as part of mixed greens.
cockatiel.portion: One or two sprigs
cockatiel.frequency: Two or three times a week
prep: Rinse thoroughly
Offer plain sprigs or chop them into a vegetable mix
Avoid serving large bunches on their own
Take away leftovers after a few hours
cockatiel.benefits: Parsley adds beta-carotene, vitamin C and vitamin K, and whole sprigs are good for foraging.
cockatiel.risks: Parsley contains compounds that can cause photosensitivity. This was documented in ostriches and ducks that ate large amounts; it has not been reported in cockatiels, so moderation is the safeguard.

faq.q: Can cockatiels eat parsley every day?
faq.a: It is safer as one of several rotating greens a few times a week rather than a daily staple, because of reports of sun sensitivity in other birds that ate large amounts.

cockatiel.notes: Same evidence as for budgies: avian-vet statement that parsley is safe versus a photosensitisation report in ostriches and ducks. 'limit' chosen for caution.

hamster.short: Yes, in small amounts. Fresh coriander (cilantro) is on PDSA's list of occasional treats for hamsters. A sprig now and then is plenty.
hamster.portion: One small sprig (2–3 leaves) for a Syrian; a single leaf for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: Once or twice a week
prep: Wash well
Offer fresh leaves and thin stems only
Do not use dried spice blends or seasoning mixes
Remove any uneaten herb the next day
hamster.benefits: Adds scent and variety to foraging; contains vitamins A and K.
hamster.risks: Cilantro has no known toxicity for hamsters. It is limited mainly to keep the diet balanced, and because sudden large amounts of any fresh greens can upset a hamster's digestion.

faq.q: Is coriander the same as cilantro?
faq.a: Yes. In the UK the leaves are called coriander and in North America cilantro. The fresh leaves are the part to offer.

hamster.notes: PDSA lists coriander among occasional treats; no other fetched source discusses it. Coriander seed (the spice) was not assessed.

budgie.short: Yes. Fresh cilantro (coriander leaf) is a safe herb for budgies and a good way to add variety to their greens. Wash it and offer a plain sprig.
budgie.portion: A small sprig, or about 1 teaspoon chopped
budgie.frequency: Several times a week, as part of mixed greens
prep: Wash well
Offer leaves and soft stems as a sprig or chopped
Serve fresh and plain, never from salsa or seasoned dishes
Remove leftovers after a few hours
budgie.benefits: Cilantro provides beta-carotene, vitamin C and vitamin K, and a sprig or whole plant makes good foraging enrichment.
budgie.risks: No specific toxicity is known. Wash shop-bought herbs to remove residues, and do not share cilantro from human dishes, which often contain salt, onion or garlic.

faq.q: Can budgies eat coriander seeds?
faq.a: An avian vet notes that the whole fresh plant, including its seed heads and flowers, can be given. Spice blends are best avoided because they may contain salt or other spices.

faq.q: Is cilantro the same as coriander?
faq.a: Yes. Cilantro is the leaf of the coriander plant; the name differs between countries.

budgie.notes: Only one avian-vet source (Stephanie Lamb, DABVP Avian) addresses cilantro directly and describes the entire plant as edible for pet birds. No reports of harm found. VCA cited for general produce-washing advice.

cockatiel.short: Yes. Cilantro is a safe fresh herb for cockatiels, and many enjoy picking through a whole sprig. Wash it and serve it plain.
cockatiel.portion: One or two sprigs, or about 2 teaspoons chopped
cockatiel.frequency: Several times a week, as part of mixed greens
prep: Rinse well
Offer sprigs whole for foraging or chop into a vegetable mix
Use plain herb only, not leftovers from seasoned food
Take away wilted leftovers after a few hours
cockatiel.benefits: Cilantro contains beta-carotene, vitamin C and vitamin K and is a useful foraging item.
cockatiel.risks: No known toxicity. The risks are pesticide residues on unwashed herbs and seasonings such as salt, onion and garlic in human dishes.

faq.q: Can I grow cilantro for my cockatiel?
faq.a: Yes. An avian vet recommends home-grown cilantro as a safe foraging plant, including the flowers and seed heads, as long as it is not sprayed.

cockatiel.notes: Single direct avian-vet source; no contrary evidence found.

hamster.short: Yes, in small amounts. Plain rolled oats are a common grain in hamster mixes and fine as a small extra. Keep them to a few flakes for dwarf hamsters, which are prone to diabetes.
hamster.portion: About ½ teaspoon of plain rolled oats for a Syrian; a small pinch (a few flakes) for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: 2–3 times a week
prep: Use plain, uncooked rolled or whole oats
Avoid instant oat sachets, granola and flavoured or sweetened oats
Serve dry, with no milk, sugar, honey or syrup
Scatter a few flakes to encourage foraging
hamster.benefits: Oats supply starch for energy plus some fibre and protein, and scattered flakes encourage natural foraging.
hamster.risks: Oats are mainly starch, so large amounts add calories and can crowd out the balanced pellet diet. Instant and flavoured oat products may contain sugar, salt or dried fruit.
hamster.dwarf: Campbell's, Winter White, hybrid and Chinese hamsters are prone to diabetes. Keep oats to a few flakes once or twice a week, and never use sweetened oat products.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat porridge or oatmeal?
faq.a: Plain oats cooked in water and cooled are not harmful in a tiny amount, but soft porridge spoils quickly if hoarded. Never use porridge made with milk, sugar, honey or syrup.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat granola or oat bars?
faq.a: No. These usually contain sugar, honey, syrup, chocolate or dried fruit, and bars can be sticky. Stick to plain rolled oats.

hamster.notes: No fetched veterinary source names oats specifically. San Diego Humane Society describes hamster mixes as containing grains, and Hamster Society (Singapore) uses oats in its hamster treat recipes. Status reasoned from oats being a plain, low-sugar grain; total extras should stay under about 10% of the diet (Merck, VCA). Dwarf note based on PDSA and ExoCare diabetes guidance.

budgie.short: Yes, in small amounts. Plain oats are safe for budgies, but they are starchy and low in calcium, so keep them an occasional extra rather than a staple.
budgie.portion: About 1/2 teaspoon of plain rolled oats or cooked plain oatmeal
prep: Use plain oats with no sugar, salt, flavouring or milk
Offer a small pinch of dry rolled oats, or cook them in water
Let cooked oats cool to lukewarm or room temperature
Remove cooked oats within a few hours, before they spoil
budgie.benefits: Oats supply energy, some protein and fibre, and a pinch can add variety.
budgie.risks: Grains are energy-dense and poor in calcium, and budgies are prone to obesity. Instant or flavoured oats often contain sugar and salt, and damp cooked grain left in the cage can grow bacteria or mould.

faq.q: Can budgies eat raw oats?
faq.a: Yes. Plain dry rolled oats are fine in a small pinch; they do not need cooking.

faq.q: Can budgies have porridge made with milk?
faq.a: No. Make it with water only. Birds digest lactose poorly, and sweetened porridge adds sugar they do not need.

budgie.notes: No avian-vet source names oats specifically. Inferred from sources that allow limited whole grains (Illinois: 'limited grains'; Pollock handout: whole grain products in small amounts), note grains are poor calcium sources (LafeberVet), and warn that mouldy cereal grains can carry fungal toxins (Lafeber).

cockatiel.short: Yes, in small amounts. Plain oats are a safe grain for cockatiels, dry or cooked in water, but they add starch rather than the vitamins and calcium cockatiels most need.
cockatiel.portion: About 1 teaspoon of plain rolled oats or cooked plain oatmeal
prep: Choose plain oats with nothing added
Serve a pinch dry, or cook in water only
Cool cooked oats before serving
Clear away leftovers within a few hours
cockatiel.benefits: Oats provide energy and fibre and make a soft, warm-texture food some cockatiels like.
cockatiel.risks: Oats are starchy and low in calcium and vitamin A, both nutrients cockatiels often lack. Flavoured instant oats contain sugar and salt, and wet oats spoil quickly.

faq.q: Are oat groats in seed mixes good for cockatiels?
faq.a: They are safe, but like other seeds and grains they are low in key vitamins and minerals, so seed mixes should not be the main diet.

cockatiel.notes: Inferred from general guidance on limited grains; no source names oats for cockatiels.

hamster.short: Yes, in small amounts. A few grains of plain cooked rice are not harmful, but rice adds starch and little else, spoils fast when hoarded, and must never be seasoned.
hamster.portion: 3–5 grains of plain cooked rice for a Syrian; 1–2 grains for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: Once a week at most
prep: Cook in plain water with no salt, oil, butter or stock
Let it cool completely
Offer a few separate grains, not a sticky clump
Remove leftovers within a few hours, as cooked rice spoils quickly
hamster.benefits: A bland, easily digested starch. It offers little that a pellet diet does not already provide.
hamster.risks: Cooked rice is starchy, low in fibre and goes off quickly if stored in the nest or cheek pouches. Leftover rice from human meals often contains salt, oil, soy sauce, onion or garlic, which are not suitable for pets.
hamster.dwarf: For diabetes-prone dwarfs (Campbell's, Winter White, hybrids and Chinese hamsters), rice is best skipped or limited to a single grain now and then.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat fried rice or leftover takeaway rice?
faq.a: No. Fried and takeaway rice usually contain oil, salt, soy sauce, onion or garlic. Only plain, unseasoned rice is suitable.

faq.q: Is brown rice better than white rice for hamsters?
faq.a: Plain brown rice has a little more fibre, but both are starchy foods that should stay a rare extra.

hamster.notes: No fetched source discusses rice for hamsters. Verdict reasoned from starch content, spoilage of hoarded food (Blue Cross), general treat limits (Merck, VCA) and ASPCA's warnings on onion, garlic and salt.

budgie.short: Yes, in small amounts. Plain cooked rice, especially brown rice, is safe for budgies. Keep it a small side dish so it does not crowd out pellets and vegetables.
budgie.portion: About 1/2 teaspoon of cooked rice (a thumbnail-sized amount)
prep: Cook in plain water with no salt, butter, oil or seasoning
Let it cool to room temperature
Mix with finely chopped vegetables if you like
Remove leftovers within a few hours, as cooked rice spoils quickly
budgie.benefits: Brown or wild rice provides energy, some fibre and B vitamins, and mixing it with chopped vegetables can encourage a budgie to try new foods.
budgie.risks: Rice is mostly starch and low in calcium, so large amounts dilute a balanced diet. Cooked rice left at room temperature can grow bacteria, and rice cooked for people is often salted, buttered or fried.

faq.q: Is white rice as good as brown rice for budgies?
faq.a: White rice is safe but less nutritious. Brown or wild rice keeps more fibre and B vitamins.

faq.q: Can I give my budgie leftover rice from dinner?
faq.a: Only if it was cooked completely plain. Fried rice, seasoned rice or rice cooked in stock can contain salt, oil, onion or garlic.

budgie.notes: VCA lists brown rice among suitable foods for budgies; the LafeberVet handout (Pollock) lists wild rice among foods for small amounts; Illinois advises limited grains.

cockatiel.short: Yes, in small amounts. Plain cooked rice is safe for cockatiels, and brown rice is the better choice. Serve it cool and unseasoned, as a small extra.
cockatiel.portion: About 1 teaspoon of cooked rice
prep: Cook in unsalted water with no butter or oil
Cool completely before serving
Stir in chopped vegetables to add nutrients
Discard leftovers within a few hours
cockatiel.benefits: Brown or wild rice adds energy, fibre and B vitamins and is a useful base for mixing in vegetables.
cockatiel.risks: Rice is starchy and low in calcium and vitamin A. It spoils quickly once cooked, and restaurant or family rice dishes often contain salt, fat, onion or garlic.

faq.q: Can cockatiels eat uncooked rice?
faq.a: Cooked rice is the better option. Dry raw rice is hard and offers little; cooked plain rice or a little brown rice mixed with vegetables is more useful.

cockatiel.notes: VCA's pet-bird list includes brown rice; Pollock handout lists wild rice. The FAQ avoids repeating the unverified 'rice expands in the stomach' claim either way.

hamster.short: Yes, in small amounts. Vets list plain whole wheat bread as a hamster treat. Keep it tiny and dry, and never offer bread with butter, spreads, garlic or raisins.
hamster.portion: A cube about 1 cm (⅜ in) across of plain wholemeal bread for a Syrian; a crumb about half that size for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: Once a week at most
prep: Choose plain wholemeal (whole wheat) bread
Offer it dry or lightly toasted rather than soft and doughy
Add no butter, jam, peanut butter or other spreads
Remove uneaten pieces before they go mouldy
hamster.benefits: Wholemeal bread supplies some fibre and carbohydrate and is a handy hand-feeding treat for taming.
hamster.risks: Bread is starchy and often salty, soft bread can form a doughy lump in the cheek pouches, and hoarded bread goes mouldy. Garlic bread, raisin bread and sweet or chocolate spreads add real risks. Raw yeast dough is dangerous because it expands and produces alcohol.
hamster.dwarf: Diabetes-prone dwarfs are better off with a crumb at most, or none. Skip white, sweet or enriched breads entirely.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat white bread?
faq.a: A crumb is not harmful, but white bread is more refined and lower in fibre than wholemeal. If you offer bread at all, choose plain wholemeal.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat bread with butter or peanut butter?
faq.a: No. Spreads add fat, salt and sometimes sugar or sweeteners, and sticky spreads can cling inside the cheek pouches.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat raw bread dough?
faq.a: No. Raw yeast dough can expand in the stomach, and the yeast produces alcohol, which is toxic to pets. Contact a vet if your hamster eats some.

hamster.notes: MedVet and San Diego Humane Society list whole wheat bread as a treat. PetMD advises avoiding most human foods other than fresh produce, so we chose 'limit' with small, infrequent portions. The soft-bread cheek-pouch concern is reasoned from Blue Cross's description of impacted pouches; no fetched source names bread as a cause. Yeast dough warning from ASPCA.

budgie.short: Yes, in small amounts. A crumb of plain wholegrain bread or toast is not harmful, but bread offers little and often contains salt and sugar. Never offer mouldy bread.
budgie.portion: A crumb about 1 cm (⅜ in) square of plain wholegrain bread or toast
prep: Choose plain wholegrain bread with no garlic, onion, chocolate, sweet toppings or sugar-free sweeteners
Check that it is completely free of mould
Toast it lightly and let it cool; dry pieces are less sticky
Do not soak bread in milk or water
Remove any leftover pieces the same day
budgie.benefits: Wholegrain bread provides some carbohydrate and fibre; its main value is as a familiar, occasional treat.
budgie.risks: Most bread contains added salt and often sugar and fat, which small birds do not need. Mouldy bread can contain fungal toxins, and soft or soaked bread spoils quickly in the cage. Raw bread dough is dangerous because the yeast keeps rising and produces alcohol.

faq.q: Is bread bad for budgies?
faq.a: A crumb of plain wholegrain bread is not harmful, and an avian vet includes wholegrain bread or toast among foods that can be given in small amounts. It is a low-value filler, though, so vegetables are a better use of a budgie's appetite.

faq.q: Can budgies eat white bread?
faq.a: A crumb will not hurt, but white bread has less fibre and fewer nutrients than wholegrain, so there is no reason to make it a habit.

budgie.notes: LafeberVet handout (Pollock, DABVP Avian) lists whole grain bread or toast among foods that may be offered in small amounts. VCA advises avoiding processed foods but does not name bread. Mould concern from Lafeber's note on mouldy cereal grains; raw dough hazard from ASPCA. The widely repeated idea that soft bread sticks in the crop was not found in any avian-vet source; toasting is suggested only as a simple precaution.

cockatiel.short: Yes, in small amounts. Plain wholegrain bread or toast is safe for cockatiels as a rare treat, but it is low in nutrients and usually salted. Never give mouldy bread or raw dough.
cockatiel.portion: A piece about 2 cm (3/4 in) square of plain wholegrain bread or toast
prep: Use plain wholegrain bread without garlic, onion, chocolate, sweet toppings or sugar-free sweeteners
Make sure there is no mould anywhere on the loaf
Toast lightly and cool
Offer a small dry piece rather than soaked bread
Remove leftovers the same day
cockatiel.benefits: Wholegrain toast gives a little fibre and is an easy food to share as a treat.
cockatiel.risks: Bread is mostly starch with added salt, and often sugar and fat, so it adds calories without the vitamin A and calcium cockatiels need. Mould can produce toxins, and uncooked yeast dough can expand and produce alcohol.

faq.q: Can cockatiels eat bread every day?
faq.a: No. Treat it as an occasional crumb. Daily bread would displace pellets and vegetables and add unnecessary salt.

faq.q: What kind of bread is best for cockatiels?
faq.a: Plain wholegrain bread or toast with no toppings, seeds coated in salt, or garlic. Sweet breads and flavoured crackers are not suitable.

cockatiel.notes: VCA's cockatiel page says to avoid processed foods like cookies, crackers or chips (bread not named); Pollock handout allows whole grain bread or toast in small amounts.

hamster.short: Yes, in small amounts. VCA lists pasta among occasional hamster treats. Offer it plain, with no sauce, salt, oil, garlic or cheese.
hamster.portion: One or two small pieces of plain cooked pasta, about 1 cm (⅜ in), for a Syrian; one tiny piece for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: Once a week
prep: Cook in unsalted water with no oil
Let it cool
Cut into small pieces
Remove leftovers the same day
hamster.benefits: A bland carbohydrate treat; wholewheat pasta adds a little fibre.
hamster.risks: Pasta is starchy and adds calories without much nutrition. Leftover pasta from human meals usually carries salt, oil, sauce, onion, garlic or cheese, which are not suitable.
hamster.dwarf: For diabetes-prone dwarfs, keep pasta to a tiny piece now and then, or skip it.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat uncooked pasta?
faq.a: Cooked plain pasta is the safer choice. Dry pasta snaps into hard, sharp shards that could scratch or pierce the cheek pouches, so if you offer it dry at all, use a small, smooth piece and count it as a treat.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat pasta with sauce?
faq.a: No. Sauces usually contain salt, sugar, oil, onion, garlic or cheese. Only plain pasta is suitable.

hamster.notes: VCA, MedVet and Veterinary Partner all mention pasta as an acceptable small extra; VCA does not say whether cooked or dry. PetMD's general advice to avoid human foods is the more cautious view, so portions here are small and infrequent.

budgie.short: Yes, in small amounts. Plain cooked pasta is safe for budgies and many enjoy it, but take their portion out before any sauce, salt, butter or cheese goes on.
budgie.portion: One or two pieces of a small pasta shape, or about 1/2 teaspoon
prep: Cook in unsalted water
Take the budgie's portion out before adding sauce, butter, oil or cheese
Cut into small pieces and let it cool
Remove leftovers within a few hours
budgie.benefits: Plain pasta gives energy and a soft texture birds often accept readily, and wholewheat pasta adds fibre. Veterinary guides suggest moist foods such as pasta as a carrier for crushed pellets when converting a bird from seeds.
budgie.risks: Pasta is starchy and low in calcium and vitamin A, so it should stay a small extra. The real dangers are the additions: salt, butter, oil, garlic, onion and cheese sauces.

faq.q: Can budgies eat spaghetti with sauce?
faq.a: No. Pasta sauces usually contain onion, garlic, salt and oil. Offer a plain noodle taken out before the sauce is added.

faq.q: Is wholewheat pasta better for budgies?
faq.a: Yes. It has more fibre, although either kind should remain an occasional extra.

budgie.notes: VCA uses cooked pasta as a moist carrier for pellet conversion; Lafeber (Pollock) suggests a plain noodle before sauce, salt or butter; Pollock handout lists pasta among foods for small amounts.

cockatiel.short: Yes, in small amounts. Cockatiels can have plain cooked pasta as an occasional treat. Serve it cool, unsalted and before any sauce, butter or cheese is added.
cockatiel.portion: Two or three small pieces, about 1 teaspoon
prep: Boil in water without salt
Set the cockatiel's share aside before adding anything
Cool and chop into small pieces
Clear away leftovers within a few hours
cockatiel.benefits: Plain pasta is an easy, soft food, and sprinkling crushed pellets on it can help a seed-eating cockatiel accept pellets.
cockatiel.risks: It is mainly starch with little vitamin A or calcium. Sauces, salt, butter, garlic, onion and cheese are what make human pasta dishes unsuitable.

faq.q: Can cockatiels eat pasta with pesto or tomato sauce?
faq.a: No. These sauces contain garlic, salt, oil and often cheese. Only plain, unseasoned pasta is suitable.

cockatiel.notes: VCA's cockatiel page uses cooked pasta as a moist carrier for crushed pellets.

hamster.short: Yes, in small amounts. VCA lists unsalted popcorn as a hamster treat. It must be plain and air-popped, with no butter, salt, sugar or flavouring, and hard kernels removed.
hamster.portion: One or two plain popped pieces for a Syrian; one small piece for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: Once a week at most
prep: Air-pop plain kernels with no oil, butter, salt or sugar
Do not use microwave-bag, caramel, cheese or buttered popcorn
Remove unpopped and half-popped kernels and loose hulls
Break into small pieces
hamster.benefits: A light treat that hamsters enjoy carrying and foraging for.
hamster.risks: Buttered, salted, caramel or flavoured popcorn adds fat, sodium and sugar. Hard unpopped kernels and sharp hull fragments are a concern because sharp pieces of food can occasionally pierce the cheek pouches.
hamster.dwarf: Popcorn is starch from corn. For diabetes-prone dwarfs, keep it to a single small piece now and then.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat salted or buttered popcorn?
faq.a: No. Salt and butter make it unsuitable. Only plain, air-popped popcorn is appropriate, and only a piece or two.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat unpopped popcorn kernels?
faq.a: Better not. They are very hard, offer no benefit and could injure the cheek pouches. Remove them before offering popcorn.

hamster.notes: VCA explicitly names 'unsalted popcorn' as an occasional treat. The kernel/hull caution is reasoned from Blue Cross's note that sharp pieces of food can pierce the cheek pouches.

budgie.short: Better not. Veterinary guides list popcorn among salty foods never to feed budgies. Plain air-popped popcorn is not toxic, but most popcorn is salted, buttered or flavoured.
budgie.portion: Not recommended. If offered at all, one plain, fully popped piece with no salt, butter or oil
prep: Never share cinema, microwave or flavoured popcorn
If you offer any, air-pop plain kernels with no oil, salt or butter
Remove unpopped kernels and loose hulls
Give a single piece and remove leftovers
budgie.risks: Most popcorn carries salt, butter, oil, sugar or flavourings, and small birds are sensitive to salt. Plain popcorn itself is not poisonous but offers almost nothing nutritionally, and unpopped kernels are very hard.
budgie.ifEaten: One piece of plain popcorn needs no action. If your budgie ate salted or buttered popcorn, make sure fresh water is available and watch over the next day for heavy drinking, very wet droppings, wobbliness or lethargy. Contact an avian vet if you see these or if it ate more than a small piece.

faq.q: Is plain air-popped popcorn safe for budgies?
faq.a: It is not toxic, and some bird keepers use it as a treat, but it offers little nutrition and veterinary feeding guides advise against popcorn for budgies. Fresh vegetables or a little spray millet make better treats.

faq.q: What if my budgie ate a piece of salted popcorn?
faq.a: A single piece is unlikely to cause harm. Provide fresh water and watch for heavy drinking or wobbliness; call an avian vet if it ate several pieces or seems unwell.

budgie.notes: Disagreement with popular advice: many owner-facing websites recommend plain air-popped popcorn as a treat. VCA's budgie page lists popcorn with chips and pretzels as very salty foods that should never be fed; the Veterinary Center for Birds and Exotics lists popcorn among salty snacks. No avian-vet source found endorsing popcorn. Chose 'avoid' as the cautious status.

cockatiel.short: Better not. Popcorn as people eat it is salty, buttery or sugary, which cockatiels should not have. Plain air-popped popcorn is not toxic, but it adds nothing useful.
cockatiel.portion: Not recommended. If offered at all, one or two plain, fully popped pieces with no salt, butter or oil
prep: Do not share cinema, microwave, caramel or flavoured popcorn
If you offer any, air-pop plain kernels with no fat or salt
Pick out unpopped kernels and hulls
Offer only a piece or two and remove leftovers
cockatiel.risks: Salted and buttered popcorn gives a small bird a load of salt and fat; caramel and kettle corn add sugar. Plain popcorn is mostly starch with little nutritional value, and unpopped kernels are hard.
cockatiel.ifEaten: A piece of plain popcorn needs no action. After salted, buttered or sweet popcorn, provide fresh water and watch for heavy drinking, watery droppings, weakness or wobbling, and call an avian vet if they appear or if a large amount was eaten.

faq.q: Why do some sites say popcorn is fine for cockatiels?
faq.a: Plain air-popped popcorn is not poisonous, so some keepers use it as a treat. Veterinary sources group popcorn with salty snacks to avoid, and it offers little nutrition, so we suggest other treats.

cockatiel.notes: VCA's cockatiel page does not name popcorn but says to avoid processed snacks like chips; VCA's budgie page and VCBE list popcorn among salty foods. 'avoid' chosen for caution; differs from common internet advice.

hamster.short: Yes, in small amounts. Millet is a small seed found in many hamster mixes. It is fine as a treat, but seeds should be limited so they do not replace the balanced pellets.
hamster.portion: A small pinch of loose millet, or a 1–2 cm (½–¾ in) piece of millet spray, for a Syrian; about half that for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: 1–2 times a week
prep: Use plain millet or millet spray, not seed sticks bound with honey or molasses
Scatter or hide it to encourage foraging
Count it as a treat, not part of the main ration
hamster.benefits: Encourages natural foraging, and millet is much lower in fat than oil seeds such as sunflower.
hamster.risks: Millet is mostly starch. Hamsters that fill up on seeds may skip their pellets, which can lead to an unbalanced diet and weight gain. Seed sticks and bars are often bound with honey or molasses, adding sugar.
hamster.dwarf: Keep millet to a few grains now and then for Campbell's, Winter White, hybrid and Chinese hamsters, and avoid honey- or molasses-coated millet treats completely.

faq.q: Is millet spray safe for hamsters?
faq.a: Yes, a small piece occasionally. Choose plain millet spray rather than sticks or bars bound with honey or molasses, which Blue Cross advises avoiding.

hamster.notes: No fetched source names millet specifically. VCA lists seeds as occasional treats, Merck says seeds should be limited, and Blue Cross suggests seed sprays for foraging while warning against seed sticks containing molasses or honey. Veterinary Partner advises largely avoiding high-fat seeds; millet is relatively low in fat, so 'limit' was chosen.

budgie.short: Yes, in small amounts. Millet is a budgie favourite but is low in many nutrients, and budgies that fill up on it can become poorly nourished or overweight.
budgie.portion: About 2–3 cm (1 in) of spray millet, or a small pinch (about 1/4 teaspoon) of loose millet
budgie.frequency: Spray millet only occasionally (one veterinary guide suggests once or twice a month for pellet-fed budgies); loose millet can be part of a small daily seed portion of no more than about a tenth of the diet
prep: Break off a short piece rather than hanging a whole spray
Check that it is dry, clean and free of mould or insects
Use it for training or foraging rather than filling the bowl
Count it as part of the day's seed, not an extra
budgie.benefits: Millet is very palatable, which makes small pieces useful for hand-taming, training and foraging games.
budgie.risks: Millet is low in vitamin A, calcium and protein and high in carbohydrate. Budgies choose it over better foods, and seed-heavy diets are linked to obesity, fatty liver, lipomas, iodine deficiency (goitre) and vitamin A deficiency.

faq.q: Can budgies eat millet every day?
faq.a: A small pinch of loose millet can be part of a daily seed ration, but spray millet is best kept as an occasional treat. Most of the diet should be pellets plus vegetables.

faq.q: Why does my budgie only eat millet?
faq.a: Budgies prefer tasty, high-carbohydrate seeds. Offer other foods first and millet only as a reward, and ask an avian vet about a gradual switch to pellets.

budgie.notes: Sources disagree on how much seed small parrots should get: Merck (Hoppes) suggests 40–50% pellets and 30–40% seed mix for budgerigars and cockatiels; RSPCA says small parrots need some seed daily but no more than a tenth of the diet; VCA says millet spray only once or twice a month. Portion and frequency follow the more cautious VCA/RSPCA end. PDSA's budgie diet page (reported by search to call millet sprays a very occasional treat) could not be opened and is not cited.

cockatiel.short: Yes, in small amounts. Cockatiels love millet, but it is nutritionally poor, and seed-heavy diets leave cockatiels short of vitamin A and calcium. Use it as a treat or training reward.
cockatiel.portion: About 3–5 cm (1–2 in) of spray millet, or a small pinch (about 1/2 teaspoon) of loose millet
cockatiel.frequency: Spray millet a few times a month as a treat; loose millet can be part of a small daily seed portion of no more than about a tenth of the diet
prep: Offer a short length, not a whole spray
Make sure it is dry and free of mould or insects
Use pieces as training rewards or hide them for foraging
Reduce other seeds on days you give millet
cockatiel.benefits: Millet is highly motivating, which makes it an excellent training reward and foraging item.
cockatiel.risks: Millet is low in vitamin A, calcium and protein. Cockatiels are prone to vitamin A deficiency, calcium deficiency and egg-binding, and diets built mainly on seed are linked to obesity and fatty liver disease.

faq.q: Is spray millet bad for cockatiels?
faq.a: Not in small amounts. The problem is quantity: a cockatiel given unlimited millet tends to eat little else.

faq.q: How much seed should a cockatiel eat?
faq.a: Veterinary and welfare advice varies. A cautious guide is seed at no more than about a tenth of a small parrot's diet, with pellets and vegetables making up the rest.

cockatiel.notes: Same disagreement on seed proportion as for budgies (Merck 30–40% seed mix vs RSPCA 10% vs VCA 'very small part'). VCA's cockatiel page gives no specific millet frequency; the budgie page's once-or-twice-a-month figure was adapted loosely.

hamster.short: Yes, in small amounts. Plain, unsalted sunflower seeds are a classic hamster treat, but they are about half fat, so one or two a few times a week is plenty.
hamster.portion: 1–2 seeds for a Syrian; 1 seed for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: 2–3 times a week at most
prep: Use plain raw or dry-roasted seeds with no salt or flavouring
Shelled or in-shell seeds are both fine
Hand-feed or hide them rather than adding them to the bowl
Cut back if the main food is already a seed-heavy mix
hamster.benefits: Hamsters love them, which makes them useful for hand-taming, and they contain protein and vitamin E.
hamster.risks: Sunflower seeds are about half fat by weight. Hamsters readily pick seeds over pellets, and VCA notes that seeds are high in fat and poor in overall nutrition, and that hamsters are prone to obesity. Salted or flavoured seeds add sodium and seasonings.
hamster.dwarf: Dwarf hamsters are small and prone to diabetes, which extra weight does not help. One seed at a time, a few times a week, is enough.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat salted sunflower seeds?
faq.a: No. Choose unsalted, unflavoured seeds. Snack-style seeds are often heavily salted or coated in seasoning.

faq.q: My hamster only eats the sunflower seeds from its mix. Is that a problem?
faq.a: Yes, it can be. Selective eating of seeds leads to an unbalanced, high-fat diet. Vets and welfare charities recommend a pelleted food as the main diet, with seeds only as treats; ask your vet how to switch gradually.

hamster.notes: PetMD calls plain sunflower seeds 'a great occasional treat'; VCA lists seeds as occasional treats; Merck says seeds should be limited; Veterinary Partner says high-fat nuts and seeds 'should largely be avoided'. 'Limit' with very small portions reconciles these. The 'about half fat' figure is standard food-composition knowledge, not from a fetched hamster source.

budgie.short: Yes, in small amounts. Sunflower seeds are very high in fat and low in calcium, and budgies are prone to obesity and fatty tumours, so treat them as a rare reward.
budgie.portion: One or two hulled kernels, or one seed in its shell
budgie.frequency: Once or twice a week, ideally as a training reward
prep: Use plain, raw, unsalted seeds
Never use roasted, salted or flavoured snack seeds
Break a kernel into pieces for a small budgie
Store seeds dry and discard any that smell rancid or look mouldy
budgie.benefits: Sunflower kernels provide vitamin E and energy and are highly motivating as training rewards.
budgie.risks: Sunflower seeds are high in fat, low in calcium and short of key amino acids. Birds pick them out ahead of healthier foods, and high-fat seed diets are linked to obesity, fatty liver and lipomas, which budgies commonly develop.

faq.q: Are sunflower seeds bad for budgies?
faq.a: They are not toxic, but they are a high-fat treat. One or two kernels, once or twice a week, is plenty for a budgie; a mix that is mostly sunflower is not a suitable diet.

faq.q: Can budgies eat salted sunflower seeds?
faq.a: No. Snack seeds are salted or flavoured, and small birds are sensitive to salt.

budgie.notes: Merck: sunflower seeds are selected preferentially, low in calcium, deficient in essential amino acids and high in fat. VCA: lipomas common in budgies and linked to high-fat, all-seed diets.

cockatiel.short: Yes, in small amounts. Cockatiels love sunflower seeds, but they are fatty and low in calcium, and cockatiels that fill up on them often become overweight or short of nutrients.
cockatiel.portion: Two to four seeds
cockatiel.frequency: A few times a week, used as training rewards
prep: Use plain, raw, unsalted seeds
Avoid roasted, salted or flavoured snack seeds
Hand them out one at a time as rewards rather than in the bowl
Discard seeds that smell rancid or look mouldy
cockatiel.benefits: Sunflower seeds are energy-rich and contain vitamin E; their high appeal makes them effective training rewards.
cockatiel.risks: Seed mixes heavy in sunflower are high in fat and low in calcium and vitamin A. Cockatiels are prone to calcium and vitamin A deficiency, fatty liver disease and lipomas, and they tend to pick sunflower over healthier food.

faq.q: My cockatiel's seed mix is mostly sunflower. Is that a problem?
faq.a: Yes, if it is the main food. Veterinary sources describe sunflower-heavy diets as high in fat and deficient in calcium and other nutrients. Talk to an avian vet about gradually moving to pellets.

faq.q: Black or striped sunflower seeds for cockatiels?
faq.a: Either is fine as an occasional treat; the fat content matters more than the type.

cockatiel.notes: VCA's cockatiel page notes that black sunflower seeds are commonly offered but deficient in many nutrients.

hamster.short: Yes, in small amounts. A plain, unsalted pumpkin seed is fine as a treat, but like other seeds it is high in fat, so keep it to one now and then.
hamster.portion: 1 seed for a Syrian; half a shelled (green) seed for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: Once or twice a week
prep: Use raw or plain dry-roasted seeds with no salt, oil, sugar or spice
Rinse and dry seeds from a fresh pumpkin before offering
For small hamsters, use shelled green seeds broken into pieces
hamster.benefits: Contains protein, zinc and fibre (in the hull), and a seed in its shell gives some gnawing and foraging work.
hamster.risks: Pumpkin seeds are high in fat, so regular handfuls contribute to obesity. Salted, spiced or sugar-coated seeds are unsuitable. Whole seeds are large for the smallest dwarfs to pouch.
hamster.dwarf: For dwarfs, and especially tiny Roborovskis, offer only a small piece of a shelled seed, and not every week.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat seeds from a carved pumpkin?
faq.a: Yes, if the pumpkin was fresh, unpainted and not left out to go mouldy. Rinse and dry the seeds, and offer one plain seed occasionally.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat roasted pumpkin seeds?
faq.a: Only if they are roasted plain, without oil, salt or seasoning. Most shop-bought roasted pumpkin seeds are salted, so check the label.

hamster.notes: No fetched source names pumpkin seeds. Verdict follows general guidance on seeds: VCA (occasional treats; seeds high in fat), Merck (limit seeds), Veterinary Partner (largely avoid high-fat seeds).

budgie.short: Yes, in small amounts. Plain raw pumpkin seeds are not harmful, but like other oily seeds they are rich in fat, so a budgie needs only a fragment now and then.
budgie.portion: One seed, broken into small pieces
prep: Use plain, raw, unsalted seeds, either from a fresh pumpkin or shelled pepitas
If taken from a pumpkin, rinse off the pulp and use the same day or dry them fully
Never use roasted, salted or spiced snack seeds
Break into budgie-sized pieces
budgie.benefits: Pumpkin seeds contain protein, zinc, magnesium and unsaturated fat.
budgie.risks: They are energy-dense and fatty, which matters for a small bird prone to obesity and lipomas. Seeds sold as snacks are often roasted with salt or spices, and damp seeds can go mouldy.

faq.q: Can budgies eat pumpkin seeds with the shell on?
faq.a: They can pick at a whole seed, but the hull is tough for a small beak. A shelled seed broken into pieces is easier.

faq.q: Are pumpkin seeds better than sunflower seeds for budgies?
faq.a: Both are fatty treats. Neither should be a regular part of a budgie's diet; one small piece now and then is enough.

budgie.notes: No avian-vet source discusses pumpkin seeds specifically. Inferred from guidance that seeds and nuts should be small, occasional treats (RSPCA, Merck) and the fat sensitivity of budgies (VCA). Nutrient composition is general food-composition knowledge.

cockatiel.short: Yes, in small amounts. Plain raw pumpkin seeds are a safe occasional treat for cockatiels, but they are fatty, so one or two at a time is enough.
cockatiel.portion: One or two seeds
prep: Use raw, unsalted seeds or plain pepitas
Rinse and dry seeds taken from a fresh pumpkin
Skip roasted, salted or spiced seeds
Offer as a reward or hide in a foraging toy
cockatiel.benefits: Pumpkin seeds provide protein, zinc and magnesium, and cracking them gives cockatiels something to work on.
cockatiel.risks: High fat content adds calories quickly, and cockatiels are prone to obesity, fatty liver and lipomas. Salted snack seeds add sodium, and damp seeds can grow mould.

faq.q: Can cockatiels eat pumpkin flesh too?
faq.a: Yes. Plain raw or cooked pumpkin flesh is a nutritious vegetable for cockatiels and can be fed more freely than the seeds.

cockatiel.notes: No source names pumpkin seeds; VCA lists pumpkin (the vegetable) among suitable foods.

hamster.short: Yes, in small amounts. Plain, unsalted peanuts are fine as a rare treat, but they are high in fat. Never give salted, flavoured or mouldy peanuts, or peanut butter from the jar.
hamster.portion: Half a shelled peanut for a Syrian; a crumb-sized piece for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: Once a week
prep: Use plain, unsalted peanuts sold for people, raw or dry-roasted
Throw away any that look shrivelled, discoloured or mouldy
Break into small pieces
Do not give peanut butter straight from the jar
hamster.benefits: Provides protein and fat for energy, and hamsters find peanuts very tempting, which helps with hand-taming.
hamster.risks: Peanuts are high in fat and add weight quickly in a small animal. Mouldy peanuts can carry aflatoxins, which damage the liver, so use only fresh, human-grade nuts. Peanut butter is sticky and may cling inside the cheek pouches, and some brands contain salt, sugar or xylitol.
hamster.dwarf: Diabetes-prone dwarfs should have no more than a crumb-sized piece, and not every week.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat salted or honey-roasted peanuts?
faq.a: No. Salted, honey-roasted, chocolate-coated and flavoured peanuts add salt, sugar and other unsuitable ingredients. Use plain, unsalted peanuts only.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat peanut butter?
faq.a: Not by the lick. It is sticky, so it can stay lodged in the cheek pouches, and many brands contain salt, sugar or, occasionally, xylitol. If you use a tiny amount in a baked hamster treat, choose a plain peanut butter whose only ingredient is peanuts, with no salt, sugar, xylitol or other sweeteners. 'Sugar-free' and 'reduced-sugar' spreads are the ones most likely to contain xylitol.

faq.q: Are peanuts in the shell OK?
faq.a: Plain, unsalted in-shell peanuts sold for people are fine occasionally for a Syrian. Check that shells are clean and dry, and remember a whole peanut is more than a single portion.

hamster.notes: PDSA and VCA list 'nuts' as occasional treats without naming peanuts; Hamster Society (Singapore) uses unsalted, sugar-free peanut butter in a baked treat and warns about salt and sugar in commercial brands. Veterinary Partner advises largely avoiding high-fat nuts. The sticky-peanut-butter/cheek-pouch concern is reasoned from Blue Cross's description of impacted pouches; no fetched vet source names peanut butter specifically. Aflatoxin on peanuts from Merck.

budgie.short: Better not. Peanuts can carry aflatoxin, a mould toxin linked to liver damage in pet birds, and they are very fatty for a small budgie. Never give salted or coated peanuts.
budgie.portion: Not recommended. If given at all, a crumb of fresh, plain, human-grade peanut
prep: Choose safer treats such as a little millet or vegetables
Never offer salted, flavoured, candied or chocolate-coated peanuts
Never offer peanuts that look discoloured, shrivelled or mouldy
Do not use peanut butter, which is fatty and sticky and may contain salt, sugar or xylitol
budgie.risks: Peanuts, especially poorly stored or pet-grade ones, can be contaminated by moulds that produce aflatoxin. A veterinary reference links liver fibrosis and cirrhosis in pet birds to aflatoxin from improperly stored seed and pet-grade peanuts. Peanuts are also high in fat, and budgies are prone to obesity, fatty liver and lipomas.
budgie.ifEaten: A bite of a fresh, plain peanut is not an emergency. If your budgie ate salted peanuts, give fresh water and watch for heavy drinking or wobbliness. If it has been eating old or possibly mouldy peanuts, tell your avian vet, and seek help promptly for fluffed-up posture, poor appetite or unusual droppings.

faq.q: Are peanuts poisonous to budgies?
faq.a: Fresh, human-grade peanuts are not poisonous in themselves. The concern is aflatoxin from mould, which you cannot reliably see or smell, plus the high fat. An avian vet lists peanuts as not recommended.

faq.q: Can budgies eat peanut butter?
faq.a: Better not. It is very fatty, can contain salt and sugar, and some brands contain xylitol, which is dangerous to animals.

budgie.notes: Lafeber (Pollock) lists peanuts under 'not recommended but sometimes fed without incident'; Merck links hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis to aflatoxicosis from improperly stored seed and pet-grade peanuts; Merck Food Hazards notes xylitol in some peanut and nut butters. Note: the RSPCA suggests peanut butter as a flavour to coax parrots onto new foods during diet change, a minor disagreement. Human-grade, fresh peanuts carry lower but not zero risk. 'avoid' chosen over 'limit' for caution.

cockatiel.short: Better not. Peanuts are fatty and can carry aflatoxin, a mould toxin linked to liver disease in pet birds. They are common in cockatiel mixes, but safer treats exist.
cockatiel.portion: Not recommended. If given at all, a small piece of fresh, plain, human-grade peanut
prep: Pick seed mixes without peanuts, or remove them
Never offer salted, roasted-flavoured, candied or chocolate-coated peanuts
Never feed peanuts that are discoloured, shrivelled, musty or mouldy
Skip peanut butter, which may contain salt, sugar or xylitol
cockatiel.risks: Aflatoxin-producing moulds can grow on peanuts that are poorly stored, and chronic exposure has been linked to liver fibrosis and cirrhosis in pet birds. Peanuts are also high in fat, and cockatiels are prone to obesity, fatty liver disease and lipomas.
cockatiel.ifEaten: A piece of fresh, plain peanut is not an emergency. After salted peanuts, provide water and watch for heavy drinking or weakness. If your cockatiel has had regular access to old or mouldy peanuts, mention it to your avian vet, and get prompt help for lethargy, poor appetite or abnormal droppings.

faq.q: My cockatiel's seed mix contains peanuts. Should I remove them?
faq.a: It is sensible to. Peanuts add a lot of fat, and lower-grade peanuts are a recognised source of aflatoxin. If you keep them, buy fresh mixes and store them cool and dry.

faq.q: Are peanuts in the shell safer?
faq.a: The shell does not guarantee freedom from mould, and shells can themselves carry mould. Human-grade, fresh nuts are lower risk, but peanuts are still best kept out of the diet.

cockatiel.notes: As for budgies. 'Shells can carry mould' is general knowledge about stored peanuts, not a cited bird-specific finding.

hamster.short: Better not. A vet-reviewed guide lists almonds among foods hamsters should avoid. Bitter almonds contain cyanide-forming compounds, and even sweet almonds are hard, fatty nuts.
prep: Offer a small piece of plain unsalted peanut or a sunflower seed instead
Keep bitter almonds, almond extract, marzipan and apricot kernels away from your hamster
hamster.risks: Bitter almonds contain amygdalin, which releases hydrogen cyanide; one study measured roughly 40 times more cyanide in bitter than in sweet almonds. Sweet snack almonds contain far less, but they are high in fat and very hard, and salted or flavoured versions add further problems.
hamster.ifEaten: A small piece of plain sweet almond is not usually an emergency: remove the rest, make sure your hamster can empty its cheek pouches, and watch for diarrhoea or lethargy over the next day. If it ate a bitter almond, an apricot kernel or almond extract, or you see weakness, breathing difficulty, wobbliness or collapse, call a vet straight away.

faq.q: Are sweet almonds safe for hamsters?
faq.a: Sweet almonds are not highly toxic the way bitter almonds are, and some owners do offer them. We still suggest choosing another treat, because a vet-reviewed guide lists almonds as a food to avoid, and they are hard, fatty nuts that add nothing a pellet diet lacks.

faq.q: Can hamsters have almond butter or almond milk?
faq.a: No. Almond butter is sticky and fatty, and almond drinks often contain sugar or other additives. Neither is useful for hamsters.

hamster.notes: Sources disagree: PDSA and VCA list 'nuts' in general as occasional treats, and much popular advice says sweet almonds are fine in moderation, while PetMD (DVM-reviewed) lists almonds as a toxic food to avoid. We followed the more cautious source. PetMD does not distinguish sweet from bitter almonds. Chaouali et al. (2013) measured about 1062 mg/kg HCN in bitter almonds versus about 25 mg/kg in sweet almonds. No hamster-specific toxic dose was found. Not graded 'no' because plain sweet almond is not acutely toxic; the ifEaten text treats bitter almond or apricot kernel as a vet call.

budgie.short: Better not. Almonds are not toxic, but they are about half fat, and budgies are tiny birds prone to obesity and fatty tumours. If your budgie steals a sliver, it will not come to harm.
budgie.portion: Not needed. At most a sliver about the size of a grain of rice
prep: Offer vegetables or a little millet as treats instead
If you give any, use plain almond with no salt or flavouring
Shave off a tiny sliver
Never give salted, smoked, sugared or chocolate-coated almonds
budgie.benefits: Almonds contain vitamin E, calcium and unsaturated fat, but a budgie gets these more safely from pellets and greens.
budgie.risks: The concern is fat and calories rather than poison. Budgies commonly develop obesity, fatty liver disease and lipomas on high-fat diets, and even a small piece of nut is a large portion for such a small bird. Flavoured almonds add salt and sugar.
budgie.ifEaten: No action is needed for a nibble of plain almond. If your budgie ate salted or flavoured almonds, make sure fresh water is available and watch for heavy drinking, wobbliness or lethargy over the next day; call an avian vet if you see these.

faq.q: Do almonds contain cyanide that can poison budgies?
faq.a: Sweet almonds sold for eating contain only trace amounts of the compound that releases cyanide; bitter almonds contain much more and should never be given. The main reason to skip almonds for budgies is their fat.

faq.q: Can I give my budgie almond milk?
faq.a: No. It adds nothing a budgie needs, and many versions contain sugar or additives. Fresh water is the only drink it needs.

budgie.notes: No avian-vet source discusses almonds for budgies specifically. RSPCA and Merck allow nuts in very small amounts as occasional treats for parrots; the Veterinary Center for Birds and Exotics warns that the smaller the bird, the higher the risk from even a few bites of high-fat or high-salt food. Budgie: cautious 'avoid'; cockatiel: 'limit'. Popular advice often lists almonds as a healthy budgie treat. Sweet vs bitter almond chemistry is general knowledge.

cockatiel.short: Yes, in small amounts. A sliver of plain almond makes a good occasional reward for cockatiels, but almonds are high in fat, and cockatiels are prone to fatty liver and lipomas.
cockatiel.portion: A sliver about a quarter of one almond
prep: Use plain raw or dry-roasted almonds with no salt or flavouring
Chop into small slivers
Use pieces as training rewards rather than a bowl treat
Never give chocolate-, sugar- or salt-coated almonds
cockatiel.benefits: Almonds provide vitamin E, some calcium and unsaturated fat, and their crunch makes them a satisfying reward.
cockatiel.risks: Almonds are about half fat, so frequent or large portions add calories quickly, and high-fat diets are linked to obesity, fatty liver disease and lipomas in cockatiels. Salted and flavoured almonds add sodium and sugar.

faq.q: Can cockatiels eat almonds in the shell?
faq.a: Most cockatiels struggle to crack almond shells. Offer shelled slivers instead.

faq.q: Are almonds poisonous to cockatiels because of cyanide?
faq.a: No. Sweet almonds sold for eating contain only traces of the cyanide-releasing compound. Bitter almonds should never be given.

cockatiel.notes: Nuts are allowed in small amounts for parrots by RSPCA, Merck and the Pollock handout (which names walnuts and palm nuts, not almonds).

hamster.short: Yes, in small amounts. Plain shelled walnut is not known to be toxic to hamsters, but it is one of the fattiest nuts, and mouldy walnuts can carry dangerous toxins.
hamster.portion: A piece about the size of a pea for a Syrian; a crumb for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: Once a week at most
prep: Use fresh, plain, unsalted shelled walnuts sold for people
Throw away any that smell rancid or show mould or dark discolouration
Never offer walnuts picked up from the ground
Break into pea-sized pieces
hamster.benefits: Walnuts contain protein and polyunsaturated fats, and a small piece makes a high-value taming treat.
hamster.risks: Walnuts are very high in fat, which can contribute to obesity and digestive upset. Mouldy walnuts can contain tremorgenic mycotoxins, which cause tremors and seizures in dogs; that is the reason to use only fresh, human-grade nuts.
hamster.dwarf: For dwarfs, which are small and prone to diabetes, keep walnut to a crumb once in a while.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat walnuts in the shell?
faq.a: Whole walnuts are too big and hard for most hamsters, and old shells can hide mould. Offer a small piece of shelled walnut instead.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat candied or salted walnuts?
faq.a: No. Sugar, honey and salt coatings make them unsuitable.

hamster.notes: PDSA and VCA list 'nuts' as occasional treats but do not name walnuts; Veterinary Partner advises largely avoiding high-fat nuts. ASPCA names walnuts among high-fat nuts that can cause digestive upset in pets. Tremorgenic mycotoxin evidence comes from dogs (Merck); no hamster data found.

budgie.short: Better not. Walnuts contain healthy fats, but they are still very rich for a bird as small as a budgie, which is prone to obesity and lipomas. A crumb will not hurt.
budgie.portion: Not needed. At most a crumb about the size of a grain of rice
prep: Offer vegetables or a little millet as treats instead
If you give any, use a fresh, plain, unsalted walnut
Check the nut smells fresh, not rancid or musty
Crumble a tiny piece
budgie.benefits: Walnuts contain omega-3 alpha-linolenic acid and vitamin E.
budgie.risks: The issue is fat and calories. Budgies are prone to obesity, fatty liver and lipomas on high-fat diets, and a piece of walnut is a large dose of fat for such a small bird. Old walnuts can turn rancid or grow mould, and candied or salted walnuts add sugar and salt.
budgie.ifEaten: No action is needed for a nibble of plain walnut. If your budgie ate a large piece, salted or candied walnuts, or a mouldy nut, watch for lethargy, heavy drinking, wobbliness or changes in the droppings and call an avian vet if anything seems wrong.

faq.q: Aren't walnuts healthy for birds?
faq.a: They contain useful fats, and an avian vet lists walnuts among foods parrots can have in small amounts. For a budgie, though, even a small piece is a lot of fat, so they are best left out or kept to a crumb.

budgie.notes: Disagreement: the Pollock handout lists walnuts among foods that can be offered to pet birds in small amounts; VCBE cautions that the smaller the bird, the higher the risk from even a few bites of high-fat food. Budgie: cautious 'avoid'; cockatiel: 'limit'.

cockatiel.short: Yes, in small amounts. A pea-sized piece of plain walnut is a fine occasional treat for cockatiels, but walnuts are fatty, and cockatiels are prone to fatty liver and lipomas.
cockatiel.portion: A piece about the size of a pea
prep: Use fresh, plain, unsalted walnut halves
Check for a fresh smell; discard rancid, musty or mouldy nuts
Break into pea-sized pieces
Use as a training reward or foraging treat
cockatiel.benefits: Walnuts provide omega-3 alpha-linolenic acid and vitamin E, and an avian vet lists them among foods pet birds can have in small amounts.
cockatiel.risks: Walnuts are high in fat, so regular or large portions add up quickly. Rancid or mouldy nuts should never be fed, and candied or salted walnuts add sugar and salt.

faq.q: Can cockatiels crack walnuts?
faq.a: Most cannot crack a whole walnut shell. Offer shelled pieces, or a cracked shell with a little nut left inside as a foraging puzzle.

cockatiel.notes: Pollock handout names walnuts; RSPCA and Merck allow nuts as occasional treats; VCBE's caution about high-fat food in small birds applies to a lesser degree to cockatiels.

hamster.short: Yes, in small amounts. Plain, unsalted cashews are not known to be toxic to hamsters, but they are fatty, and most snack cashews are salted or flavoured.
hamster.portion: A quarter to half of one cashew for a Syrian; a crumb for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: Once a week at most
prep: Use plain, unsalted cashews sold for people
