Avoid salted, honey-roasted, spiced or chocolate-covered cashews
Break into small pieces
hamster.benefits: Provides protein and fat; useful as an occasional high-value treat.
hamster.risks: Cashews are high in fat, which can contribute to obesity. Salted and flavoured cashews add sodium, sugar or seasonings such as onion and garlic powder. Cashews are sold shelled because the shell contains irritant oils, so never offer anything from a whole cashew shell.
hamster.dwarf: For diabetes-prone dwarfs, a crumb-sized piece now and then is the most to give.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat salted cashews?
faq.a: No. Use only plain, unsalted cashews, and only a small piece.

faq.q: Are 'raw' cashews from the shop safe?
faq.a: Cashews sold as 'raw' have already been removed from the shell and processed for eating, so a small plain piece is fine. Never offer cashews still in their shell.

hamster.notes: No fetched source names cashews for hamsters; verdict follows general guidance on nuts (PDSA, VCA treats; Veterinary Partner largely avoid high-fat nuts). The shell-irritant point is general food knowledge, not from a fetched veterinary source.

budgie.short: Better not. Plain cashews are not toxic, but they are fatty and usually sold salted or roasted in oil, which makes them a poor choice for small budgies.
budgie.portion: Not needed. At most a crumb about the size of a grain of rice of plain, unsalted cashew
prep: Offer vegetables or a little millet as treats instead
If you give any, use plain, unsalted cashew
Never offer salted, honey-roasted or flavoured cashews
Crumble a tiny piece
budgie.risks: Cashews are high in fat, and budgies are prone to obesity, fatty liver and lipomas. Most cashews sold as snacks are salted or roasted in oil, and small birds are sensitive to salt.
budgie.ifEaten: No action is needed for a nibble of plain cashew. After salted or flavoured cashews, provide fresh water and watch for heavy drinking, wobbliness or lethargy, and call an avian vet if you see them.

faq.q: Are raw cashews toxic to budgies?
faq.a: Cashews sold as 'raw' in shops have already been shelled and heat-treated to remove the irritating shell oil, so they are not poisonous. The real issue for budgies is fat and, in snack cashews, salt.

budgie.notes: No avian-vet source discusses cashews specifically. The cashew shell-oil point is general food-processing knowledge; some internet lists wrongly call shop-bought raw cashews toxic to birds.

cockatiel.short: Yes, in small amounts. A small piece of plain, unsalted cashew is safe for cockatiels as an occasional treat, but cashews are fatty and usually sold salted, so choose carefully.
cockatiel.portion: A piece about a quarter of one cashew
prep: Buy plain, unsalted cashews
Never offer salted, honey-roasted or spiced cashews
Break into small pieces
Use as a reward rather than a bowl food
cockatiel.benefits: Cashews provide energy, some protein and minerals such as magnesium and zinc, and their soft crunch is popular as a reward.
cockatiel.risks: Cashews are high in fat, and cockatiels are prone to obesity, fatty liver and lipomas. Snack cashews add salt and sometimes sugar.

faq.q: Are raw cashews safe for cockatiels?
faq.a: Yes. Shop-bought 'raw' cashews have already had the irritating shell oil removed by processing. Choose unsalted ones and keep portions small.

cockatiel.notes: Inferred from general guidance on nuts for parrots; no source names cashews.

hamster.short: Yes, in small amounts. PDSA and Blue Cross list boiled egg as a good occasional protein treat for hamsters. Always cook it fully and serve it plain.
hamster.portion: A piece of hard-boiled egg about the size of your hamster's ear, roughly 1 cm (⅜ in), for a Syrian; about half that for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: Once or twice a week
prep: Hard-boil until both white and yolk are firm
Cool and peel, then offer white, yolk or a little of both
Add no salt, butter, mayonnaise or seasoning
Remove any uneaten egg within a few hours
hamster.benefits: Egg is an easily digested source of high-quality protein that adds variety alongside the pellet diet.
hamster.risks: Raw or undercooked egg can carry Salmonella, and raw egg white contains a protein (avidin) that binds the B vitamin biotin, so only fully cooked egg should be used. Yolk is rich in fat, and cooked egg spoils quickly if hoarded.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat raw egg?
faq.a: No. Raw egg can carry Salmonella, and raw egg white contains a protein that binds the B vitamin biotin. Always hard-boil the egg.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat scrambled egg?
faq.a: Plain scrambled egg cooked without butter, oil, milk or salt is similar to boiled egg and fine in a small piece. Most scrambled egg made for people contains butter and salt, so boiled is simpler.

hamster.notes: PDSA and Blue Cross both name boiled egg. PetMD says protein should come mainly from pellets and advises against most human foods, hence 'limit' rather than 'yes'. Raw egg risks from ASPCA (general pet guidance).

budgie.short: Yes, in small amounts. Hard-boiled egg is a good protein source that avian vets suggest for pet birds, but the yolk is rich, so offer a small crumbled portion.
budgie.portion: About 1/2 teaspoon of chopped hard-boiled egg (a thumbnail-sized amount)
budgie.frequency: Once or twice a week; your avian vet may suggest more for breeding or moulting birds
prep: Boil the egg until both white and yolk are completely firm
Cool it fully
Chop or mash finely; a little finely crushed boiled shell adds calcium
Add no salt, butter, oil or mayonnaise
Remove leftovers within an hour or two
budgie.benefits: Egg provides high-quality protein, which birds need more of during moult and egg laying, and cooked egg with its shell is a calcium source for pet birds.
budgie.risks: Egg yolk is rich in fat and cholesterol, so large or frequent portions add calories budgies do not need. Raw or undercooked egg can carry Salmonella, and cooked egg spoils quickly if left in the cage.

faq.q: Can budgies eat raw egg?
faq.a: No. Always cook egg until firm. Raw egg can carry Salmonella, and raw egg white contains a protein that binds the B vitamin biotin.

faq.q: Can budgies eat scrambled egg?
faq.a: Yes, if it is cooked through with no butter, oil, milk or salt. Hard-boiling is simplest.

budgie.notes: VCA uses cooked egg as a moist carrier food for budgies; the Pollock handout lists hard-boiled or scrambled egg with the shell as a calcium source; Merck notes higher protein needs during moult and laying. Raw egg risks from ASPCA (general pets).

cockatiel.short: Yes, in small amounts. Cockatiels can have a little hard-boiled egg as a nutritious treat. It is rich, so keep portions small and always cook it fully.
cockatiel.portion: About 1 teaspoon of chopped hard-boiled egg
cockatiel.frequency: Once or twice a week; your avian vet may suggest more for breeding or moulting birds
prep: Hard-boil until the yolk is completely set
Let it cool
Chop finely, with a little finely crushed boiled shell if you like
Serve with no salt, butter or seasoning
Take away leftovers within an hour or two
cockatiel.benefits: Egg is an excellent protein source, and hard-boiled egg with shell provides calcium, which is useful for cockatiels, a species prone to calcium deficiency.
cockatiel.risks: Yolk is fatty and cholesterol-rich, so too much adds unwanted calories. Raw egg can carry Salmonella and contains a biotin-binding protein, and cooked egg spoils fast at room temperature.

faq.q: Is egg good for a cockatiel that is laying eggs?
faq.a: Egg can help supply protein and, with shell, calcium, but a laying hen needs a vet-guided plan. Chronic laying depletes calcium and is linked to egg-binding in cockatiels.

faq.q: Can cockatiels eat egg shells?
faq.a: Boiled, finely crushed shell is a recognised calcium source for pet birds. Never offer raw shell.

cockatiel.notes: VCA's cockatiel page mentions cooked egg as an occasional table food and as a moist carrier for pellets.

hamster.short: Yes, in small amounts. Blue Cross lists lean cooked meat as a suitable fresh food for hamsters. Serve plain, fully cooked chicken with no skin, bones, salt or seasoning.
hamster.portion: A shred about 1 cm (⅜ in) long for a Syrian; about half that for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: Once or twice a week
prep: Boil, steam or bake the chicken plainly, with no salt, oil, onion, garlic or stock
Cook it thoroughly
Remove skin, fat and every bone
Shred into tiny pieces and remove leftovers within a few hours
hamster.benefits: Lean protein that suits a hamster's omnivorous diet and adds variety.
hamster.risks: Raw chicken can carry Salmonella and other bacteria. Seasoned or leftover chicken often contains salt, onion or garlic, which can damage red blood cells in pets, and cooked bones can splinter. Meat spoils quickly if hoarded in the nest.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat rotisserie or leftover chicken?
faq.a: Usually not. Rotisserie and leftover chicken is typically salted and seasoned, often with garlic or onion. Cook a plain piece specially instead.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat raw chicken?
faq.a: No. Raw chicken can carry Salmonella and other bacteria. Only thoroughly cooked, plain chicken is suitable.

hamster.notes: Blue Cross ('lean cooked meat') and MedVet ('cooked lean meats') support small portions. Onion/garlic and raw-meat warnings are from ASPCA's general pet guidance; the red-blood-cell effect is documented in cats and dogs rather than hamsters.

budgie.short: Yes, in small amounts. A shred of plain cooked chicken is safe for budgies now and then, but they are seed and plant eaters and get the protein they need from pellets.
budgie.portion: One or two small shreds, together about the size of a pea
prep: Use lean breast meat cooked right through
Remove skin and bones; add no salt, seasoning, oil or sauce
Cool and shred finely
Never offer raw or undercooked chicken
Remove leftovers within an hour or two
budgie.benefits: Lean chicken provides protein, which birds need more of during moult and breeding.
budgie.risks: Meat is not a natural part of a budgie's diet, and meat-heavy diets are discouraged for plant-eating parrots; they have been linked to iron storage disease in grey parrots. Raw chicken can carry Salmonella and E. coli, and skin or seasoned meat adds fat and salt.

faq.q: Do budgies need meat?
faq.a: No. Budgies are mainly seed and plant eaters, and a good pellet diet covers their protein needs. Meat is an optional, occasional extra.

faq.q: Can budgies eat chicken nuggets or seasoned chicken?
faq.a: No. Breaded, fried or seasoned chicken contains salt, fat and often onion or garlic. Only plain, unseasoned cooked meat is suitable.

budgie.notes: VCA's budgie page allows small portions of wholesome human food without naming meat; VCA's cockatiel page mentions small amounts of lean cooked meat (cited as the closest species evidence). Merck warns against carnivorous diets in herbivorous parrots (iron storage disease in grey parrots). VCBE warns fatty meat contributes to fat deposits. No source addresses meat for budgies directly.

cockatiel.short: Yes, in small amounts. Veterinary guides note some cockatiels enjoy a little lean cooked meat. Offer an occasional shred of plain cooked chicken, never raw, seasoned or fatty meat.
cockatiel.portion: A few small shreds, no more than about 1 teaspoon in total
prep: Use lean, skinless breast meat cooked through
Remove all bones
Add no salt, seasoning, oil or sauce
Shred finely and serve cool
Clear away leftovers within an hour or two
cockatiel.benefits: Plain chicken adds high-quality protein, which can be useful during moult.
cockatiel.risks: Cockatiels are mainly seed and plant eaters, and a meat-heavy diet is discouraged in plant-eating parrots because it has been linked to iron storage disease. Raw chicken can carry Salmonella and E. coli, and fatty or seasoned meat adds fat and salt.

faq.q: Is it strange for a cockatiel to eat chicken?
faq.a: Cockatiels are not meat eaters by nature, but a small amount of lean cooked meat is safe. It should stay a rare extra, not a regular part of the diet.

faq.q: Can cockatiels have chicken bones?
faq.a: No. Offer only boneless meat; cooked bones can splinter.

cockatiel.notes: VCA cockatiel: 'Some birds occasionally even enjoy a small amount of lean cooked meat'. Merck cautions against carnivorous diets for herbivorous parrots. Bone-splinter advice is a general precaution, not a cited bird-specific finding.

hamster.short: Yes, in small amounts. PDSA and Blue Cross list mealworms as a good protein treat for hamsters. They are rich in fat, so one or two a few times a week is enough.
hamster.portion: 1–2 dried mealworms for a Syrian; 1 for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: 2–3 times a week
prep: Buy mealworms sold as pet food or live food
Dried or freeze-dried mealworms are the simplest option
If you use live mealworms, hand-feed one at a time and never leave live insects loose in the enclosure
Check the nest so live worms are not being stored
hamster.benefits: A natural protein source; wild hamsters eat insects, and hand-feeding mealworms is enriching and helps build trust.
hamster.risks: Mealworms are high in fat, so too many contribute to weight gain. PetMD advises against live prey because hoarded live insects can injure a hamster or infest the enclosure.

faq.q: Are live or dried mealworms better for hamsters?
faq.a: Dried mealworms are easier and cannot escape or bite. If you prefer live ones, hand-feed them one at a time so none end up stored alive in the nest.

faq.q: How many mealworms can a hamster eat?
faq.a: A Syrian can have one or two a few times a week, and a dwarf one. Their high fat content is the reason to keep numbers low.

hamster.notes: PDSA and Blue Cross name mealworms; PetMD accepts freeze-dried mealworms but advises against live prey. We recommend dried mealworms as the default and hand-feeding if live ones are used.

budgie.short: Yes, in small amounts. A mealworm is not harmful to a budgie, but insects are poor in calcium, dried ones are calorie-dense, and pellet-fed budgies do not need them.
budgie.portion: One or two mealworms, live or dried
prep: Buy mealworms sold as animal food from a reliable supplier
Never collect wild insects, which may carry pesticides or parasites
Soak dried mealworms briefly in warm water if you like
Offer by hand or in a dish so you know how many were eaten
budgie.benefits: Mealworms are rich in protein and can be a novel foraging treat.
budgie.risks: Insects, including mealworms, are poor sources of calcium, and dried insects pack a lot of calories into a small piece. Budgies are mainly seed and plant eaters, so regular insect treats add energy without improving a pellet-based diet.

faq.q: Do budgies need mealworms for protein?
faq.a: No. A good pellet diet provides enough protein for a pet budgie. Mealworms are optional.

faq.q: Are dried mealworms better than live ones for budgies?
faq.a: Either is fine in tiny amounts. Dried ones are more concentrated, so one dried mealworm is plenty.

budgie.notes: No avian-vet source discusses mealworms for budgies or cockatiels. LafeberVet (Pollock): invertebrates are generally poor calcium sources; Finke (2015): commercial feeder insects including mealworms were poor calcium sources; Merck: some psittacines eat insects as a small part of the diet. Fat content was not quoted because no fetched source gives a mealworm figure.

cockatiel.short: Yes, in small amounts. Cockatiels can have the odd mealworm as a protein treat, but insects are poor in calcium, a nutrient cockatiels often lack, so keep them occasional.
cockatiel.portion: Two or three mealworms, live or dried
prep: Buy mealworms sold as animal food, never wild-caught insects
Rehydrate dried mealworms briefly in warm water if you like
Hand-feed or place in a foraging toy
Remove any uneaten live mealworms so they do not escape into the cage
cockatiel.benefits: Mealworms are high in protein and make an interesting foraging item.
cockatiel.risks: Insects are poor calcium sources, and cockatiels are prone to calcium deficiency and egg-binding. Dried mealworms are calorie-dense, and pellet-fed cockatiels do not need extra animal protein.

faq.q: Can mealworms help my cockatiel during moult?
faq.a: A few can add protein, but a balanced pellet diet already meets most needs. Ask your avian vet before adding extra protein for moult or breeding.

cockatiel.notes: As for budgies; no source addresses mealworms for cockatiels directly.

hamster.short: Yes, in small amounts. Hamster Society (Singapore) uses tofu in a protein treat for hamsters. Use plain tofu with no marinade, salt or sauce.
hamster.portion: A 1 cm (⅜ in) cube for a Syrian; about half that for a dwarf.
hamster.frequency: Once or twice a week
prep: Choose plain firm or silken tofu with no flavouring
Drain and pat dry
Do not use fried, smoked or marinated tofu, or anything with soy sauce, garlic or onion
Remove uneaten tofu within a few hours
hamster.benefits: A plant-based protein source that adds variety, useful for owners who prefer not to handle meat or insects.
hamster.risks: Plain tofu is not known to be harmful in small amounts. Flavoured and fried tofu often contains salt, soy sauce, oil, garlic or onion. Fresh tofu spoils quickly if hoarded.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat tofu straight from the pack?
faq.a: Yes. Tofu is cooked during manufacture, so a small piece of plain tofu can be offered without further cooking.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat fried or marinated tofu?
faq.a: No. Fried and marinated tofu usually contains oil, salt, soy sauce, garlic or onion. Use only plain tofu.

hamster.notes: Only Hamster Society (Singapore) discusses tofu for hamsters, as an ingredient in a baked protein treat; no veterinary source was found. Effects of soy compounds in pet hamsters are not addressed in the sources reviewed; small, infrequent portions keep any such concern minimal.

budgie.short: Yes, in small amounts. Plain tofu is a safe, lactose-free protein for budgies. Use unseasoned tofu and offer only a small cube now and then.
budgie.portion: A cube about 1 cm (⅜ in) across
prep: Use plain firm tofu with no marinade, salt, soy sauce or spices
Rinse and pat dry
Cut a small cube or crumble it; serve it as it comes or plainly steamed
Remove leftovers within a couple of hours, as tofu spoils quickly
budgie.benefits: Tofu provides plant protein, and tofu set with calcium sulfate also contains calcium.
budgie.risks: Tofu has no known toxicity for birds, but it is a processed food. Flavoured, fried or marinated tofu brings salt, oil and seasonings such as garlic or onion, and like any moist protein food it spoils if left out.

faq.q: Can budgies eat flavoured or fried tofu?
faq.a: No. Marinades and frying add salt, oil and seasonings. Only plain tofu is suitable.

faq.q: Is tofu a good protein source for budgies?
faq.a: It is a safe occasional extra, but pellet-fed budgies do not need added protein; vegetables should come first among fresh foods.

budgie.notes: No avian-vet source found that discusses tofu. Inferred: plain tofu is soybean curd with a coagulant; risks come from seasoning and spoilage. VCA (small portions of wholesome human food, avoid processed and oily foods) and Lafeber (avoid high-salt, high-fat table food) cited for the general principles only.

cockatiel.short: Yes, in small amounts. Plain, unseasoned tofu is a safe occasional protein for cockatiels and contains no lactose. Keep it a small extra alongside pellets and vegetables.
cockatiel.portion: A cube about 1.5 cm (1/2 to 3/4 in) across
prep: Choose plain firm tofu, ideally calcium-set
Rinse, pat dry and cut into small cubes or crumble
Add no soy sauce, salt, oil or spices
Discard leftovers within a couple of hours
cockatiel.benefits: Tofu offers plant protein, and calcium-set tofu adds some calcium, a mineral cockatiels often lack.
cockatiel.risks: Tofu is not known to be harmful, but seasoned, fried or marinated versions contain salt, oil and flavourings such as garlic. It spoils quickly once out of the fridge.

faq.q: Is tofu safer than cheese for cockatiels?
faq.a: In one respect, yes: tofu contains no lactose, which birds digest poorly. Plain tofu is also lower in salt than most cheeses.

cockatiel.notes: No source discusses tofu for cockatiels; reasoning as for budgies.

hamster.short: Better not. Cheese is high in fat and salt, and dairy can upset digestion. One vet hospital lists it as a treat, but safer protein treats such as boiled egg are available.
prep: Offer a small piece of hard-boiled egg, plain cooked chicken or a mealworm instead
Keep cheese snacks out of reach during free-roam time
hamster.benefits: Cheese contains protein and calcium, but a pelleted hamster food already supplies these.
hamster.risks: Most cheeses are high in fat and salt. Pets generally have little lactase, the enzyme that digests milk sugar, so dairy can cause diarrhoea or other digestive upset. Soft cheese can also smear inside the cheek pouches and spoils quickly if hoarded.
hamster.ifEaten: A crumb of plain cheese is not an emergency. Remove any leftovers, make sure your hamster has water, and watch for diarrhoea or a wet, dirty bottom over the next day or two. Contact a vet promptly if diarrhoea develops, as it can become serious quickly in hamsters.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat a little cheese?
faq.a: A crumb will not poison a hamster, and one veterinary hospital lists cheese among possible treats. Because of its fat, salt and lactose, we suggest boiled egg, cooked chicken or mealworms instead.

faq.q: Is low-fat cheese or cottage cheese better?
faq.a: Lower-fat cheese reduces one problem, but it still contains lactose and often salt. It is still not a useful food for hamsters.

hamster.notes: Sources disagree: MedVet lists cheese among treat ideas, while PetMD advises avoiding most human foods and ASPCA warns that dairy can cause diarrhoea in pets. Following the more cautious view, we chose 'avoid'. The lactase statement is ASPCA's general pet guidance, not hamster-specific research. UC Davis notes hamster diarrhoea ('wet tail') can be fatal within 24 hours, which supports prompt vet contact.

budgie.short: Better not. Birds digest lactose poorly, and cheese is also salty and fatty, which suits a tiny budgie badly. A crumb is unlikely to cause harm.
budgie.portion: Not recommended. At most a crumb smaller than a lentil of plain, mild cheese
prep: Offer hard-boiled egg or vegetables instead
Never give blue, strongly flavoured, heavily salted or processed cheese
If you offer a crumb, make it plain, mild hard cheese
Remove any leftovers promptly
budgie.benefits: Cheese contains protein and calcium, but pellets, greens and egg supply these without the fat, salt and lactose.
budgie.risks: Birds lack the enzyme to digest much lactose, so dairy can cause diarrhoea as the amount rises. Most cheeses are also high in fat and salt, and budgies are prone to obesity and sensitive to salt.
budgie.ifEaten: A crumb needs no action. If your budgie ate a larger amount you may see loose droppings for a day; keep fresh water available and contact an avian vet if diarrhoea persists or your budgie seems fluffed up, stops eating or drinks excessively.

faq.q: Is cheese toxic to budgies?
faq.a: No, it is not poisonous. Some veterinary guides allow very small amounts of cheese for pet birds, while a leading veterinary reference advises owners to avoid milk products. Given a budgie's size and sensitivity to fat and salt, it is best left out.

faq.q: Is low-lactose cheese all right for budgies?
faq.a: Aged hard cheeses contain little lactose, but they are still fatty and salty. A crumb is not harmful; it just offers nothing a budgie needs.

budgie.notes: Disagreement: VCA (cockatiel page) allows 'very small amounts of cheese' and dairy in moderation; Lafeber (Pollock) says low-lactose cheeses and yogurts can be occasional small treats; Merck (Hoppes) lists milk products among foods owners should avoid. Cautious 'avoid' chosen. Popular advice often says small pieces of cheese are fine.

cockatiel.short: Better not. Some vets allow a tiny taste, but birds digest lactose poorly and cheese is salty and fatty. A crumb will not hurt a cockatiel, but it is not a useful treat.
cockatiel.portion: Not recommended. At most a crumb about the size of a lentil of plain, mild cheese
prep: Choose egg, vegetables or a seed reward instead
Avoid blue, processed, smoked or heavily salted cheese
If you do share a crumb, keep it plain and mild
Remove leftovers promptly
cockatiel.benefits: Cheese supplies protein and calcium, but cockatiels get these more safely from pellets, egg and greens.
cockatiel.risks: Birds have little ability to digest lactose, so larger amounts of dairy can cause diarrhoea. Cheese is also high in fat and salt; cockatiels are prone to obesity and fatty liver, and small birds are sensitive to salt.
cockatiel.ifEaten: No action is needed for a crumb. After a larger amount, watch for loose droppings over the next day; contact an avian vet if diarrhoea persists or your cockatiel seems quiet, fluffed up or off its food.

faq.q: Some vets say cockatiels can have a little cheese. Why 'better not'?
faq.a: One veterinary feeding guide does allow very small amounts, but a leading veterinary reference lists milk products among foods to avoid. When credible sources differ we lean cautious, and cheese adds fat, salt and lactose without adding anything cockatiels need.

cockatiel.notes: Direct disagreement: VCA cockatiel page ('very small amounts of cheese') vs Merck (avoid milk products). Cautious status chosen.

hamster.short: Better not. Yogurt is a dairy food that can upset a hamster's digestion, and flavoured yogurts and yogurt drops add sugar, a particular problem for diabetes-prone dwarfs.
prep: Choose a protein treat such as boiled egg or a mealworm instead
Skip yogurt drops and yogurt-coated treats, which are typically high in sugar and fat
hamster.risks: Pets generally have little lactase, the enzyme that digests milk sugar, so dairy can cause diarrhoea. Flavoured yogurts, yogurt drops and yogurt-coated treats add sugar and fat, and some contain artificial sweeteners. Yogurt also spoils quickly if hoarded.
hamster.dwarf: Campbell's, Winter White, hybrid and Chinese hamsters are prone to diabetes. Sweetened yogurt and yogurt drops should be avoided completely.
hamster.ifEaten: A lick of plain yogurt is not an emergency. Remove any leftovers and watch for diarrhoea or a wet, dirty bottom over the next day or two. Call a vet if diarrhoea appears, or if your hamster seems lethargic or stops eating.

faq.q: Are yogurt drops safe for hamsters?
faq.a: They are sold as hamster treats, but they are typically high in sugar and fat. Blue Cross advises avoiding sugary, fatty treats, and dwarf hamsters are prone to diabetes, so we recommend skipping them.

faq.q: Does yogurt help a hamster with diarrhoea?
faq.a: No home remedy replaces a vet. Diarrhoea (wet tail) in hamsters can be fatal within a day or two, so contact a vet promptly rather than trying yogurt.

hamster.notes: No fetched source discusses yogurt for hamsters specifically. Verdict reasoned from ASPCA's general dairy warning, Blue Cross's advice to avoid sugary, fatty treats, and the diabetes risk in dwarfs (PDSA, ExoCare). Pet shops and many websites promote yogurt drops as hamster treats; we disagree for these reasons.

budgie.short: Better not. Yogurt has less lactose than milk, but birds still digest dairy poorly, and flavoured yogurts add sugar or sweeteners. A lick of plain yogurt is not harmful.
budgie.portion: Not recommended. At most a fingertip dab of plain, unsweetened yogurt
prep: Never offer flavoured, sweetened or 'light' yogurt, which may contain sugar or xylitol
If you offer any, use plain unsweetened yogurt only
Give a dab on a spoon rather than a dish
Remove leftovers promptly; yogurt spoils quickly in a warm room
budgie.benefits: Plain yogurt contains protein and calcium, and some owners offer it for its live cultures, though a benefit for birds has not been shown.
budgie.risks: Birds have little lactase, so dairy can cause diarrhoea as the amount increases. Flavoured yogurts add sugar, and some low-sugar products use xylitol, a sweetener that is dangerous to animals.
budgie.ifEaten: A dab of plain yogurt needs no action. If your budgie ate a spoonful or more, watch for loose droppings over the next day. If the yogurt was sugar-free or artificially sweetened, check the label for xylitol and call an avian vet if it is listed.

faq.q: Is yogurt a good probiotic for budgies?
faq.a: There is little evidence that yogurt cultures help birds. If your budgie needs a probiotic, ask an avian vet about a product made for birds.

faq.q: Can budgies eat Greek yogurt?
faq.a: Plain Greek yogurt is lower in lactose than milk but still dairy and fairly fatty. A dab will not hurt, but it is not a useful regular food.

budgie.notes: Disagreement: Lafeber (Pollock) says some yogurts are low in lactose and can be an occasional small treat; VCA says dairy in moderation; Merck lists milk products among foods to avoid. Cautious 'avoid' chosen. Popular advice often recommends plain yogurt as a probiotic treat; no bird-specific evidence for that benefit was found.

cockatiel.short: Better not. Birds digest dairy poorly, and most yogurts are sweetened. A small taste of plain yogurt will not hurt a cockatiel, but it offers little they need.
cockatiel.portion: Not recommended. At most a small dab (about 1/4 teaspoon) of plain, unsweetened yogurt
prep: Avoid flavoured, fruit, sweetened or sugar-free yogurts
If you share any, use plain unsweetened yogurt
Offer a dab on a spoon
Remove leftovers quickly
cockatiel.benefits: Plain yogurt contains protein and calcium; claimed probiotic benefits for birds are unproven.
cockatiel.risks: Lactose is poorly digested by birds, and larger amounts of dairy can cause diarrhoea. Sweetened yogurts add sugar, and sugar-free versions may contain xylitol.
cockatiel.ifEaten: A small taste of plain yogurt needs no action; watch for loose droppings after a larger amount. If the yogurt was sugar-free, look for xylitol on the label and contact an avian vet if it is present.

faq.q: Can cockatiels have yogurt drops or yogurt-coated treats?
faq.a: Better not. Yogurt coatings are mostly sugar and fat with added dairy, and offer nothing useful.

cockatiel.notes: Same disagreement as for budgies. Claim about yogurt-coated treats being mostly sugar and fat is general knowledge of such products.

hamster.short: No. Chocolate contains theobromine and caffeine, stimulants that can cause tremors, heart rhythm problems, seizures and death in animals. A hamster's tiny body makes small amounts risky.
hamster.risks: Chocolate's methylxanthines (theobromine and caffeine) overstimulate the nervous system and heart. Dark chocolate, baking chocolate and cocoa powder contain the most; white chocolate the least, though it is still sugary and fatty. No safe dose has been established for hamsters; the effects are documented mainly in dogs.
hamster.ifEaten: Call your vet or an animal poison helpline straight away, even if your hamster seems fine. Note the type of chocolate (dark, milk, white or cocoa) and roughly how much is missing. Rodents cannot vomit, so do not try home remedies. Remove any chocolate from the nest, and watch for restlessness, rapid breathing, trembling, wobbliness, diarrhoea or seizures.

faq.q: Is white chocolate safe for hamsters?
faq.a: No. White chocolate has the lowest theobromine content, but it is still sugary and fatty and offers nothing a hamster needs. Treat all chocolate as off-limits.

faq.q: My hamster ate a tiny crumb of chocolate. What should I do?
faq.a: Phone your vet for advice. A crumb of milk chocolate may cause no problems, but hamsters are so small that professional advice is worthwhile, especially for dark chocolate or cocoa.

hamster.notes: San Diego Humane Society lists chocolate among foods to avoid for hamsters. Toxicology (Merck, ASPCA) is documented mainly in dogs; Merck notes many species are susceptible. No hamster-specific toxic dose was found. Horn et al. (2013) conclude that the inability to vomit is a general property of rodents.

budgie.short: No. Chocolate contains theobromine and caffeine, which can cause heart rhythm problems, seizures and death in birds. A budgie is so small that even a little is dangerous.
budgie.risks: Theobromine and caffeine (methylxanthines) overstimulate the heart and nervous system, causing hyperactivity, a racing or irregular heart, tremors, seizures and potentially death. Dark chocolate and cocoa powder contain the most. A wild kea parrot died of methylxanthine poisoning after eating dark chocolate.
budgie.ifEaten: Call an avian vet or an animal poison control line straight away, even if your budgie seems fine, and have the packaging ready so you can say what type and roughly how much was eaten. Watch for restlessness, regurgitation, diarrhoea, trembling, rapid breathing and seizures. Do not try home remedies or try to make your bird bring food up.

faq.q: How much chocolate is toxic to a budgie?
faq.a: No safe dose has been established for birds. Because budgies are so small, even a small piece could be significant, so any amount is a reason to call your vet.

faq.q: Is white chocolate safe for budgies?
faq.a: White chocolate contains very little theobromine, but it is still fatty and sugary, and it is easy to misjudge what a product contains. Do not feed it, and call your vet if your budgie ate chocolate of any kind.

budgie.notes: Unanimous across sources. Kea case: Gartrell & Reid 2007 (about 20 g dark chocolate; acute methylxanthine toxicity). White-chocolate note from Merck Food Hazards.

cockatiel.short: No. Chocolate is toxic to cockatiels. Its theobromine and caffeine can trigger a racing heart, tremors, seizures and death, and darker chocolate is the most dangerous.
cockatiel.risks: Chocolate contains the methylxanthines theobromine and caffeine, which stimulate the heart and nervous system. Signs in birds include hyperactivity, increased heart rate, tremors and seizures, and death has been documented in a wild parrot that ate dark chocolate. Cocoa powder and dark chocolate carry the highest doses.
cockatiel.ifEaten: Treat any chocolate as an emergency: call an avian vet or animal poison control line immediately and keep the wrapper to report the type and amount. Watch for restlessness, trembling, rapid breathing, diarrhoea or seizures. Do not attempt home treatment.

faq.q: My cockatiel licked some chocolate. Is that serious?
faq.a: Call your vet for advice. A lick of milk chocolate is a much smaller dose than a piece of dark chocolate, but only a vet can judge the risk for your bird's weight and the product involved.

faq.q: Are chocolate-flavoured bird treats safe?
faq.a: Avoid anything containing cocoa or chocolate. There is no need to risk it when plenty of safe treats exist.

cockatiel.notes: VCA cockatiel page: never offer chocolate. Unanimous across sources.

hamster.short: No. Coffee, tea, energy drinks and cola contain caffeine, a stimulant that can cause hyperactivity, tremors, abnormal heart rhythm, seizures and death in pets. Keep grounds and drinks away.
hamster.risks: Caffeine is a methylxanthine, like the theobromine in chocolate, and it overstimulates the nervous system and heart. Coffee grounds and beans, tea leaves and bags, caffeine tablets and energy drinks are the most concentrated sources. No hamster-specific safe dose exists; the concern rests on its well-documented effects in other pets and the hamster's tiny size.
hamster.ifEaten: Call your vet or an animal poison helpline straight away, especially if your hamster ate coffee grounds, beans, tea leaves or a caffeine tablet, or drank more than a lick of a caffeinated drink. Rodents cannot vomit, so do not try home remedies. Watch for restlessness, rapid breathing, trembling or seizures.

faq.q: Can hamsters have decaf coffee or tea?
faq.a: No. Decaffeinated drinks still contain small amounts of caffeine and offer nothing a hamster needs. Fresh water is the only drink a hamster requires.

faq.q: Is herbal tea OK for hamsters?
faq.a: It is not needed, and herbal blends can contain plants that are not suitable for hamsters. Stick to fresh water.

hamster.notes: No fetched source discusses caffeine for hamsters specifically; verdict based on ASPCA and Merck guidance on methylxanthines in pets. The mechanism is well established across mammals.

budgie.short: No. Coffee, tea, cola and energy drinks contain caffeine, which can cause a racing heart, arrhythmias and hyperactivity in birds. Even a few sips can be dangerous for a budgie.
budgie.risks: Caffeine is a methylxanthine, like theobromine in chocolate. It overstimulates the heart and nervous system and can cause arrhythmias, hyperactivity, tremors and, in serious cases, cardiac arrest. Coffee grounds, tea leaves and caffeine tablets are concentrated sources.
budgie.ifEaten: Contact an avian vet straight away if your budgie drank coffee, tea, cola or an energy drink, or pecked at coffee grounds, tea leaves or caffeine tablets. Watch for restlessness, trembling, rapid breathing and seizures, and keep your bird warm and quiet on the way.

faq.q: Is herbal tea safe for budgies?
faq.a: Caffeine-free herbal teas are not covered by this warning, but some herbs have effects of their own. Fresh water is the only drink a budgie needs; ask your avian vet before using any herbal preparation.

faq.q: Can budgies drink decaf coffee?
faq.a: Better not. Decaffeinated coffee still contains a little caffeine and offers nothing a budgie needs.

budgie.notes: VCA lists caffeine products (coffee, tea, soda) among foods never to feed budgies; VCBE warns even a few sips can be extremely hazardous.

cockatiel.short: No. Caffeine in coffee, tea, cola and energy drinks can cause a fast or irregular heartbeat, hyperactivity and even cardiac arrest in birds. Keep cups and grounds away from cockatiels.
cockatiel.risks: Caffeine stimulates the heart and nervous system. Birds can develop an increased heart rate, arrhythmias, hyperactivity, tremors and potentially fatal heart problems. Loose tea, coffee grounds and caffeine pills are especially concentrated.
cockatiel.ifEaten: Call an avian vet promptly if your cockatiel drank a caffeinated drink or ate coffee grounds, tea leaves or caffeine tablets. Note what and how much, keep the bird calm and warm, and watch for agitation, trembling, fast breathing or seizures.

faq.q: My cockatiel likes to sip from my cup. Is a little tea all right?
faq.a: No. Even small amounts of caffeine can be hazardous for a bird this size. Keep drinks covered and offer fresh water instead.

faq.q: Is green tea safer than coffee?
faq.a: Green tea contains less caffeine than coffee but still contains it, so it is not safe for cockatiels.

cockatiel.notes: VCA cockatiel page: never offer products containing caffeine. Green tea contains less caffeine than coffee is general knowledge.

hamster.short: No. Alcohol is rapidly absorbed and can cause incoordination, depression, breathing difficulty, tremors, coma and death in pets. For an animal as small as a hamster, even a lick matters.
hamster.risks: Ethanol depresses the nervous system and disturbs blood chemistry. Beer, wine, spirits, liqueur chocolates, alcohol-soaked cakes, fermenting fruit and raw yeast dough (which produces alcohol as it ferments) are all sources.
hamster.ifEaten: Call your vet or an animal poison helpline immediately, because alcohol is absorbed quickly. Keep your hamster warm and quiet in a secure box on the way. Watch for wobbliness, weakness, slow breathing or unresponsiveness.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat fermented or overripe fruit?
faq.a: Fruit that has started to ferment can contain alcohol and may also be mouldy. Remove old fruit from the enclosure promptly and only offer fresh pieces.

faq.q: Is a drop of beer harmful to a hamster?
faq.a: It can be. A hamster weighs a tiny fraction of what a person or even a small dog weighs, so a small amount of alcohol is a large dose for its size. Never offer alcohol.

hamster.notes: No hamster-specific source; verdict based on ASPCA and Merck guidance for pets. Alcohol toxicity is well established across mammals.

budgie.short: No. Alcohol depresses the nervous system and can cause loss of coordination, breathing problems and death. For a bird as small as a budgie, even a few sips of a drink could be a large dose.
budgie.risks: Ethanol is absorbed quickly and depresses the brain and breathing. In pets it can cause vomiting, incoordination, depression, difficulty breathing, tremors, changes in blood chemistry, coma and death. An unsteady bird can also be injured falling from a perch. Raw yeast dough produces alcohol as it ferments.
budgie.ifEaten: Treat this as an emergency and call an avian vet at once. While you arrange care, move your budgie to a small, warm, quiet cage with a low perch or none, to prevent falls, and do not force food or water.

faq.q: What if my budgie drank from my glass of wine or beer?
faq.a: Call an avian vet immediately, even if it seems normal, because signs can appear quickly. Keep drinks covered or out of reach whenever your bird is out of its cage.

faq.q: Can fermenting fruit give a budgie alcohol?
faq.a: Very overripe fruit can ferment and contain some alcohol. Remove fresh fruit after a few hours and do not offer fruit that smells boozy.

budgie.notes: VCA: alcoholic beverages should never be fed to budgies; Merck: avoid alcohol; ASPCA and Merck Food Hazards describe ethanol effects in pets and raw dough fermentation. No bird-specific dose data were found; 'even a few sips could be a large dose' is reasoning from body size.

cockatiel.short: No. Alcohol is toxic to cockatiels. It depresses the brain and breathing and can cause wobbling, collapse, coma and death, and a small bird can be badly affected by a small amount.
cockatiel.risks: Ethanol is rapidly absorbed and acts on the nervous system. Signs in pets include incoordination, depression, breathing difficulty, tremors, coma and death. Intoxicated birds are also at risk of injury from falls. Uncooked yeast dough and fermenting fruit can produce alcohol.
cockatiel.ifEaten: Call an avian vet immediately. Keep your cockatiel warm and quiet in a small cage with low or no perches so it cannot fall, and do not give food or drink by force.

faq.q: Is a drop of alcohol in food, such as a sauce or cake, a problem?
faq.a: Food made with alcohol is not suitable for cockatiels. Cooking does not always remove all the alcohol, and such foods usually contain sugar, fat or salt too.

faq.q: How can I prevent accidents?
faq.a: Keep glasses covered or out of reach when your cockatiel is out, and remove fruit before it starts to ferment.

cockatiel.notes: VCA cockatiel page: never offer alcoholic beverages. 'Cooking does not always remove all alcohol' is general food-science knowledge.

hamster.short: Better not. Potato chips (crisps) are salty, fatty junk food with no benefit for hamsters, and flavoured kinds may contain onion or garlic powder. A stolen crumb is not usually an emergency.
prep: Offer a piece of plain air-popped popcorn or a vegetable instead
Keep snack bowls out of reach during free-roam time
hamster.risks: Chips are high in salt and fat. Too much salt causes thirst and, in larger amounts, salt poisoning, which is more likely if water is not available. Dwarf hamsters weigh about the same as a budgie, so for them even one or two chips is a lot of salt. Flavourings such as onion and garlic powder can damage red blood cells in pets, and sharp shards could injure the cheek pouches.
hamster.ifEaten: A crumb of plain chip is unlikely to cause harm: remove the rest, make sure fresh water is available, and watch your hamster for a day. Call a vet if it ate more than a crumb or a flavoured variety, or if you notice heavy drinking, wobbliness, trembling, lethargy or diarrhoea.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat unsalted potato chips?
faq.a: Unsalted chips are still fried and fatty and offer no benefit. A piece of plain, air-popped popcorn is a better crunchy treat.

hamster.notes: San Diego Humane Society lists 'junk food' among foods to avoid; Blue Cross advises avoiding sugary, fatty treats; PetMD advises avoiding processed human foods. None names potato chips specifically. Salt toxicosis (Merck) and allium effects (ASPCA) come from general veterinary toxicology, not hamster studies. Graded 'avoid' rather than 'no' because a crumb is not acutely dangerous.

budgie.short: No. Potato chips are loaded with salt and fat. Veterinary guides list chips among foods never to feed budgies, and for a bird this small a few chips can hold a harmful amount of salt.
budgie.risks: Birds are sensitive to salt. Excess sodium upsets electrolyte balance, causing thirst, dehydration and kidney problems, and in severe cases weakness, loss of coordination and death. In a study of house sparrows, relatively small amounts of salt caused rapid depression, loss of coordination and deaths. Chips are also fatty, and flavoured chips often contain onion or garlic powder.
budgie.ifEaten: A nibble of one plain chip is unlikely to cause harm; make sure fresh water is available. If your budgie ate more than a small piece, or a heavily salted or flavoured chip, call an avian vet for advice. Signs of salt poisoning include heavy drinking, very wet droppings, weakness, wobbling or falling off the perch, and trembling.

faq.q: What about unsalted or baked chips?
faq.a: They are still processed, fatty and low in nutrition, and many are seasoned with onion or garlic powder. Crunchy vegetables make a far better treat.

faq.q: My budgie stole a crumb of a crisp. Should I panic?
faq.a: No. A crumb is a very small amount of salt. Offer fresh water and watch for heavy drinking or wobbliness; call a vet if you see either.

budgie.notes: Status debate 'no' vs 'avoid': Lafeber (Pollock) calls high-salt, high-fat foods 'not technically toxic'; VCA says chips should never be fed to budgies; VCBE (avian practice) says a few chips or pretzels can contain potentially toxic amounts of salt for a small bird; Merck lists junk food (salt, sweets) among foods to avoid. Bollinger et al. (2005), house sparrows: clinical signs at oral NaCl of 1,500 mg/kg and above, approximate LD50 3,000–3,500 mg/kg in water-deprived birds. Rough internal estimate only: a budgie of about 35 g would reach 1,500 mg/kg with about 50 mg of salt, roughly two to three typical salted chips; parrots may differ and water access matters. Chose 'no' as the cautious status.

cockatiel.short: No. Chips are very salty and fatty, and veterinary sources say not to feed them to pet birds. Small birds are sensitive to salt, and a handful of chips can be a harmful dose.
cockatiel.risks: Too much salt disturbs a bird's electrolyte balance, leading to thirst, dehydration, kidney damage and, at higher doses, weakness, incoordination and death, as shown in a study of house sparrows. Chips also add fat, and many flavours contain onion or garlic powder.
cockatiel.ifEaten: A crumb of a plain chip is unlikely to cause harm; provide fresh water. If your cockatiel ate a whole chip or more, or a strongly seasoned one, call an avian vet for advice. Watch for heavy drinking, very wet droppings, weakness, wobbling, trembling or collapse.

faq.q: Are tortilla chips or pretzels any better?
faq.a: No. They are also salty processed snacks and should not be fed to cockatiels.

faq.q: What is a good crunchy treat instead?
faq.a: Try a small piece of raw carrot, bell pepper or broccoli stalk, or a sliver of plain unsalted nut.

cockatiel.notes: VCA cockatiel page: avoid processed foods like chips. VCBE warns a few chips can contain potentially toxic salt for a small bird. Rough internal estimate using the sparrow data: a 90 g cockatiel would reach 1,500 mg/kg with about 135 mg salt (several typical chips). 'no' chosen for caution over 'avoid'.

hamster.short: No. Sweets offer nothing but sugar, sticky sweets can lodge in the cheek pouches, and chocolate or sugar-free sweets with xylitol add poisoning risks. Dwarf hamsters are also prone to diabetes.
hamster.risks: Sugar adds empty calories and is a particular concern for diabetes-prone dwarfs. Chewy sweets, toffee, jelly sweets and gum can cling inside the cheek pouches. Chocolate sweets contain theobromine and caffeine. Xylitol in sugar-free gum and sweets causes dangerous low blood sugar and liver damage in dogs; its effect on hamsters has not been studied, so treat it as dangerous.
hamster.dwarf: Campbell's, Winter White and their hybrids, and Chinese hamsters, have an inherited tendency to diabetes. Keep all sugary foods away from them.
hamster.ifEaten: If the sweet contained chocolate or xylitol, or your hamster ate more than a crumb, call your vet or an animal poison helpline straight away. For a lick of a plain sugar sweet, remove the rest, look for sticky pieces in the nest, and watch for diarrhoea, lethargy or a cheek that stays swollen or will not empty, which needs a vet.

faq.q: Can hamsters eat sugar-free sweets?
faq.a: No. Sugar-free sweets and gum often contain xylitol or other sweeteners. Xylitol is known to be dangerous to dogs and its effects on hamsters are unknown, so treat it as unsafe.

faq.q: Are honey sticks and other sweet hamster treats OK?
faq.a: Blue Cross advises avoiding sugary, fatty treats, including seed sticks made with molasses or honey. They are best skipped, especially for dwarf hamsters.

faq.q: What sweet treat can I give instead?
faq.a: For a Syrian, a tiny piece of fresh fruit now and then is a better choice than any sweet. For dwarf hamsters, a small piece of vegetable or a mealworm is safer.

hamster.notes: San Diego Humane Society lists candy among foods to avoid for hamsters. Graded 'no' rather than 'avoid' because the category includes chocolate, xylitol-containing products and sticky sweets; a lick of plain sugar candy is not itself known to be toxic, and the ifEaten text reflects that. Xylitol toxicity is documented in dogs (Merck, ASPCA); no hamster data found. Diabetes predisposition: PDSA (Russian dwarfs), ExoCare (Campbell's and hybrids), Voss et al. 1978 (Djungarian colony), Frankel et al. 1974 (Chinese hamster sublines). Blue Cross says only Syrian hamsters should have fruit as an occasional treat.

budgie.short: No. Sweets are just sugar and fat, chocolate candies are toxic, and sugar-free sweets and gum may contain xylitol, which is the suspected cause of death in a group of wild birds. Keep all candy away from budgies.
budgie.risks: Sugary sweets add empty calories to a bird prone to obesity and can upset the gut. Sugar-free products often contain xylitol, which causes dangerously low blood sugar and liver damage in dogs; it has not been studied in parrots, but 29 wild Cape sugarbirds died shortly after drinking xylitol-sweetened nectar. Chocolate sweets add theobromine and caffeine.
budgie.ifEaten: If the sweet was sugar-free, contained chocolate, or you are not sure, call an avian vet or animal poison control line right away and keep the wrapper. Xylitol can lower blood sugar within minutes, so watch for weakness, wobbliness, falling from the perch or collapse. A lick of ordinary sugar candy is less serious: offer water and watch for loose droppings.

faq.q: Can budgies have honey or honey sticks?
faq.a: Honey sticks are seeds glued together with sugar and honey, and most avian vets do not recommend them. Honey itself is concentrated sugar that a budgie does not need.

faq.q: What about sugar-free gum?
faq.a: Never. Gum is a common source of xylitol and could also stick in or block a small bird's mouth or throat.

budgie.notes: Status reflects the whole category: ordinary sugar candy alone would be 'avoid'-level, but xylitol and chocolate products justify 'no'. Xylitol evidence in birds is limited: presumptive fatal toxicosis in Cape sugarbirds (Gardner & Mitchell 2017) versus poultry feeding trials in which broiler chicks tolerated dietary xylitol (e.g., Takahashi et al. 2000, PMID 10824964, not in registry). Avian-vet sources (Lafeber/Pollock, VCBE) advise keeping sugar-free products away from birds. The gum-choking point is a precaution, not a cited finding.

cockatiel.short: No. Candy gives cockatiels sugar and fat and nothing useful, chocolate sweets are toxic, and sugar-free sweets and gum may contain xylitol, a sweetener linked to bird deaths.
cockatiel.risks: Sugar-rich sweets can irritate the gut and add calories to a bird prone to obesity and fatty liver. Xylitol, common in sugar-free gum, mints and sweets, causes severe low blood sugar and liver damage in dogs; its effects in parrots are unknown, but it was the presumed cause of death in a group of wild nectar-feeding birds. Chocolate adds theobromine and caffeine.
cockatiel.ifEaten: Call an avian vet or animal poison control line at once if the candy was sugar-free, contained chocolate, or you cannot tell, and keep the packaging. Watch for weakness, stumbling, trembling or collapse. If it was a lick of ordinary sugar candy, offer water and watch for loose droppings.

faq.q: Are sugary bird treats from pet shops safe?
faq.a: Treats coated in sugar or honey add calories without nutrition. Vegetables, a little millet or a sliver of plain nut are better rewards.

faq.q: Can cockatiels eat marshmallows or jelly sweets?
faq.a: No. They are almost pure sugar, may contain colourings or sweeteners, and are sticky enough to cling to the beak.
